teile.einleitung: If you order something from abroad, you sometimes pay more than the price in the online shop. At customs, VAT and fees can be added.
wichtigste: For parcels from abroad, customs charges **Swiss VAT** depending on the value.
On top of that there is often a **fee** from the parcel service for customs clearance.
The **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** (FOCBS) is responsible.
If the VAT is very small, it is not charged.
The costs are usually paid by the person who receives the parcel.
Before ordering, it is worth adding up all the costs.

abschnitte.text: A T-shirt from a foreign online shop can look cheap. When the parcel arrives in Switzerland, **customs** checks it. Depending on the value, you have to pay **VAT**, just as when you shop in a Swiss store. On top of that, the parcel service often charges a **customs clearance fee**. That way a small order can become considerably more expensive than you thought.

In Switzerland, customs is the job of the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security**, **FOCBS** for short (BAZG in German). It checks which goods come into the country and collects the charges. Customs also protects against dangerous or forbidden goods. It can, for example, hold back and destroy fake branded goods.

**VAT** is a tax on almost all goods and services. It is calculated on the value of the goods and the delivery costs. If the amount of tax is very small, customs does not charge it, because the effort is not worth it. Since 2024, Switzerland no longer charges actual **customs duty** on most industrial goods. But customs duty can still be charged on foods such as meat or cheese.

Before ordering from abroad, it is worth adding up all the costs: price, delivery, VAT and fees. Some shops already charge Swiss VAT when you buy. Then there is often nothing more to pay at customs. If you are unsure, the FOCBS website has a calculator for the charges.

gewusst: With small orders, the parcel service’s fee can be higher than the VAT itself.
Where Switzerland still charges customs duty, it is usually calculated by the weight of the goods and not by their price.

teile.einleitung: Saving means not spending all your money straight away, but keeping part of it for later. That way you can afford something bigger at some point or are prepared for emergencies. The most important thing about saving is patience.
wichtigste: Saving means not spending money straight away, but keeping it for later.
If you spend all your pocket money straight away, you have nothing left when you need something later.
A savings goal is an amount you want to save up in order to buy something particular.
If you put some money aside every week, you can later make even expensive wishes come true.
Above all, successful saving takes patience.
You keep saved money in a money box or safely in a savings account.
In a savings account, money can grow through interest.

abschnitte.text: When **saving**, you put part of your money aside instead of spending it straight away. This can be pocket money, birthday money or, later on, your wages. Saved money is available when you really need it. So saving means doing without something now in order to have more possibilities later.

A **savings goal** makes saving easier. If, for example, you want a bike for 300 francs, you know exactly how much you need. If you put 10 francs aside every week, you will have the money after 30 weeks. It helps to write the goal down or to hang up a picture of it.

If you always spend everything straight away, you can only afford small things. If you wait, you can afford something **bigger** that really matters to you. Researchers have found that children who are good at waiting often find life easier. This is known from the so-called **marshmallow test**, in which children could wait for a second marshmallow.

A proven trick is to save first and spend afterwards, in other words to put something aside as soon as you get your pocket money. A simple rule is to save a third and spend the rest. A **budget**, in which you note what you spend money on, also helps. Before every purchase you can ask yourself whether you really need it.

In a **savings account**, the bank pays you interest on your money. If you do not withdraw the interest, the next year you also get interest on the interest. This is called **compound interest**, and over many years it makes a big difference. That is why it is worth starting to save early.

In Switzerland, many people save very diligently. For old age there is a separate savings system with three pillars: AVS, the pension fund and **pillar 3a**. With pillar 3a you can save voluntarily and pay less tax in return. World Savings Day at the end of October also reminds people every year how important saving is.

begriffe.erklaerung: An amount you want to collect for a particular wish.
Interest you receive on interest you have already received.
A plan of how much money you have and what you spend it on.
Voluntary saving for old age in Switzerland with a tax advantage.

gewusst: World Savings Day was launched in 1924 in Milan at an international congress of savings banks.
In the marshmallow test in the 1960s, children could have a second marshmallow if they waited a few minutes with the first one.
If you save just one franc every day, you will already have 365 francs after a year.

teile.einleitung: A prepaid card is a payment card that you first have to load with money. Prepaid means “paid in advance”. You can only spend as much with it as was loaded onto it beforehand.
wichtigste: Prepaid means “paid in advance”.
You first have to load a prepaid card with money.
You can only spend what was loaded onto it beforehand.
This means you cannot get into debt with the card.
Prepaid cards are well suited to teenagers and to travelling.
In shops and on the internet they work much like a credit card.

abschnitte.text: With a **prepaid card**, you first load **money** onto the card. You can do this, for example, by **transfer** from your own account or in an app. Only then can you pay with the card. You can only spend as much as you loaded onto it beforehand. If the balance is empty, the payment is refused.

In Switzerland you normally only get a proper **credit card** from the age of 18. A prepaid card is often available for **teenagers** already. Because you only spend what is already there, you **cannot get into debt**. Parents can load pocket money onto the card. This way you learn to handle money and keep track of it.

Prepaid cards are practical when **travelling** and for shopping on the **internet**. They often carry the **Visa** or **Mastercard** logo and are therefore accepted in many places. If the card is lost, at most the loaded balance is at risk. You can still have it blocked. Some cards cost an annual fee or charge fees when you load them.

With a **credit card**, you pay first and get a bill later. With a **debit card**, the money is taken directly from your **account**. With a **prepaid card**, the money is already on the card beforehand. All three cards often look similar. It is important to know how your own card works.

gewusst: Gift cards from shops also work on the prepaid principle.
The word “prepaid” is also familiar from mobile phone plans where you pay for your credit in advance.

teile.einleitung: A money box is a small container with a slot into which you put coins and notes to collect money. The best-known form is the piggy bank. In Switzerland people often call it a Kässeli.
wichtigste: A money box is a container in which you collect and save money.
The best-known form is the piggy bank.
Money is put in through a slot but is not easy to take out again.
In Switzerland it is often called a Kässeli.
Money boxes help children learn to save.
In many cultures the pig is a symbol of luck and wealth.
Larger amounts are better taken to a savings account.

abschnitte.text: A **money box** is a container made of clay, porcelain, metal or plastic with a narrow slot. Through this slot you drop coins or folded notes. Taking them out is deliberately difficult, so that you do not spend the money again straight away. In Switzerland it is usually called a **Kässeli** in everyday speech.

The best known is the **piggy bank**, but there are money boxes in all shapes. Some look like houses, animals, letterboxes or characters from films. There are also money boxes with a counter that shows how much money is already inside. Some old piggy banks have to be smashed to get at the money.

Even in ancient times, people kept coins in clay pots. In Central Europe the **pig** was considered a lucky symbol from early on, because a farmer with many pigs was thought to be rich. Later, many banks gave children small money boxes. When the box was full, you took it to the bank and the money went into a savings account.

A piggy bank helps you collect money instead of spending it straight away. If you have a **savings goal**, for example a new toy, you can see the money slowly growing. That way children learn patience and the value of money. You can also have several money boxes, for example one for saving and one for giving to charity.

In a money box, the money earns no **interest**. It can also be lost or stolen. That is why it is worth taking larger amounts to a savings account at the bank. But for small goals and for learning, the money box is ideal.

begriffe.erklaerung: A Swiss German word for a small money box.
Something you are collecting money for, with a fixed amount.
A sign that is meant to bring luck, like the pig or clover.
Money the bank gives you for keeping your savings with it.

gewusst: At New Year, people in Switzerland and Germany often give each other little lucky pigs.
Some piggy banks have no opening at all and have to be broken so that you cannot get at the money too early.
With counters in money boxes you can see at any time how much you have already saved.

teile.einleitung: Compound interest means that you get interest not only on your original money, but also on interest you received earlier. As a result, an amount grows faster and faster over time. Compound interest is the reason why saving early pays off, but also why debts can become dangerous.
wichtigste: With compound interest, you also get interest on interest received earlier.
The interest is added to the capital and then earns interest too.
The longer you save, the stronger the effect of compound interest.
A higher interest rate makes money grow considerably faster.
Compound interest also works with debts, which then grow quickly.
With the rule of 72 you can estimate when an amount will double.

abschnitte.text: If you put money into a savings account, the bank pays **interest** on it. If this interest stays in the account, it becomes part of the balance the next year. Then you get interest on this interest too; this is called **compound interest**. That way the money does not grow evenly, but a little faster each time.

Suppose you invest 1000 francs at 5 per cent interest. After one year you have 1050 francs; in the second year you get 5 per cent of 1050, which is 52.50 francs. After 10 years it is already about 1629 francs, without you having added anything. Without compound interest it would only be 1500 francs. The formula is: **final capital** equals starting capital times (1 plus interest rate) to the power of the number of years.

abschnitte.titel: Time is the most important factor
abschnitte.text: Compound interest works most strongly over long periods. If you start saving when you are young, you benefit much more than someone who starts late. That is why people are often advised to invest even small amounts regularly. With the **rule of 72** you can estimate the time it takes to double: 72 divided by the interest rate gives roughly the number of years, for example 72 divided by 6 equals 12 years.

Compound interest also works against you if you have **debts**. If, for example, you do not pay a credit card bill, interest is charged, and then interest on that interest. That way a small amount can become a huge mountain of debt over time. In Switzerland, interest on credit cards and small loans is allowed up to a legal **maximum interest rate**, which is far above savings interest rates.

Today, interest on savings accounts in Switzerland is often low, so compound interest has only a weak effect there. But with long-term investments such as equity funds or in **retirement provision**, the same effect plays a big role. Returns that are reinvested bring new returns themselves. Pillar 3a also uses this effect over many decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: The price for borrowed money that the bank pays or charges.
The money that you have invested or lent.
How many per cent of interest there is per year.
The profit that an investment brings.

gewusst: At 3 per cent interest, an amount doubles in about 24 years thanks to compound interest.
If a single centime earned 10 per cent interest for 100 years, it would have become more than 137 francs.
Even the ancient Babylonians knew calculations with interest and compound interest.

teile.einleitung: If you do not pay a bill on time, you can be in default (Verzug). Default is a term from the Code of Obligations. It has consequences, for example default interest.
wichtigste: Default means you have not paid a debt that was due on time.
The rules are set out in the Code of Obligations.
Normally, default begins with a reminder.
If a fixed payment date was agreed, no reminder is needed.
Anyone in default owes default interest.
After that the creditor can start debt enforcement proceedings.

abschnitte.text: A debt is **due** as soon as it has to be paid. If you do not pay, you are in **default**. This means that you have not fulfilled your duty under the contract on time. Default is governed by the **Code of Obligations**, the Swiss law on contracts.

Default usually begins with a **reminder**. In it, the creditor asks the debtor to pay at last. But if a **fixed date** was agreed, for example “payable by 30 April”, default begins **without a reminder**. Such a day is called a **due date** (Verfalltag). Once it has passed, you are immediately in default.

Anyone in default with a debt of money must pay **default interest**. Unless something else has been agreed, it is **5 per cent a year**. Many companies also charge **reminder fees** if this is in the contract. If you still do not pay, the creditor can start **debt enforcement proceedings**. This is entered in the debt enforcement register.

It is best to pay bills as soon as they arrive or to put the **payment date** in your calendar. With e-banking you can set up payments in advance for a particular date. If you cannot pay a bill, get in touch with the company early. **Payment by instalments** or a delay is often possible.

gewusst: You can also be in default if you deliver late instead of paying late.
Many Swiss bills have a payment deadline of 30 days.

teile.einleitung: A bank account is not always free. The bank looks after the money, records payments and provides cards and online banking. For this it often charges fees. This is called account management.
wichtigste: Account management means the bank looks after your account and all its transactions.
Many banks charge monthly or yearly fees for this.
Cards can also have their own fees.
For young people and people in training, accounts are often free.
It is worth comparing banks.
The bank statement shows all the transactions in the account.

abschnitte.text: In **account management**, the bank records every deposit, every payment and every withdrawal. It makes sure the **account balance** is always correct. It provides **online banking**, an app and cards. It also regularly sends a **bank statement**. Many banks charge money for this work.

**Account fees** are costs the bank charges for running the account. They are usually taken directly from the account every month or every year. Sometimes there are also fees for the **debit card** or the credit card. A paper bank statement can cost something too. How high the fees are varies from bank to bank.

Many banks in Switzerland offer **youth accounts** or accounts for students and apprentices. These are often **free of charge**. The banks hope that young customers will stay with them later. When you finish your training, you should check from when fees will be charged. The offer often changes at a certain age.

If you **compare** different banks, you can save money every year. You look at account fees, card fees and the cost of cash withdrawals. It is also important to think about which services you really need. Some banks waive fees if there is enough money in the account. Switching accounts is allowed in Switzerland and is usually easy.

gewusst: Many banks waive fees if you give up paper and do everything in online banking.
Some banks offer accounts with no branches at all, which work only through an app.

teile.einleitung: Paying means giving money for goods or a service. Today there are many ways to do it: with cash, by card, with your phone or by invoice.
wichtigste: In a shop you pay with cash or by card.
You can often pay with your phone too, in Switzerland for example with TWINT.
With a debit card, the money leaves your own account directly.
In Switzerland, bills are paid with the QR bill or eBill.
When you pay, you should quickly check the change or the amount.

abschnitte.text: When paying with **cash**, you hand over coins and notes. If the amount is less than the money you give, you get **change**. Cash is simple, and you can see exactly how much you still have. It is worth quickly counting your change.

With a **debit card**, the amount is taken from your own account. With a **credit card**, you only pay later, usually once a month. Many cards work **contactlessly**: you just hold them briefly to the machine. For larger amounts you have to enter your PIN.

More and more people pay with their **phone**. In Switzerland, the app **TWINT** is very widespread. With it you can pay in shops, online or send money to friends. There are also solutions where a card is stored in the phone. For children, the parents decide whether they may pay this way.

Some things are paid for later with an **invoice**, for example the rent or a phone contract. In Switzerland, the **QR bill** completely replaced the old payment slip in 2022. You scan the QR code in e-banking and pay. With **eBill**, the bill even comes straight into your e-banking.

gewusst: In the past, people also paid with shells, salt or livestock.
The word “salary” recalls the Latin word for salt.

teile.einleitung: Today, many people pay without coins and notes, for example by card or phone. You do not see the money, but it is still real. It is taken directly from the bank account.
wichtigste: Cash is coins and notes that you can touch.
Money in a bank account is called book money.
With a card or phone, you pay with money from your account.
With a debit card, the money is taken straight away.
With a credit card, the bill comes later.
Invisible money is also gone once you have paid.

abschnitte.text: Instead of paying with **cash**, many people pay with a **card**, a **phone** or a watch. You hold the card to the machine at the till, and it is paid. On the internet, too, people usually pay without cash. This is practical, but you do not see the money getting less.

Most money is not kept as notes in a safe, but is stored as a number in a **bank account**. This money is called **book money**. When Mum pays by card, the amount is **taken** from her account and credited to the shop’s account. So it is real money that changes hands.

With a **debit card**, the money is taken from the account straight away or after a short time. With a **credit card**, the bank collects the purchases, and you pay for them later with a **monthly bill**. If you do not pay the bill in full, you often have to pay high interest. Payment apps on phones are also linked to an account or a card.

Because you cannot see the money, people often spend **more** by card than with cash. That is why it is important to check your **account balance** regularly. Many banks show all payments in an app. A tip for children: with cash in your purse, it is easier to notice how much you still have.

gewusst: In Switzerland, more and more payments are made without cash, but cash remains legal tender.
Even the money that banks transfer to each other only flows as numbers from computer to computer.

teile.einleitung: Changing money means swapping money for other notes or coins of the same value. A 10-franc note can, for example, become five 2-franc pieces. You can also change money into another currency.
wichtigste: When you change money, the value stays the same.
You can change a 10-franc note for five 2-franc pieces.
In Switzerland there are coins from 5 centimes to 5 francs.
Notes come in values from 10 to 1000 francs.
For travelling, you change francs into a foreign currency.
When changing into foreign money, an exchange rate applies.

abschnitte.text: When **changing** money, you swap money for money of the **same value**. Leo can change his 10-franc note for **five 2-franc pieces**, or for ten 1-franc pieces. Afterwards he has neither more nor less money. You can change money at a bank counter, sometimes in a shop, or with family and friends.

In Switzerland there are **coins** worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The coins are made by **Swissmint** in Bern. **Banknotes** come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. They are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**. If you know the values, you can easily change money correctly.

Money is changed at the till too. If you pay for an exercise book costing 3 francs with a 5-franc coin, you get 2 francs **change**. So the cashier changes your large coin. If you have small money with you, you make it easier for her. You should always quickly count your change.

For holidays abroad, you change **francs** into **euros**, for example. An **exchange rate** applies, which says how much you get for one franc. It changes all the time. Banks and bureaux de change often charge a **fee** or give a worse rate. That is why it is worth comparing.

gewusst: The 5-centime piece is one of the smallest coins in Switzerland; 1-centime pieces have not been valid since 2007.
The Swiss 1000-franc note is one of the banknotes with the highest value in the world.

teile.einleitung: You do not have to buy everything yourself. If you share, swap or borrow, you can use lots of things without spending money. This saves money and is also good for the environment.
wichtigste: Games, books and tools can often be borrowed.
In a toy library you can borrow games.
The library has books, comics and often films too.
You can swap things with friends.
Sharing saves money, and fewer things have to be made.
You return borrowed things carefully and on time.

abschnitte.text: A **toy library** (Ludothek) is like a library, but for **games and toys**. There you can borrow board games, puzzles or ride-on toys for little money. That way you can try out lots of games without buying them. In Switzerland, many municipalities have a toy library. If you especially like a game, you can still ask for it as a present.

In the **library** you borrow books, comics, audiobooks and often films too. For children, borrowing is usually free or very cheap. After a certain time you bring everything back. If you are late, you sometimes have to pay a small **fee**.

With friends you can **swap** or **lend** games, books or clothes. Then both of you have something new without spending money. It is important to agree clearly how long you will keep something. You treat borrowed things **carefully**, because they belong to someone else.

When many people use one thing together, fewer things have to be made. This saves **raw materials** and energy. Adults, for example, share cars through **car sharing** or borrow tools from a neighbour. That way not everyone has to buy a drill that they only rarely need.

gewusst: Some municipalities have swap shelves where you put books and take others away.
On average, a drill is used only very rarely in a household, which is why borrowing one is often worth it.

teile.einleitung: A Bankomat is a machine that gives out cash from your own account. You need your bank card and your secret PIN code for it. In Switzerland people often also say Bancomat.
wichtigste: At the Bankomat you get cash from your own account.
You need your bank card and your PIN code.
The Bankomat only gives out as much as there is in the account.
When typing your PIN, you cover the keys with your hand.
After withdrawing money, always take your card and the money with you.
If the machine keeps the card, tell your parents or the bank straight away.

abschnitte.text: At the **Bankomat** you put in your **bank card** and type your **PIN code**. Then you choose the amount, and the machine gives out notes. The money is taken from your own account. If there is nothing in the account, there is no money either. At many cash machines you can also see your account balance.

Cash machines are where lots of people are out and about: at **banks**, at **railway stations** and in **shopping centres**. Some are outside on the wall of a building, others in a room that you open with your card. That way you can get money in the evening or on a Sunday too.

Nobody should see which numbers you type. That is why you cover the keys with your **hand**. If someone is standing right behind you, wait or ask them to keep their **distance**. You never write the PIN down and never tell it to anyone. The bank never asks for it either.

Always take your **card** first and then the **money**. Only then do you walk away. Put the money straight into your purse. If the cash machine keeps your card or something does not work, tell your parents straight away. They can tell the bank and have the card blocked if necessary.

gewusst: Many cash machines no longer give back a card that has been forgotten after a short time, and keep it for safety.
There are also machines at which you can pay in cash.

teile.einleitung: If you have a lot of small change, you can pack it into coin rolls. A coin roll is a paper roll that always holds the same number of coins of the same kind. This makes it quick to count small change and keep it tidy.
wichtigste: A coin roll is a paper roll holding the same number of identical coins.
Each roll contains only one kind of coin.
This lets you count a lot of small change quickly.
Shops need coin rolls so they have change in the till.
Banks accept coins and hand out coin rolls, sometimes for a fee.

abschnitte.text: A **coin roll** is a firm roll made of paper or plastic film. It always holds **the same number** of coins of **the same kind**. The coins lie exactly on top of each other, like a little tower. The roll often says which coins are inside and how much the whole roll is worth. That way you know straight away how much money you are holding.

Counting lots of single coins takes a long time. With coin rolls it is much **quicker**. You simply count the rolls and add them up. Coins in rolls are also easy to **carry neatly** and to store. Nothing rolls away and nothing gets lost.

Above all, **shops**, restaurants and kiosks need coin rolls. They must always have enough **change** in the till. That is why they collect rolls of coins from the bank. The other way round, they take too much small change to the bank. There it is counted by **counting machines** and credited to the account.

Children can also take their **money box** to the bank. Some banks have machines into which you pour coins. The machine counts them and pays the money into your account. For large amounts of coins, some banks charge a **fee**. It is worth asking your own bank first.

gewusst: Counting machines recognise coins by their size, thickness and weight and sort them very quickly.

teile.einleitung: Banks charge fees for many services. If you know them and compare them, you can save a lot of money. For children and teenagers, many offers are cheaper or even free.
wichtigste: Fees are amounts that the bank charges for its services.
You pay the account fee for having the account managed.
Cards often have an annual fee too.
When paying in a foreign currency, extra fees can be charged.
With youth accounts, many fees do not apply.
When comparing banks, you look at interest and fees together.

abschnitte.text: A bank offers many services: it manages accounts, issues cards and carries out payments. For this it often charges **fees**. The best known is the **account fee**, which you pay every month or every year. Which fees a bank charges is stated in its **price list**.

For a **debit card** or **credit card**, you often pay an annual fee. Withdrawing cash from another bank’s machine can also cost something. A new card after a loss is sometimes not free either. If you know this, you can plan better.

If you pay in **euros** or another currency, the bank has to convert the amount. For this it often charges a **foreign currency fee**, usually a small percentage of the amount. Withdrawing cash abroad often costs even more. If you travel often, it is worth choosing a cheap card.

Good **interest** is of little use if high fees eat it up. That is why you always compare both. For children, teenagers and students there are often special offers with no account fee. On the internet there are comparison websites that show the costs of different banks.

gewusst: A few francs in fees per month add up to a large amount over many years.
Many banks charge lower fees if you receive your bank statements digitally instead of on paper.

teile.einleitung: Inflation, also called Teuerung in Switzerland, means that prices rise in general. You can then buy less with the same money. In Switzerland, the National Bank makes sure that inflation stays low.
wichtigste: Inflation means that prices rise in general.
Money loses purchasing power as a result.
Inflation is measured using a basket of many products.
In Switzerland, the Federal Statistical Office calculates the Swiss Consumer Price Index.
The Swiss National Bank wants to keep inflation below 2 per cent.
The opposite of inflation is called deflation.

abschnitte.text: If a loaf of bread costs more today than a few years ago, and other things have become more expensive too, this is called **inflation**. The word comes from Latin and means “blowing up” or “swelling”. In Switzerland people often say **Teuerung**. If only a single price rises, that is not yet inflation.

With inflation, **purchasing power** falls. For 100 francs you get fewer goods than before. Anyone who has money in an account and gets hardly any interest slowly loses value this way. That is why high inflation is a problem for many people.

Every month, the **Federal Statistical Office** watches the prices of many things. These include food, rents, clothes, electricity and travel. Together they form a **basket of goods**. From this comes the **Swiss Consumer Price Index**, which shows how much prices have risen.

abschnitte.titel: The role of the National Bank
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** has the task of ensuring **stable prices**. By this it means inflation of less than 2 per cent a year. If prices rise too much, it can, for example, **raise interest rates**. Then borrowing money becomes more expensive, and prices rise more slowly.

gewusst: Compared with many other countries, Switzerland has mostly had low inflation in recent decades.
When prices rise extremely fast, this is called hyperinflation, as happened in Germany in 1923.

teile.einleitung: With barter, you give one thing away and get another in return. Long before there were coins, people traded like this. Because swapping was often complicated, money came into being later.
wichtigste: Barter means: goods for goods, without money.
In the past, people swapped grain for tools, for example.
Both sides had to want exactly what the other was offering.
Later, sought-after things such as shells or metal were used as a means of payment.
Coins made trading much easier.
Even today, people sometimes still swap.

abschnitte.text: With **barter** there is no money. A farmer, for example, swaps grain for a tool, and a fisherman swaps fish for furs. Each gives something they have spare and gets something they need. That is how people traded with each other even in very early times.

Swapping only works if **both** want exactly what the other is offering. But if the fisherman does not want any grain, there is no deal. Another difficult question is how much something is worth: how many fish is a cow worth? And you cannot divide a cow into small pieces to buy a loaf of bread with it.

That is why people used certain things that everyone liked to have as a **means of payment**. These were, for example, **shells**, salt or pieces of metal. Later, **coins** made of gold, silver or bronze appeared. The first coins came into being about 2,600 years ago in Asia Minor, in what is now Turkey. With money you can easily compare, save and pay in small amounts.

People still swap today. Children swap **stickers** or toys. At **swap meets**, people pass on clothes or books. Sometimes people also swap help: I help you in the garden, and you help me move house. But for most purchases, money is much more practical.

gewusst: Cowrie shells were used as money for a long time in various parts of the world.
The Latin word for money, “pecunia”, comes from “pecus”, which means livestock.

teile.einleitung: Phishing is an internet scam in which criminals “fish” for passwords, card details or other personal data. They send fake emails, text messages or chat messages that look as if they come from a bank, the post office or an online shop. If you know the tricks, you will not fall for them.
wichtigste: With phishing, fraudsters fish for passwords and other data.
The word is a variation of the English word “fishing”.
Phishing comes by email, text message, messenger or phone.
The messages often put you under pressure, for example by threatening to block your account.
Real banks never ask for passwords or your PIN by email or text message.
You should never click on links in suspicious messages.
In Switzerland you can report phishing to the Federal Office for Cyber Security.

abschnitte.text: With **phishing**, fraudsters try to trick people into giving away their secret data. They pretend to be a well-known company, such as a bank, PostFinance, Swisscom, Netflix or a parcel service. The message contains a link to a fake website that looks real. Anyone who enters their password or card details there sends them straight to the criminals.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the word come from?
abschnitte.text: The word is a variation of the English **fishing**. The fraudsters cast lots of bait and hope that someone will bite. The spelling with “ph” comes from the language of hackers in the 1990s. There are also variants such as **smishing** by text message and vishing by phone call.

Phishing messages often create **time pressure**, for example with sentences such as “Your account will be blocked in 24 hours”. They often contain spelling mistakes, an impersonal greeting or a strange sender address. If you move the mouse over the link, you often see an unfamiliar internet address. So-called prizes or unpaid parcel fees are also typical **bait**.

Never click on links in suspicious messages and do not open unknown attachments. Only enter passwords on websites that you have opened yourself using the address you know. **Two-factor authentication** makes things much harder for fraudsters, even if they have a password. If you are unsure, ask an adult you trust or call the company on its official number.

In Switzerland, the **Federal Office for Cyber Security** (NCSC) collects reports of phishing and warns the public. You can report suspicious messages to it online. If you have already entered data, you should change your password straight away and, if bank details are involved, call the bank and have the card blocked. If there is damage, you can report it to the **police**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fraud in which fake messages are used to fish for data.
Phishing by text message.
Logging in with two proofs, for example a password and a code sent to your mobile phone.
A clickable reference to a website.

gewusst: Phishing sites often look deceptively real, because the fraudsters copy the logos and colours of the real company.
Some fraudsters even phone people and pretend to be bank staff or police officers.
Many phishing emails are sent to millions of addresses at the same time.

teile.einleitung: A savings goal is something you put money aside for, for example a ball, a camera or your driving licence. With a clear goal, saving is easier. You can even work out how long you need to save.
wichtigste: A good savings goal has a clear amount and a date.
You work out the saving time like this: target amount divided by the amount saved each time.
If you save 15 francs a month, you will have 120 francs after 8 months.
There are short-term and long-term savings goals.
Visible progress is motivating, for example with a list.

abschnitte.text: A savings goal works best when it is **precise**. Instead of “I’m saving something”, you say: “I’m saving 120 francs for a camera by the summer.” If you know the **amount** and the **date**, you can work out how much you need to save regularly. That turns a wish into a plan.

The rule is: **target amount divided by the amount saved each time gives the time**. A ball costs 12 francs, and Ella saves 2 francs every week. 12 divided by 2 gives **6 weeks**. Jana wants a camera for 120 francs and saves 15 francs a month. 120 divided by 15 gives **8 months**. With patience, small amounts become big.

You reach **short-term** goals in a few days or weeks, for example a comic or a ball. **Long-term** goals take months or years. For teenagers these might be a bike of their own or their **driving licence**. For big goals it is worth starting early.

If you can see your savings growing, you are more likely to keep going. A **list** on which you note every amount you save helps with this. A picture of the goal on the wall or a **savings app** can also be motivating. And when you have reached your goal, you can be really pleased.

gewusst: If you save 2 francs every week, you will have 104 francs after a year, because a year has 52 weeks.

teile.einleitung: Helvetia is a female figure who represents Switzerland. You can see her on coins, stamps and monuments. On the 1-franc coin she stands with a spear and a shield.
wichtigste: Helvetia is a symbolic figure for Switzerland.
The standing Helvetia can be seen on the 1-franc, 2-franc and half-franc coins.
She holds a spear and a shield with the Swiss cross.
The name recalls the Helvetii, a Celtic people.
The abbreviation CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, the Swiss Confederation.

abschnitte.text: **Helvetia** is not a real person, but a **symbolic figure**. She shows Switzerland as a woman. Other countries have figures like this too, for example Marianne in France. Helvetia became popular above all in the 19th century, when the modern federal state came into being.

On the **1-franc coin** you can see the **standing Helvetia**. The same picture is also on the 2-franc and half-franc coins. In one hand she holds a **spear**, and with the other she leans on a **shield** with the Swiss cross. Stars are arranged all around her.

The name comes from the **Helvetii**. They were a **Celtic people** who lived about 2000 years ago in the area of what is now Switzerland. The Romans named the area after them. From this came the Latin name for Switzerland: **Confoederatio Helvetica**.

You see the abbreviation **CH** on cars, in internet addresses and in the IBAN. Swiss **stamps** bear the word “Helvetia”, because it is understood in all the national languages. Monuments and paintings also show Helvetia. So you come across her more often than you might think.

gewusst: Older Swiss coins also showed a seated Helvetia.
Because Switzerland has four national languages, the Latin name “Helvetia” is a neutral solution for everyone.

teile.einleitung: FINMA is the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority. In Switzerland it supervises banks, insurance companies and other financial companies. This is meant to protect customers and the whole financial centre.
wichtigste: FINMA stands for the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority.
It supervises banks, insurance companies and financial markets in Switzerland.
Anyone who accepts customers’ money on a commercial basis needs a licence from FINMA.
FINMA can take action against providers without a licence.
Its website has lists of licensed institutions and a warning list.
FINMA is independent and is based in Bern.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority**, **FINMA** for short, is a federal authority. It began its work in 2009 and is based in **Bern**. FINMA is **independent**, which means it does not receive instructions from the government on how to decide individual cases. It is financed mainly through fees and charges paid by the companies it supervises.

FINMA **supervises** banks, insurance companies, stock exchanges and other financial companies. It grants **licences**: only those with a licence may, for example, operate as a bank. After that it checks whether the rules are being followed, for instance whether a bank has enough capital of its own. This is meant to protect **customers’ money** and keep the financial centre stable.

Anyone in Switzerland who accepts money from the public **on a commercial basis** needs a licence from FINMA. Such money is called **public deposits**. FINMA can take action against providers without a licence, for example by banning their activities. It also publicly **warns** about suspicious companies.

FINMA’s website has **lists** of all licensed banks, insurance companies and other institutions. There is also a **warning list** of providers that may be operating without a licence. Before you invest money, you can check there. That is more reliable than any advert. Memory aid: check with FINMA first, then invest money.

gewusst: FINMA was created in 2009 by merging three earlier supervisory authorities.
FINMA does not help with individual disputes between customers and banks; that is what the banking ombudsman is for.

teile.einleitung: A banknote is money made of special paper or plastic that is issued by a central bank. In Switzerland, this is the Swiss National Bank. Each note has a value in francs printed on it.
wichtigste: Swiss banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
There are notes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs.
There is no 500-franc note in Switzerland.
The texts on the notes are in all four national languages.
You check whether a note is genuine by tilting it, feeling it and holding it up to the light.
The current series is the ninth series of banknotes.

abschnitte.text: A **banknote** is a printed note of money. It is **legal tender**, which means you can pay with it. In Switzerland, only the **Swiss National Bank** may issue banknotes. Coins, on the other hand, are minted by Swissmint on behalf of the federal government.

In Switzerland there are notes of **10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs**. There is no 500-franc note, even though other countries have such values. Each note has its own colour; for example, the 10-franc note is yellow and the 1000-franc note is purple. That way you can recognise the values quickly.

The texts on Swiss notes are in **German, French, Italian and Romansh**. That way all four **national languages** are represented. The ninth series was introduced between 2016 and 2019. Each note shows a theme that is typical of Switzerland, for example water, wind or language.

Genuine notes have many **security features**. When you **tilt** them, certain pictures and colours change. If you hold the note up to the **light**, hidden signs become visible. The paper also feels special, and some areas are printed so that they are raised and can be felt. The National Bank explains these features on its website.

gewusst: The Swiss 1000-franc note is one of the banknotes with the highest value in the world.
The ninth series no longer has portraits of famous people.

teile.einleitung: Change is the money you get back when paying if you hand over more money than the goods cost. If, for example, you buy an exercise book for 7.50 francs with a 20-franc note, you get 12.50 francs back. Counting your change is a simple but very useful habit.
wichtigste: Change is the amount you get back when you hand over too much money.
You calculate it like this: amount paid minus price.
In Switzerland, change is made up of francs and centimes (Rappen).
One franc has 100 centimes.
With cash, amounts in Switzerland are usually rounded to 5 centimes.
It is worth always counting your change straight away at the till.
If you pay by card or app, you get no change, because exactly the right amount is taken.

abschnitte.text: **Change** comes about when you pay with a note or coin that is worth more than the price. The shop assistant then gives back the difference. If an ice cream costs 3.50 francs and you pay with 5 francs, you get 1.50 francs back. The German word Wechselgeld comes from “wechseln”, to change, because a large note is changed into smaller money.

The calculation is a simple **subtraction**: amount paid minus price gives the change. But many cashiers prefer to count forwards, from the price up to the amount paid. If something costs 6.30 francs and you give 10 francs, they count: 6.30 plus 20 centimes makes 6.50, plus 50 centimes makes 7, plus 3 francs makes 10. This counting forwards is also called the **shopkeeper’s method**.

Switzerland’s money is the **Swiss franc**. There are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. Banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. The smallest coin today is the 5-centime piece, which is why cash amounts are **rounded** to 5 centimes.

Mistakes happen at the till too, for example when it is busy. That is why you should count your change **right at the till** before you leave. If something is missing, say so politely straight away. Later it is difficult to prove that you were given too little. The **receipt** also helps with checking.

Today many people pay by **debit card**, credit card or TWINT. Then exactly the right amount is taken, and there is no change. Even so, cash is still popular in Switzerland, especially for small amounts. But being able to do sums in your head always helps you compare prices and keep track.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money you get back when you pay more than something costs.
The smaller part of the franc; 100 Rappen make 1 franc.
The amount is rounded up or down to the nearest 5 centimes.
A slip that shows what you bought and paid.

gewusst: The 1-centime coin has no longer been legal tender in Switzerland since 2007.
In dialect, the half-franc coin is often called a “Füfzgi”.
If you try to buy a bread roll with a 1000-franc note, you may be turned away because the till does not have that much change.

teile.einleitung: A fixed-rate mortgage is a loan for a house or a flat in which the interest stays fixed for a certain period. This makes planning easier. In Switzerland it is one of the most common types of mortgage.
wichtigste: A mortgage is a loan for buying a house or a flat.
With a fixed-rate mortgage, the interest stays the same for the whole term.
The term is set when the mortgage is taken out, often between 2 and 10 years.
If interest rates rise, you benefit; if they fall, you pay more than necessary.
Anyone who wants to get out early usually has to pay compensation.
The house or flat serves as security for the bank.

abschnitte.text: A house costs a lot of money, often more than you have saved. That is why you borrow part of it from a bank. This loan is called a **mortgage**. The house itself serves as security. In Switzerland you usually have to contribute at least 20 per cent of the purchase price yourself, known as **own funds**.

With a **fixed-rate mortgage**, you agree an interest rate and a **term** with the bank. As long as the term lasts, the interest does not change. That way you know exactly how much you have to pay each year. This helps with planning the family budget.

If interest rates on the market rise, you keep paying the lower, fixed interest. But if interest rates fall, you stay with the higher interest. Anyone who wants to end the fixed-rate mortgage before the end of the term usually pays an **early repayment penalty**. This is a kind of compensation for the bank.

As well as fixed-rate mortgages, there are mortgages with **variable interest**. There the interest adjusts continuously, for example with the **SARON mortgage**. It can be cheaper, but it is harder to plan for. Many people split their mortgage and combine different types.

gewusst: The word “mortgage” in German, “Hypothek”, comes from Greek and means roughly “pledge”.
At the end of a fixed-rate mortgage, you can renew it or switch to another bank.

teile.einleitung: On the back of many cards there is a short number, usually made up of three digits. This is the card security code. You need it above all when paying on the internet, and it must be kept secret.
wichtigste: The card security code is usually on the back of the card.
It often consists of three digits and is called CVV or CVC.
You need it for payments on the internet.
Only enter it in secure online shops.
Never tell it to strangers by phone or email.
Often you also have to confirm a payment in the bank’s app.

abschnitte.text: The **card security code** is a short number, usually with **three digits**. It is often on the back, near the signature strip. Depending on the card company, it is called **CVV** or **CVC**. On some cards it has four digits and is on the front.

When shopping on the **internet**, the shop cannot see the card. That is why it asks for the card number, expiry date and **security code**. The security code shows that you really have the card in your hand. It is an extra **security step**.

Anyone who knows the card number, expiry date and security code can shop on the internet. That is why you only enter these details in **secure shops**. Never give them by phone, text message or email. Fraudsters sometimes pretend to be the bank in order to get such data. This is called **phishing**.

Many payments on the internet also have to be confirmed in the bank’s **app**. That way you notice straight away if someone else is using the card. You can also see in the app which payments have been made. If something seems odd, report it to the bank.

gewusst: The security code is not stored in the card’s magnetic stripe or chip, so that it cannot be read when paying in a shop.
Reputable online shops do not store the security code permanently.

teile.einleitung: With an inheritance, the assets of a person who has died pass to other people, the heirs. This includes the money in their bank accounts. But the bank only releases it once it is clear who inherits.
wichtigste: Heirs are the people who receive the assets of a person who has died.
When the bank learns of the death, it usually blocks the account.
Only with proof such as a certificate of inheritance can the heirs use the account.
In Switzerland, who inherits is governed by the Civil Code or a will.
The bank card of the person who has died may no longer be used.

abschnitte.text: When a person dies, their **assets** pass to the **heirs**. In Switzerland, the **Civil Code** decides who inherits if nothing else has been laid down. Usually these are, for example, the husband or wife or the children. With a **will**, a person can decide during their lifetime who should get something. Certain legal limits apply.

When the bank learns of a customer’s death, it usually **blocks** the account. That way nobody can simply withdraw money. The cards of the person who has died may no longer be used either. Important payments, for example for the funeral, can often still be made after agreement with the bank.

So that the heirs can use the account, they need **proof**. In Switzerland this is the **certificate of inheritance**. It shows who the heirs are. Depending on the canton, it is issued by an authority or by a notary. With the certificate of inheritance, the heirs can divide up the money together.

gewusst: The rules on inheritance are set out in the Swiss Civil Code, which has applied since 1912.
Inheritance law in Switzerland was changed on some points in 2023.

teile.einleitung: Shares and bonds are two important ways of investing money. Both help companies to raise money. But they work very differently: a share is a part of the company, a bond is a loan.
wichtigste: With a **share** you become the **owner** of part of the company.
With a **bond** you lend the company money and become a **creditor**.
For a bond you regularly receive **interest**.
At the end of the **term** you get the money you lent back.
Shares can bring more profit, but they are usually **riskier**.
The federal government and cantons also issue bonds.

abschnitte.titel: The share: part of the company
abschnitte.text: Anyone who buys a **share** becomes a **co-owner** of the company. They have a share in the profit, often in the form of a **dividend**, and may have a say at the general meeting. How much the share is worth depends on the company’s success. The share price can rise sharply, but it can also fall sharply.

A **bond** (Obligation) is also called an **Anleihe** in German. Anyone who buys one lends money to the company or the state. In return they receive a fixed **interest** payment every year. After a certain time, the **term**, the borrower pays the money back. So you are a **creditor** and not an owner, and that is why you do not have a say.

Bonds are usually considered **safer** than shares. The interest is known in advance. If a company goes bust, the creditors are paid before the shareholders. Shares go up and down more, but over a long time they often bring higher returns. That is why many investors mix both, in order to **spread the risk**.

It is not only companies that issue bonds, but also the **Swiss Confederation**, cantons and municipalities. That is how they borrow money, for example for roads or school buildings. Because Switzerland is considered a very reliable borrower, its bonds are popular. In return they usually pay fairly low interest.

gewusst: In Germany, bonds are usually called Anleihen.
With very safe borrowers the interest is often lower; with unsafe ones it is higher.

teile.einleitung: A bank account is like a safe compartment at a bank in which you can keep, receive and pass on money. Almost all adults in Switzerland have one, because wages, rent and bills usually go through an account. Many banks offer youth accounts especially for young people, often without fees.
wichtigste: In a bank account, money is kept safely at a bank.
Every account has its own number, the IBAN.
With a card you can pay from the account or withdraw cash.
Many banks offer youth accounts, often without fees.
There are different kinds of account, for example private accounts and savings accounts.
Deposits of up to 100,000 francs per person and bank are protected by deposit protection.
With e-banking or an app you can check your account at any time.

abschnitte.text: A **bank account** is an agreement between a person and a bank. The bank manages the money and records every payment in and out. The money is not kept in a box of its own; instead the bank keeps an exact record. The current amount in the account is called the **account balance**.

The **private account** is meant for everyday use; for example, your wages arrive there and you pay bills from it. The **savings account** is meant for putting money aside for longer. There are also accounts for retirement provision, such as the pillar 3a account. Companies have their own business accounts.

Many Swiss banks, including cantonal banks, Raiffeisen banks and PostFinance, offer **youth accounts**. These often have no account fees and sometimes slightly better interest. For children, the parents usually open the account. Later, young people often get their own debit card and access to a banking app, with which they learn to make their own decisions about money.

Every account has an **IBAN**, an international account number. A Swiss IBAN begins with CH and is 21 characters long. With the IBAN, someone can transfer money into the account. The account usually comes with a **debit card**, with which you can pay in shops and withdraw cash at a cash machine.

Money in Swiss bank accounts is protected up to 100,000 francs per person and bank by **deposit protection** in case a bank goes bust. You must not tell anyone your e-banking login details or your card’s PIN. It is worth checking the movements in your account regularly. Before opening an account, you can compare the fees and offers of different banks.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much money is in the account at the moment.
International account number; in Switzerland it begins with CH.
A bank card with which you pay directly from your own account.
Money that the bank charges for managing the account.

gewusst: The IBAN contains two check digits so that typing mistakes are usually spotted.
An account can also go into the red; this is called an overdraft, and the bank charges interest for it.
Under Swiss law, young people may in principle manage wages they have earned themselves.

teile.einleitung: We use electricity every day for lights, the fridge, computers and much more. Electricity costs money, and producing it uses raw materials and energy. With small habits, every family can save.
wichtigste: Electricity is measured and paid for in kilowatt hours.
Switching off the light when you leave a room saves electricity.
LED bulbs use much less electricity than old light bulbs.
Appliances on standby keep using electricity.
The energy label shows how economical an appliance is.
Saving hot water also saves energy and money.

abschnitte.text: Electricity use is measured in **kilowatt hours** (kWh). An **electricity meter** in the house counts how much a family uses. The electricity company then sends a bill. The price per kilowatt hour differs from municipality to municipality and is given in centimes. The less you use, the smaller the bill.

When you leave a room, you can **switch off the light**. **LED bulbs** use much less electricity than old light bulbs and last longer. Many appliances such as televisions or games consoles are on **standby** when they only seem to be switched off. Even then they use electricity. A power strip with a switch makes it easy to switch everything off completely.

New appliances such as fridges or washing machines have an **energy label** stuck on them. It uses letters and colours to show how much electricity an appliance uses. Green and the letter A mean very economical. An economical appliance may cost more to buy, but it saves money over many years.

**Hot water** also uses a lot of energy, because it has to be heated. A short shower instead of a bath saves water and energy. When airing a room, it is better to open the window wide for a short time than to leave it tilted open for a long time. If you put a lid on the pan when cooking, you also use less electricity.

gewusst: In Switzerland, a large part of the electricity comes from hydropower.
A fridge runs day and night, so being economical matters especially with it.
A charger left in the socket without a phone can still use a little electricity.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who invests money wants to make a profit. This profit is called the return. But the greater the chance of a high return, the greater the risk of losing money usually is too.
wichtigste: The return is what an investment earns, usually as a percentage per year.
Risk means that you can also lose money.
Higher chances of a return usually mean higher risk.
Safe investments usually earn less.
There is no such thing as a high return without risk.
Promises like that are typical of investment fraud.

abschnitte.text: The **return** is what an investment **earns**. It is usually given as a **percentage per year**. If you invest 100 francs and have 103 francs after a year, you have a return of 3 per cent. A return can come from **interest**, **dividends** or rising prices. But it can also be negative if you lose money.

**Risk** means that the value of an investment can **go up and down**. It can rise, but it can also **fall**. **Shares**, for example, often go up and down a lot. In good years they earn a lot; in bad years they can lose a lot. A **savings account**, on the other hand, does not go up and down, but pays little interest.

Between risk and return the rule is usually: **higher chances of a return mean higher risk**. Investments with big chances of profit go up and down more and can also bring **losses**. **Safe investments**, in return, usually **earn less**. If you need money soon, it is better to choose a safe investment. If you can wait a long time, you can more easily cope with ups and downs.

You can reduce the risk by **spreading** your money. This is called **diversification**. Instead of putting everything into one single company, you buy shares in many different companies and countries. If one company does badly, not everything is lost at once. A well-known saying about this is: “Don't put all your eggs in one basket.”

An offer promises a **20 per cent return** a year, without any risk? That is **very suspicious** and probably **fraud**. There is no such thing as a high return without risk. Promises like that are typical of **investment fraud**, often on the internet or on social media. In Switzerland, the financial market supervisory authority **FINMA** warns about unauthorised providers.

gewusst: Experts call the link between risk, return and how quickly you can get at your money the “magic triangle” of investing.
Inflation also affects the return: if prices rise faster than the interest, money in a savings account loses purchasing power.

teile.einleitung: The QR-bill is Switzerland's payment slip with a square code that you can scan with your mobile phone. It has replaced the old orange and red payment slips. In the middle of the code there is a small Swiss cross.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, the QR-bill has replaced the old orange payment slip.
It was introduced on 30 June 2020.
Since October 2022 the old payment slips are no longer valid.
The Swiss QR Code contains all the payment details such as IBAN, amount and reference.
A Swiss cross is shown in the middle of the code.
You can pay a QR-bill by scanning it with your banking app, at the post office counter or with a payment order.
Scanning prevents typing mistakes with long numbers.

abschnitte.text: A **QR-bill** is a bill with a payment part attached. On it a **Swiss QR Code** is printed, a square pattern of black and white dots. All the important details are stored in the code: recipient, account, amount and a reference number. Next to it, the same details are also printed in readable text.

For decades, bills in Switzerland were paid with the orange or red **payment slip**. On 30 June 2020 the QR-bill was introduced. Until 30 September 2022 both forms could be used. Since then only the QR-bill has been valid; the old slips are no longer accepted.

The easiest way is to scan the code with your **banking app**; then all the details are filled in straight away. You check them, confirm the payment and the money is transferred. If you do not use online banking, you can pay the QR-bill in cash at the **post office counter** or send it to the bank by post as a payment order. Today many bills also arrive digitally as an eBill directly in online banking.

abschnitte.titel: How the payment part is laid out
abschnitte.text: The payment part is at the bottom of the bill and can be torn off along a **perforation**. On the left is the receipt, on the right the actual payment part with the QR code. The Swiss cross in the middle of the code shows that it follows the Swiss standard. For companies there is a special **QR-IBAN**, with which payments can be matched automatically.

Because you do not have to type anything in, fewer **mistakes** happen with long account numbers and references. The QR-bill can be sent on paper or as a PDF. It fits in with the IBAN, which is valid worldwide, and with modern payment systems. For companies, it makes bookkeeping simpler and faster.

begriffe.erklaerung: A square code that stores information and is read with a camera.
A form used in the past to pay a bill.
A number that matches a payment to a bill.
An electronic bill that arrives directly in online banking.

gewusst: QR stands for “Quick Response”.
The QR code was invented in Japan in 1994 by a company working for the car industry.
On bills, the amount in the payment part can also be left blank; then you fill it in yourself, for example for donations.

teile.einleitung: Withdrawing money means taking money out of your own bank account and getting it in your hand as cash. You can do this at a cash machine or at the bank counter. Afterwards there is less money in the account.
wichtigste: When **withdrawing**, you take money out of your account.
Afterwards the **account balance** is lower.
You can only withdraw what is in the account.
In Switzerland, people usually withdraw money at a **cash machine** (Bankomat).
For this you need a **card** and a secret **PIN code**.
The opposite of withdrawing is **paying in**.

abschnitte.text: The **cash machine** (Bankomat) is a machine that gives out cash round the clock. You put your **bank card** in and type in your **PIN code**. Then you choose the amount, for example 20 or 50 francs. The machine gives you back your card and the notes. At the same time, the amount is taken from your account.

The **PIN** is a secret number, usually with four or six digits. Only you may know it. You do not write it on the card and you do not show it to anyone. When typing it in, you cover the keypad with your hand. If the PIN is entered wrongly several times, the card is blocked.

If Ben has 10 francs in his account, he cannot withdraw 50 francs. A **youth account** does not give out more than is in it. Many cards also have a **limit**: you can only withdraw a certain amount per day or per month. This protects you if the card gets lost.

Every withdrawal appears on your **bank statement** or in the bank’s app. That way you can see how much money is left. It is worth only withdrawing as much cash as you really need. If you write down your expenses, you keep your budget under control better.

gewusst: The word Bankomat is common in Switzerland and Austria; in Germany people usually say Geldautomat.
Some cash machines give out euros as well as francs.

teile.einleitung: Interest is a price for borrowed money. If you save money in the bank, you get interest, and if you borrow money, you have to pay interest.
wichtigste: **Interest** is a reward for letting the bank use your money.
The **interest rate** is given as a percentage per year.
1 % of 200 francs is 2 francs.
Formula: amount times interest rate divided by 100 equals interest per year.
Anyone who takes out a **loan** has to pay the bank interest.
With **compound interest**, the interest itself earns interest too.

abschnitte.text: When you put money into a **savings account**, the bank can work with it. It lends it, for example, to other people for a house. For this it pays you **interest**. The other way round, anyone who borrows money from the bank pays interest. For loans, banks charge more interest than they pay on savings accounts. A large part of the bank’s income comes from this.

The interest rate is given as a **percentage** per year. One per cent is one hundredth. With 200 francs and 1 % interest, you calculate 200 divided by 100 times 1, which gives **2 francs**. With 3000 francs and 1.5 %, you calculate 3000 times 0.015, which gives **45 francs**. The simple rule is: amount times percentage divided by 100 equals interest.

If you leave the interest in the account, it earns interest too the next year. This is called **compound interest**. Over one year it makes little difference. But over many years it makes the money grow faster and faster. That is why it is worth starting to save early.

Interest also works with debts, but against you. Anyone who does not pay off a **loan** or a credit card bill often has to pay high interest. The debts then grow quickly. For loans for consumer goods, the **Consumer Credit Act** in Switzerland protects people with a maximum interest rate. Even so: do your sums carefully before getting into debt.

Banks set their own interest rates. In doing so, they are strongly guided by the **policy rate** of the **Swiss National Bank** (SNB). If the SNB lowers the policy rate, interest on savings accounts and loans usually falls too. If it rises, they rise as well. That is why the interest on a savings account keeps changing.

gewusst: From 2015 to 2022 the Swiss National Bank had a negative policy rate. For very large deposits, some customers even had to pay the bank something.
With the “rule of 72” you can estimate when money will double: 72 divided by the interest rate gives roughly the number of years.

teile.einleitung: A securities account (Depot) is a kind of account for securities such as shares, bonds or fund units. The bank keeps them there for its customers. But the securities remain the property of the customers.
wichtigste: In a securities account, the bank keeps securities for its customers.
If you want to buy shares, you usually need a securities account.
The securities in the account belong to the customers, not to the bank.
If a bank goes bankrupt, the securities are separated out and handed over.
Banks often charge a fee for a securities account.

abschnitte.text: A **securities account** is like an account, but not for money; it is for **securities**. These include shares, bonds and units in **funds**. In the past, securities were often kept on paper in a bank’s safe. Today they are almost always only recorded **electronically**. In the securities account you can see which securities you own and how much they are worth at the moment.

Money in an account is legally a credit balance with the bank. With securities in a securities account it is different: they remain the **property of the customers**. The bank only keeps them safe. That is why, if a bank goes **bankrupt**, the securities are **separated out**, meaning kept apart from the bank’s assets, and handed over to the customers. Memory aid: what is in your securities account belongs to you.

Many banks charge a **custody fee** for a securities account. On top of that there are often **brokerage fees** when buying and selling, which are fees per order. Prices differ greatly between providers. That is why anyone opening a securities account compares the costs. Young people usually need their parents’ consent for this.

gewusst: The word Depot comes from French and means roughly “storage” or “store”.
A securities account also brings income such as dividends, which are usually credited to an account.

teile.einleitung: The personal identification number, PIN for short, is a secret number with which you prove that you are the rightful owner of a card. You need it, for example, at the cash machine or when paying in a shop. You must always keep your PIN code secret and never tell it to anyone.
wichtigste: PIN stands for personal identification number.
A PIN usually consists of four to six digits.
You need it for bank cards, mobile phones and SIM cards.
You must keep your PIN secret and never tell it to anyone.
After three wrong entries, a card is usually blocked.
You should never write your PIN on the card or keep it together with the card.
The bank never asks for your PIN by email or phone.

abschnitte.text: A **PIN** is a number code that only the owner of a card or a device knows. It works like a password but consists only of digits. On bank cards in Switzerland it is usually four or six digits. Anyone who wants to use the card must enter the correct PIN; this is how the person is **identified**.

You need your PIN when withdrawing cash at a **cash machine** and often when paying by debit card or credit card. For small amounts you can pay contactless without a PIN; for larger amounts it is required. Mobile phones, tablets and **SIM cards** are also protected with a PIN. Some apps, such as banking apps, also ask for their own code.

The most important rule is: **keep your PIN secret** and do not tell it to anyone, not even friends. You should not write it on the card or keep it in your wallet. When typing it in, you cover the keypad with your hand. A good PIN is not a date of birth and not a simple sequence such as 1234 or 0000.

If you enter your PIN wrongly three times, the card is normally **blocked**. That way thieves cannot simply try out every number. If you have lost your card or think someone knows your PIN, you must have the card blocked by the bank straight away. If you carelessly give your PIN to someone, you may have to pay for any damage yourself.

The PIN was developed in the 1960s together with the first cash machines. The inventor is said to be the Scottish engineer **James Goodfellow**, who applied for a patent for it in 1966. Today the PIN is stored in encrypted form on the card's **chip** or at the bank. With many cards you can change your PIN yourself at the cash machine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A secret combination of numbers used to prove who you are.
Proving who you are.
To lock a card so that nobody can use it any more.
Paying by just holding the card against the device.

gewusst: A four-digit PIN has exactly 10,000 possible combinations.
Strictly speaking, “PIN number” says the same thing twice, because the N in PIN already stands for number.
Instead of a PIN, many mobile phones today can also be unlocked with a fingerprint or face recognition.

teile.einleitung: Paying in money means putting money into an account. This makes the account balance bigger. You can pay in cash or have money transferred from another account.
wichtigste: Paying in means putting money into an account.
After paying in, the account balance is bigger.
You pay in cash at the bank counter or at a deposit machine.
Lots of small payments add up to a lot.
The opposite of paying in is withdrawing.

abschnitte.text: When **paying in**, money goes into your **account**. Your **account balance** gets bigger. The opposite is **withdrawing**: then you take money out of the account. Many children, for example, pay money from their piggy bank or money they have been given into their savings account.

You can hand cash in at the **bank counter**. The bank staff count it and credit it to the account. Many banks also have **deposit machines**. There you put in your card and place the notes in a compartment. The machine counts the money and books it to the account. Not all machines accept coins.

Every payment makes the account balance bigger. If Lars pays in 5 francs and then another 5 francs, there will be 10 francs in his empty account afterwards. If you regularly pay in even small amounts, you will have a nice sum after a while. In a savings account, the bank can also credit **interest**.

gewusst: Money can also reach an account without cash, for example when wages are transferred.
When you pay money in, you often get a receipt as proof.

teile.einleitung: A standing order is a regular automatic payment that you set up once with your bank, for example for the rent. The bank then transfers the same amount to the same recipient every month or at another fixed interval. That way you do not forget any important payment.
wichtigste: A standing order is a regular automatic payment.
It is suitable for amounts of the same size that come up again and again, such as the rent.
You set it up once, and after that the bank pays automatically.
You set the amount, recipient, interval and start date.
A standing order can be changed or deleted at any time.
There must be enough money in the account on the payment day.
A standing order also helps with regular saving.

abschnitte.text: A **standing order** is an instruction to the bank to transfer the same amount to the same recipient again and again. You only have to set it up once. After that the bank carries out the **transfer** automatically on the date set. This saves time and stops you from forgetting a payment.

Typical examples are the **rent**, which is the same every month, or a contribution to a sports club. Parents sometimes also use a standing order to transfer pocket money to their child’s youth account. Many people use it to save automatically, by sending a fixed amount every month to a savings account or a pillar 3a account. It is less suitable for bills with changing amounts, such as electricity or phone bills.

You set up a standing order in **e-banking**, in the banking app or at the bank counter. You enter the recipient with their IBAN, the amount, the **interval** and the first date of payment. The interval can be, for example, weekly, monthly, quarterly or yearly. You can also set an end date if the payment is only meant to run for a certain time.

With a standing order, the account holder decides when and how much is paid. It is different with **direct debit**, which in Switzerland today is usually called eBill or LSV. There the recipient, for example an electricity supplier, takes the amount of the bill from the account itself, with permission. That is why direct debit is better suited to bills whose amount changes.

On the day of payment there must be enough money in the account, otherwise the payment may not be made or the account may go overdrawn. If the amount changes, for example after a rent increase, you have to adjust the standing order yourself. After moving house, you should delete it so that payments do not keep going to your old landlord. A look at your **bank statement** shows whether all standing orders have been carried out correctly.

begriffe.erklaerung: An automatic, regular payment of the same amount.
The person or company that receives the money.
How often payment is made, for example monthly.
Doing your banking on a computer or phone.

gewusst: In Switzerland, rent is usually paid in advance, that is by the end of the previous month.
If you save 50 francs a month by standing order, you will already have put 600 francs aside after a year.
A standing order can be set to be carried out at the end of the month or on a particular day.

teile.einleitung: The BIC is an international code that clearly identifies a bank. You need it above all for payments abroad, so that the money arrives at the right bank.
wichtigste: BIC stands for Business Identifier Code.
It is often also called the SWIFT code.
The BIC identifies a bank; the IBAN identifies a particular account.
A BIC has 8 or 11 characters made up of letters and digits.
The BIC contains, among other things, an abbreviation for the bank and for the country.

abschnitte.text: The **BIC** is like an address for a bank. It consists of 8 or 11 characters. The first four characters stand for the bank, followed by two letters for the **country**, CH for Switzerland. After that come two characters for the place and sometimes three more characters for a particular branch.
