The BIC gets the name **SWIFT code** from the organisation **SWIFT**. It runs a network through which banks all over the world exchange messages about payments. SWIFT was founded in 1973 and is based in Belgium. Thousands of banks in almost every country are connected to it.

A payment needs two pieces of information. The **IBAN** names the account of the person who receives the money. The BIC names the bank where this account is held. A memory aid helps: the IBAN names the account, the BIC the bank. For many payments within Europe, the bank now finds the BIC itself from the IBAN.

gewusst: Swiss IBANs always begin with CH and have 21 characters.
The BIC of your own bank is shown on many bank statements and in e-banking.

teile.einleitung: A bank is a company that keeps money safe, lends money and carries out payments. Banks connect people who save money with people and companies who need money.
wichtigste: A bank keeps money safe and lends money.
The money for loans comes to a large extent from savers.
The bank charges interest for loans, and it often also pays interest on savings.
Banks carry out payments, for example by card or e-banking.
To open an account you usually need an official ID document.
In Switzerland, FINMA supervises the banks.

abschnitte.text: A **bank** looks after the money of many people. You have an **account** there, in which your money is recorded. The bank carries out payments, issues cards and gives advice on saving. It also lends money, for example as a **mortgage** for a house or as a loan for a company.

Many people put money into their accounts. Not all of them need it back at the same time. That is why the bank can lend part of it to others. Anyone who borrows money pays **interest** for it. The savers still get their money back when they need it. In this way the bank brings savers and borrowers together.

Anyone who wants to open an account must prove who they are, for example with a **passport** or an **identity card**. By law, the bank must know who its customers are. Among other things, this is meant to prevent money from crime being hidden. For children, the parents usually open an account.

In Switzerland there are many kinds of bank: big banks, **cantonal banks**, Raiffeisen banks, regional banks and private banks. PostFinance also offers accounts. The **Swiss National Bank** has a special role. It issues the banknotes and makes sure that the franc stays stable. **FINMA** supervises whether the banks keep to the rules.

gewusst: The word bank comes from the Italian “banco”, the table of money changers at markets.
The Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena in Italy is considered the oldest bank in the world still in existence; it was founded in 1472.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Bank, SNB for short, is Switzerland’s central bank. It makes sure that the franc keeps its value and that prices stay stable. It also issues the banknotes.
wichtigste: The SNB is Switzerland’s central bank.
Its most important task is **price stability**.
By this it means inflation of less than 2 % a year.
It issues the Swiss **banknotes**.
It has its seats in Bern and Zurich.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** opened in 1907. It is the country’s **central bank**, a kind of bank for the banks. Private individuals cannot open an account with it. The Federal Constitution obliges it to pursue a monetary policy in the interests of the whole country. In doing so it is **independent**, which means it does not take orders from the government.

If prices rise sharply, you can buy less with a franc. This is called **inflation** (in Switzerland also “Teuerung”). The SNB wants to keep inflation **below 2 %** a year. But it also wants to prevent prices from falling all the time. Its most important tool is the **policy rate**. With it, it influences how expensive it is to borrow money.

The SNB issues Switzerland’s **banknotes**. The **coins**, on the other hand, are minted for the federal government by **Swissmint** in Bern. The SNB also manages Switzerland’s **currency reserves**, for example gold and foreign currencies. If it makes a profit, the federal government and the cantons receive a share of it.

gewusst: The SNB is a public limited company. Its shares belong mainly to the cantons and the cantonal banks.
Switzerland’s current series of banknotes does not show people, but themes such as water, wind or language.

teile.einleitung: Advertising is not always easy to recognise. Sometimes someone praises a product in a video, and it seems like an honest tip. But often the person is being paid for it.
wichtigste: Advertising is meant to get people to buy something.
If someone shows and praises a product, it may be advertising.
Sometimes the person is paid for it or is given the product as a present.
Labels such as “advertising” or “advert” help you recognise it.
Advertising only shows the good sides of a product.

abschnitte.text: There is advertising on television, on posters, in magazines, in apps and in videos. It wants you to know a **product**, like it and buy it. Advertising usually only shows the **good sides**: cheerful people, nice colours, loud music. What is not so good is not mentioned.

Not all advertising looks like advertising. In a video, someone drinks a drink and says how great it is. Perhaps a **company** has paid for this. Brands also often appear in films and games; this is called **product placement**. People who have lots of fans on the internet are called **influencers**. Many of them earn money by showing products.

Look out for labels such as **“advertising”**, **“advert”** or **“sponsored”**. Is a product shown clearly several times, or is there a **discount code**? These are strong signs of advertising. Also ask yourself: **Who benefits** if I buy this? If you are unsure, talk to your parents about it.

Seeing advertising is not a bad thing. What matters is that you **decide for yourself**. Do you really need the product, or do you only want it because it looked so great in the advert? Wait a few days before you buy something. Often the wish is already smaller by then.

gewusst: Companies spend a great deal of money on advertising every year, because it works.
Some advertising is aimed specifically at children, for example with colourful characters on packaging.

teile.einleitung: Quishing is a scam using fake QR codes. If you scan the code with your mobile phone, you end up on a false website. There you are supposed to enter payment or log-in details.
wichtigste: Quishing is fraud using fake QR codes.
The word is made up of “QR” and “phishing”.
Fake QR codes can be found, for example, on letters, posters or parking meters.
They lead to fake websites that look real.
There you are supposed to enter payment or log-in details.
Before entering any data, you always check the address of the website.

abschnitte.text: **Quishing** is a made-up word from **QR code** and **phishing**. **Phishing** means that fraudsters try to get hold of personal data such as passwords. With quishing they use **fake QR codes** to do this. If you scan the code with your mobile phone, a **fake website** opens. It often looks like the website of a bank, an authority or a well-known company.

Fake QR codes can be on **letters**, emails or **posters**. Sometimes fraudsters also stick a false code over a real one, for example on a **parking meter** or a charging station. Anyone who wants to pay then ends up on the fraudsters' website. There you are supposed to enter **card details** or **log-in details**. With these, the fraudsters steal money or take over accounts.

You cannot read a QR code with the naked eye. So you cannot see where it leads. On a small phone screen, a false **internet address** is less noticeable. Fraudsters also often put their victims under **time pressure**, for example with “Your account will be blocked”. That is why even careful people sometimes fall for it.

Before opening it, your phone usually shows the **address** that the code leads to. You should check this carefully. With letters or messages you were not expecting, it is better not to scan any code. If you are unsure, it is better to open the company's website **yourself** or call them. If you have already entered data, contact your **bank** straight away.

gewusst: The real Swiss QR-bill also contains a QR code, but it does not lead to a website; it contains the payment details.
In Switzerland you can report attempted fraud to the National Cyber Security Centre.

teile.einleitung: Many contracts, such as subscriptions, do not simply run out. If you do not cancel in time, you are often tied in for another term. This is called tacit or automatic renewal.
wichtigste: Tacit means: without you saying or doing anything.
Many subscriptions renew automatically if you do not cancel.
What matters is the term and the notice period.
If you miss the deadline, you often have to pay for a whole further term.
The rules are in the contract terms, the “small print”.
A reminder in your calendar helps you not to miss the deadline.

abschnitte.text: With **tacit renewal**, a contract carries on automatically if nobody cancels it. So you do not have to sign anything for it to continue. This is common with gym memberships, magazines, mobile phone contracts, streaming services or insurance. For the providers it is practical, because the customers stay.

The **term** says how long a contract applies at least, for example one year. The **notice period** says how long before the end you have to cancel, for example three months. If you cancel too late, you are often tied in for another term. Then you may have to pay for a whole year longer, even though you no longer need the subscription at all.

The exact rules are in the **general terms and conditions**, GTC for short. They state how long the contract runs, how to cancel and whether it renews. Some providers require written notice. It is worth reading this before signing up. That way you will not get a surprise later.

A simple trick: straight after signing up, put the last day for cancelling in your **calendar**. Make a list of all your subscriptions with their costs. Cancel important contracts in a way you can prove, for example with a registered letter. And if the provider confirms the cancellation, keep the confirmation safe.

gewusst: Lots of small subscriptions together can cost several hundred francs a year.
With some free trial subscriptions, a paid subscription starts automatically after the trial period if you do not cancel.

teile.einleitung: If you want your own bank account, you first have to open it. When you do, the bank checks carefully who the new customer is. Here you will find out how opening an account works in Switzerland.
wichtigste: To open an account, you always need an official identity document.
Valid documents include, for example, a passport or an identity card.
Because of the rules against money laundering, the bank must know who its customers are.
Children and teenagers usually need their parents' consent.
Many banks offer special youth accounts.
You can open an account at a branch or often online too.

abschnitte.text: Whenever an account is opened, the bank asks for an **official identity document**. This is a document issued by the state, for example a **passport** or an **identity card**. The bank checks whether the photo and the details are correct. It keeps a copy of the document. Without ID, there is no account.

abschnitte.titel: Why the bank checks so carefully
abschnitte.text: Switzerland has an **Anti-Money Laundering Act**. **Money laundering** means that criminals try to make money from crimes look clean by passing it through banks. To prevent this, every bank must know its customers. This is also called **identification**. The bank therefore also asks for your address, date of birth and sometimes where large sums of money come from.

Children can have a **youth account** or **savings account** from an early age. As long as you are not yet of age, your **parents** usually sign as well. Youth accounts often cost no fees. Some banks give a slightly better interest rate. At 18 you can then decide on all banking matters yourself.

In the past, you always went to the bank counter for a new account. Today you can often open an account **online** as well. You show your ID in a **video call** or hold it up to the camera using an app. The check is just as strict as at the branch. At the end you receive the account number, the **IBAN**, and often a card.

gewusst: The duty to know customers well applies not only to banks but also, for example, to asset managers.
When an account is opened online, the bank can check whether the ID is genuine, for example using security features that change when you tilt it.

teile.einleitung: With currency exchange, you change one currency into another, for example francs into euros. You need this above all for trips abroad. You can change money at banks and bureaux de change.
wichtigste: Currency exchange means swapping one currency for another.
In Italy, Germany, France and Austria, people pay in euros.
You can change francs at banks and bureaux de change.
The exchange rate decides how much you get.
For cash, a slightly worse rate usually applies than for money in an account.
It is worth comparing the rates.

abschnitte.text: If you go on holiday to Italy, you need **euros** there. You cannot pay with francs in most shops. That is why you change francs into euros. This is called **currency exchange**.

You can change money at a **bank** or at a **bureau de change**. Bureaux de change can be found, for example, at large railway stations, airports and near the border. Sometimes you have to order larger amounts in advance. You can also withdraw cash with your card from a cash machine abroad.

How many euros you get for your francs is stated by the **exchange rate**. It changes every day. Banks show two rates: a **buying rate** and a **selling rate**. The difference is what the bank earns, and sometimes there are fees as well.

At airports, the rate is often less favourable. If you compare, you get more for your money. After your holiday, you can change leftover notes back into francs. But **coins** are often not taken back, so it is best to spend them before you travel home.

gewusst: Money changers existed even in ancient times; they often sat at tables in market squares.
The word “bank” comes from the Italian “banco”, the table at which money changers used to work.

teile.einleitung: A foreign currency account is a bank account in which money is held not in francs but in another currency. This is practical for people and companies that often pay or receive money in euros or dollars.
wichtigste: In a foreign currency account, money is held, for example, in euros or dollars.
You can receive and spend money in that currency there without changing it.
This saves conversion fees if you often pay in that currency.
The value of the money in francs goes up and down with the exchange rate.
Many Swiss banks offer such accounts, often for a fee.

abschnitte.titel: An account in a foreign currency
abschnitte.text: A normal account in Switzerland is kept in **francs**. With a **foreign currency account**, the bank counts the balance in another currency. The most common are accounts in **euros** and **US dollars**. The account has its own IBAN, just like a franc account.

A foreign currency account is practical for people who work abroad or have a holiday home there. **Companies** that sell goods abroad also often receive euros or dollars. They can leave the money in the account and spend it later in the same currency. That way you do not have to keep changing money.

The value of the balance in francs depends on the **exchange rate**. If the euro becomes weaker, the money is worth less when counted in francs. If it becomes stronger, you gain. These ups and downs are called **currency risk**.

Banks often charge an **account fee** for foreign currency accounts. There may also be costs for payments in and out. If you only rarely travel abroad, you usually do not need such an account. It is worth comparing the offers.

gewusst: Some banks offer accounts in many different currencies, even in Japanese yen.
Many people from neighbouring countries work in Switzerland and commute across the border every day as cross-border commuters.

teile.einleitung: A wish is something you would like to have but do not necessarily need. If you can tell wishes apart from important things, you handle your money more wisely.
wichtigste: A wish brings joy, but it is not essential for life.
A **need** is something you really need, for example food, clothes or a roof over your head.
More of the same, such as a tenth toy figure, is usually a wish.
Nobody can fulfil all their wishes straight away.
If you save, you can fulfil a bigger wish later.
Having wishes is quite normal and nothing bad.

abschnitte.text: A wish is something nice that you would like to have. It can be a new toy, a book or an outing. But you can live perfectly well without it. That is why people say: a wish is nice, but **not necessary**.

A **need** is something you need in order to live. This includes food, drink, warm clothes and a home. A wish comes on top, once the important things are already there. An example: you need shoes for the winter, but a fifth pair of trainers is more of a wish. Sometimes the line is not entirely clear; then the question helps: Can I manage without it?

If you already have nine toy figures, you do not need a tenth. It would be nice, but it is a wish. We often wish for things that are similar to things we already have. It is worth thinking briefly about whether you would really use the new thing often. That way there is more **money** left for things that matter to you.

For many wishes you have to **save**. For example, every week you put part of your pocket money in your piggy bank. Over time, enough builds up. Some wishes also come true on your birthday or at Christmas. And sometimes, while waiting, you notice that the wish no longer seems so important at all.

gewusst: Many people notice after waiting a few days that a wish is no longer so important. That is why experts advise sleeping on it for a night before buying.
Adverts often show things in such a way that you want them straight away.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Bank, SNB for short, is a very special bank. It issues the banknotes and makes sure that prices stay stable. But it does not run accounts for private individuals.
wichtigste: The Swiss National Bank is the central bank of Switzerland.
It issues the Swiss banknotes.
Its most important task is to ensure stable prices.
It runs accounts for banks and the Confederation, not for private individuals.
It has head offices in Bern and Zurich.
The coins are not made by the National Bank but by Swissmint.

abschnitte.titel: The bank of the state and of the banks
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** is the **central bank** of Switzerland. It was founded in **1907**. As a private individual you **cannot open an account** with it. It runs accounts only for **banks** and for the **Confederation**. That is why it is sometimes called the “bank of the banks”. It has its head offices in **Bern** and **Zurich**.

Only the National Bank may issue **banknotes** in Switzerland. It makes sure there is always enough cash. The notes are protected against forgery with many **security features**. The **coins**, on the other hand, are minted by **Swissmint** in Bern. But the National Bank puts them into circulation.

The National Bank's most important task is **price stability**. This means prices should neither rise nor fall too much. If prices rise sharply, this is called **inflation**. Then money becomes worth less. To prevent this, the National Bank can, for example, change the **key interest rate**. This work is called **monetary policy**.

The National Bank is **independent**. The government may not give it orders on monetary policy. But it must account for its actions to the Confederation and the public. If it makes a profit, the **Confederation** and the **cantons** receive a share of it. A large part of the National Bank's shares belongs to the **cantons** and the cantonal banks.

gewusst: The National Bank's shares are traded on the stock exchange, even though it carries out a public task.
The National Bank also keeps large amounts of gold as a reserve.

teile.einleitung: Consumer credit is borrowed money that people use for private purchases, such as a car or furniture. In Switzerland, the Consumer Credit Act sets out exactly what is allowed. It is meant to protect people from getting into too much debt.
wichtigste: Consumer credit is a loan for private spending.
In Switzerland, the Consumer Credit Act applies to it.
Before giving the loan, the bank must check whether you can pay it back.
This creditworthiness check is meant to prevent people from getting too deeply into debt.
You can cancel the contract in writing within 14 days.
You pay interest on a loan, so it costs more than the amount you receive.

abschnitte.text: With **consumer credit**, you borrow money for private things, for example a car, furniture or a holiday. This also includes **cash loans** and many **leasing contracts**. You pay the money back in instalments. On top of that comes **interest**, so in the end a loan costs more than the amount borrowed.

In Switzerland, the **Consumer Credit Act** governs these loans. Among other things, it sets the maximum interest rate. The maximum rate is set by the Federal Council. The contract must be in writing and must show all the costs clearly.

Before a loan is granted, the bank must carry out a **creditworthiness check**. It looks at how much you earn and what expenses you have. Only if the instalments are affordable may it give the loan. This is meant to stop anyone getting **too deeply into debt**.

After signing, you have **14 days** to **cancel** the contract in writing. That way you can calmly think the decision over once more. Anyone who already has debts and does not know what to do next can get help from a **debt advice service**. These exist in many cantons.

gewusst: In Switzerland, loans are recorded in a central database so that nobody takes out too many loans from several banks at the same time.
Advertising for consumer credit must not be aggressive; that is written in the law.

teile.einleitung: Donating means giving away money or things to help other people or animals. You do not get back what you have donated. Children can also donate a small part of their pocket money.
wichtigste: Donating means giving money or things in order to help.
You do not get the donation back.
You can donate, for example, to an animal shelter, a charity or people in need.
You can also donate clothes, toys or time.
In Switzerland, the **Zewo seal of approval** shows that a charity handles donations carefully.

abschnitte.text: When you **donate**, you voluntarily give something away without asking for anything in return. It can be money, but also clothes, toys or food for an **animal shelter**. Many organisations that help others depend on donations. They are called **charities** or non-profit organisations. They help, for example, after natural disasters, with illness or with poverty.

Before you donate, you should know who gets the money. In Switzerland, the **Zewo** foundation checks charities. Organisations with the **Zewo seal of approval** handle donations carefully and honestly. Children should ask their parents before donating money, especially on the internet.

Donating does not always have to cost money. You can help an elderly neighbour with her shopping or take part in a collection campaign. Anyone who helps a club or a project without pay is doing **voluntary work**. In Switzerland, many people volunteer.

gewusst: In Switzerland, donations to charitable organisations can be deducted from your taxes up to a certain amount.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss franc is the currency of Switzerland and also of the Principality of Liechtenstein. It is divided into 100 centimes (Rappen) and has the international abbreviation CHF. The franc is considered a particularly stable and safe currency worldwide.
wichtigste: The Swiss franc is the official currency of Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
One franc has 100 centimes.
The international abbreviation is CHF, which stands for Confoederatio Helvetica franc.
There are coins from 5 centimes to 5 francs and banknotes from 10 to 1000 francs.
Coins are made of metal and meant for small amounts; banknotes are meant for larger amounts.
The banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
The franc has been the single currency of Switzerland since 1850.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss franc** is the money you pay with in Switzerland. It is also the official means of payment in Liechtenstein. Internationally it is abbreviated to **CHF**, after the Latin name for Switzerland, Confoederatio Helvetica. In French it is called franc, in Italian franco and in Romansh franc.

There are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes, as well as ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The large 5-franc piece is popularly called the **Fünfliber** and is worth more than all the smaller coins. It shows an Alpine herdsman. The coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern and are made of metal such as cupronickel.

**Banknotes** come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. The current series was introduced between 2016 and 2019 and shows the many sides of Switzerland with themes such as time, light, wind and water. Each note has its own colour: the 10-franc note is yellow, the 20 red and the 50 green. The notes are made of a special material with several layers, which is hard to forge.

Before 1848, almost every canton had its own money, which was very complicated. In 1850 the new federal state introduced the franc as a **single currency**. Since 1907 the Swiss National Bank has been responsible for the banknotes. Until 2000 the franc was tied to gold by law.

The **Swiss National Bank**, SNB for short, has its seats in Bern and Zurich. It makes sure that prices remain stable and that there is enough money in circulation. To do this, it can, for example, raise or lower the policy rate. It is independent of the government so that it can take long-term decisions.

The franc is considered a **safe haven**, because Switzerland is politically stable and has little debt. In crises, investors therefore like to buy francs, which makes the franc more expensive. A strong franc is good for holidays abroad but difficult for companies that sell abroad. That is why, from 2011 to 2015, the National Bank set a minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs to the euro.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money that is officially used in a country.
A note made of special material for larger amounts.
A dialect word for the 5-franc piece.
How much one currency is worth compared with another.

gewusst: The 1000-franc note is one of the most valuable banknotes in the world.
The edge of the Fünfliber bears the Latin saying “DOMINUS PROVIDEBIT”, which means “The Lord will provide”.
Today’s Swiss banknotes are designed in portrait format, which is rather rare for banknotes around the world.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes a bill or reminder arrives for something you never ordered. It may be a mistake, but sometimes it is an attempt at fraud. The important thing is to stay calm and defend yourself in the right way.
wichtigste: You do not have to pay for something you never ordered.
It is best to object in writing.
Keep letters, bills and receipts safe.
You do not have to send back goods that were sent to you without being ordered.
In Switzerland, debt enforcement proceedings can be started against someone without proof.
You raise an objection to a payment order within 10 days.

abschnitte.text: An **unjustified bill** is a demand for payment for something you did not order or did not receive. It can arise from a mistake, for example a mix-up. But there are also **fraudsters** who simply send out bills and hope that someone pays. First, check calmly: did I really not order anything?

If the claim is wrong, you write to the company saying that you **ordered nothing** and will not pay. It is best to do this **in writing**, for example with a registered letter. That way you can prove later that you objected. Keep all letters, bills and receipts safe. Consumer protection offices can help if you have questions.

Sometimes companies send goods that nobody ordered and then ask for money. Under the **Code of Obligations**, this is not a valid offer. You do not have to pay for the item, send it back or keep it. A contract only comes about if both sides agree.

In Switzerland, **debt enforcement proceedings** can be started against someone without proving that they owe anything. That is why a **payment order** can arrive even for a wrong claim. Then you have to react: within **10 days** you raise an **objection**. This is very simple and can even be done directly when the payment order is handed over. After that, the creditor must prove in court that the claim is correct.

gewusst: You do not have to give a reason for an objection.
Debt enforcement proceedings are entered in the debt enforcement register even if they were unjustified. But under certain conditions you can ask for them no longer to be shown.

teile.einleitung: A bank card is a small plastic card with which you can pay and withdraw cash. It is linked to your own account and belongs only to the person whose name is on it.
wichtigste: A bank card is made of hard plastic and has a chip.
You use it to pay in shops or to withdraw money at a cash machine.
The card comes with a secret PIN that you never reveal.
You never give the card to a stranger.
If the card is gone, it must be blocked immediately.
You treat it carefully and do not bend it.

abschnitte.text: A bank card is made of hard **plastic** and is roughly the same size all over the world. On the front there is a small **chip** that stores important data. Often it shows the name, a card number and the expiry date. Many cards also have a symbol for paying **contactlessly**.

With a bank card you pay in shops, in restaurants or at ticket machines. At a **cash machine** you use it to withdraw cash. Usually the card is a **debit card**: the money is taken directly from your own account. For children and teenagers there are special cards where the parents have a say.

The card comes with a **PIN**, a secret number usually made up of four to six digits. You learn it by heart and never write it on the card. When typing it in, you cover the keys with your hand. Nobody, not even the bank, asks for your PIN. The card itself belongs only to you and is never lent to anyone.

If the card is lost or stolen, it must be **blocked** immediately. Children tell their parents straight away, and the parents phone the bank. Banks have a **card-blocking number** for this, which can be reached round the clock. After that, nobody can pay with the card any more. A bent or broken card often no longer works, so you keep it safe in your purse.

gewusst: The size of bank cards is standardised worldwide, just like that of many ID cards.
Some banks now make their cards from recycled plastic.

teile.einleitung: Money laundering means disguising money from crimes so that it looks like honestly earned money. In Switzerland this is forbidden. Banks must help to uncover such cases.
wichtigste: Money laundering means hiding the criminal origin of money.
The aim is to make illegal money look legal.
In Switzerland, money laundering is a criminal offence.
Banks must know who the money belongs to and where it comes from.
They report suspicious cases to the Money Laundering Reporting Office.
The financial market supervisory authority FINMA checks whether the banks follow the rules.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who earns money through crime cannot simply spend it. Otherwise it would quickly be noticed where it comes from. That is why criminals try to “launder” the money. They move it back and forth until its origin is disguised. Then it looks like clean money. In Switzerland this is called **Geldwäscherei**, in Germany **Geldwäsche**; in English it is **money laundering**.

Experts often distinguish three steps. First the money is put into the **financial system**, for example into accounts. Then it is moved through many accounts, companies and countries so that the trail is lost. Finally it comes back as apparently honest profit. It is exactly these steps that authorities try to see through.

In Switzerland, the **Anti-Money Laundering Act** governs what banks must do. They must know their customers and ask questions about large or unusual amounts. If they have a well-founded suspicion, they report it to the **Money Laundering Reporting Office**. This is part of the Federal Office of Police.

**FINMA** supervises the banks and checks whether they follow the rules. Anyone who launders money can be punished. Banks that fail in their duties must also expect consequences. Many countries work together, because money flows quickly across borders.

gewusst: For money laundering there has to be a predicate offence: the money must come from a serious crime.
Many countries work together in an international group that sets common rules against money laundering.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who starts an apprenticeship or a job needs a salary account. The employer transfers the wages into this account every month. From there you also pay your everyday bills.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, wages are almost always transferred into an account without cash.
For this the employer needs your IBAN.
With the IBAN, the employer does not get access to the account.
The salary account, also called a personal account, is used for everyday payments.
A separate savings account is suitable for savings goals.
A savings standing order shortly after payday makes saving automatic.

abschnitte.text: Sara is starting an apprenticeship. Now above all she needs an account so that her **apprentice's wage** can be transferred. In Switzerland, wages are almost always paid **without cash** into an account. For this, Sara gives her **training company** her **IBAN**. Many banks offer special accounts without fees for apprentices.

With the IBAN, the employer can only **pay money in**. It does **not give them access** to the account. So they see neither the balance nor any other payments. Every month you also receive a **payslip**. It shows how much you earned and what was deducted, for example for the **AVS**.

The **salary account** is also called a **personal account**. It is mainly intended for everyday **payments**. This is where your wages come in. From here you pay **bills**, set up **standing orders** and pay by card. There is usually hardly any interest on this account.

abschnitte.titel: Keeping salary and savings accounts separate
abschnitte.text: It is worth keeping your **salary account** and **savings account** separate. That way you can see better what is left for saving. Money in a separate account is less easily spent in everyday life. Max gets paid on the 25th. He chooses the best date for his **savings standing order** shortly **after payday**. That way he puts the money aside before he spends it.

gewusst: What is left at the end of the month is often less than planned. That is why the tip is: save first, then spend.
In many Swiss companies, wages are paid towards the end of the month.

teile.einleitung: Every bank account has its own number, just as every house has an address. With this number the bank knows exactly where a sum of money belongs. Today the account number is usually called the IBAN.
wichtigste: Every account has its own unique number.
The international account number is called the IBAN.
A Swiss IBAN begins with the letters CH.
In Switzerland it has 21 characters.
With the IBAN, money arrives in the right account.
Anyone who knows your IBAN can pay money in, but cannot take money out.

abschnitte.text: A bank has a great many accounts. So that money arrives in the **right account**, each account has its own **account number**. It works like an address for money. If someone wants to transfer money to you, they need this number. Without it, the bank would not know whom the money belongs to.

**IBAN** is short for “International Bank Account Number”. It is used in many countries in Europe and around the world. A Swiss IBAN has **21 characters** and begins with **CH**. After that come two **check digits**, a number for the bank and the actual account number.

The two numbers after CH are called **check digits**. They are calculated from the other characters. If you type a number wrongly when making a transfer, the system usually notices straight away that the IBAN is not right. This makes it less likely that the money ends up in the wrong account. Even so, you should always give the recipient's name exactly.

abschnitte.titel: Can you give out your IBAN?
abschnitte.text: You give your IBAN, for example, to your **employer** so that they can transfer your wages. Bills with a **QR code** also show an IBAN. With the IBAN alone, nobody can take money out of your account. Even so, you only give it to people and companies you trust. Your **PIN** and **passwords**, on the other hand, must stay completely secret.

gewusst: To make it easier to read, a Swiss IBAN is written in groups of four, for example CH93 0076 2011 6238 5295 7.
In other countries the IBAN has a different length, but it always begins with the country code.

teile.einleitung: Coins are the small change in our wallets. In Switzerland there are seven different coins, from the 5-centime piece to the 5-franc piece, the “Fünfliber”. Coins are good for practising sums, because 100 centimes make 1 franc.
wichtigste: 1 franc has 100 centimes.
The coin with the highest value is the Fünfliber, worth 5 francs.
The coin with the lowest value today is the 5-centime piece.
The 5-centime piece is golden-yellow; the other coins are silvery.
Two 50-centime coins make 1 franc.
The 1-centime piece has no longer been valid since 2007.

abschnitte.text: Today there are seven coins in Switzerland: **5 centimes**, **10 centimes**, **20 centimes**, **50 centimes**, **1 franc**, **2 francs** and **5 francs**. The 50-centime coin is also called the **half franc**. The **Fünfliber** has the highest value. It is also the largest and heaviest Swiss coin. The 1-centime piece has not been valid since **2007**.

The **5-centime piece** shines **golden-yellow**. All the other coins are **silvery**. That makes it easy to recognise the smallest coin quickly. The coins from half a franc upwards show **Helvetia**. She stands with a spear and shield and is a symbol of Switzerland.

**1 franc** has **100 centimes**. So you need **2** coins of 50 centimes for 1 franc. With 20-centime coins you need **5**, because 5 times 20 centimes is 100 centimes. With 10-centime coins you need **10**. And with 5-centime coins you even need 20.

A **2-franc coin** and **four 50-centime coins** are worth the same. Four times 50 centimes is 200 centimes, which is 2 francs. If you have a 1-franc coin and a 50-centime coin, together that makes **1 franc 50**. When counting, it is best to start with the big coins. That way it is quicker and you are less likely to miscount.

gewusst: A price such as 1 franc 50 is often written as “Fr. 1.50” or “CHF 1.50”.
Because there is no longer a 1-centime coin, amounts paid in cash are rounded to 5 centimes.

teile.einleitung: Cantonal banks are banks that belong wholly or mostly to a canton. They are meant to support the economy in their own canton. Many of them have a state guarantee.
wichtigste: A cantonal bank belongs wholly or mostly to a canton.
Almost every canton has its own cantonal bank.
They are meant to support the economy in the canton.
Many cantonal banks have a state guarantee.
With the state guarantee, the canton stands behind the bank’s obligations.
Part of the profits benefits the canton.

abschnitte.text: A **cantonal bank** is a bank that belongs wholly or for the most part to a **canton**. Almost every canton has its own, for example the Zurich, the Bern or the Lucerne cantonal bank. But some cantons no longer have a cantonal bank of their own. In 2024 there were 24 cantonal banks in Switzerland.

Cantonal banks have a **mandate**: they are meant to support the economy and the population in the canton. For example, they give **mortgages** for houses and loans to companies in the region. Many people have their savings account there. Part of the profit goes to the canton.

Many cantonal banks have a **state guarantee**. This means that if the bank gets into difficulties, the canton stands behind its obligations. This gives customers extra **security**. Not all cantonal banks have this guarantee to the same extent.

The first cantonal banks came into being in the **19th century**. At that time it was difficult for farmers and craftsmen to get cheap loans. That is why the cantons founded their own banks. Many of these banks are among the big banks of Switzerland today.

gewusst: Zürcher Kantonalbank is one of the largest banks in Switzerland.
Some cantonal banks also have shares on the stock exchange, but the canton usually keeps the majority.

teile.einleitung: Taking care (Sorgfalt) means looking after your things well. If you look after your things, you can use them for longer. That way you do not have to buy them new so often, and you save money.
wichtigste: Taking care means looking after your things well.
Things that are looked after last longer.
What lasts a long time does not need to be bought new so often.
That way you save money and protect the environment.
Small damage can often be repaired.

abschnitte.text: Taking care starts in everyday life. You put toys away after playing so that nobody treads on them. You do not leave books where they can get wet. When it rains, you put your **bike** under a roof, and you pump up the tyres. Pens get their caps back so that they do not dry out. That way things stay nice for a long time.

If something breaks, you do not have to throw it away straight away. A button can be sewn back on, and a hole in a bike tyre can be patched. In many Swiss municipalities there are **repair cafés**. There, volunteers help to repair clothes, appliances or toys. Repairing saves money and is often even fun.

If you look after your things well, you have to buy something new less often. The money stays in your **purse** or money box. It can then be used for something else you would like. It also helps the **environment** if less is thrown away.

gewusst: The first repair café opened in Amsterdam in 2009. Today there are meeting places like this in many countries.

teile.einleitung: Fully comprehensive insurance (Vollkasko) protects your own car even if you cause an accident yourself. It is voluntary, but it is usually required for leasing. It costs considerably more than liability insurance alone.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, motor vehicle liability insurance is compulsory.
Liability insurance pays for damage you cause to others.
Partial cover pays, for example, for theft, fire, hail and broken glass.
Fully comprehensive cover also pays for damage to your own car in a collision you caused yourself.
Leasing companies usually require fully comprehensive insurance.
The premium belongs in your budget.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who drives a car in Switzerland needs **motor vehicle liability insurance**. It is **compulsory**. It pays for damage you cause to **others**, for example to another car or when people are injured. But it does not pay for damage to your **own** car. For that there is **casco insurance**.

**Partial cover** (Teilkasko) is voluntary. It pays for damage to your own car that is not caused by a collision. This includes, for example, **theft**, **fire**, **hail**, flooding, **broken glass**, damage by martens or a collision with animals. Exactly what is covered is stated in the contract.

**Fully comprehensive cover** (Vollkasko) includes partial cover and also pays for **collision damage** to your own car. This applies even if you **caused** the accident **yourself**, for example by driving into a wall while parking. That is why it is the most expensive option. Often a **deductible** is agreed: you pay part of the damage yourself, and in return the premium is lower.

With **leasing**, the car does not belong to the person who drives it, but to the **leasing company**. It wants its car to be well protected. That is why it usually requires **fully comprehensive insurance**. This premium comes on top of the leasing instalments, petrol and servicing. Anyone who leases a car must definitely include it in their **budget**.

gewusst: For new cars, fully comprehensive insurance often makes sense; for very old cars it is less worthwhile.
Young new drivers often pay higher premiums because, statistically, they have more accidents.

teile.einleitung: Some bills come every month, but with a different amount, for example for electricity. With the direct debit system, called LSV in Switzerland, you do not have to pay them yourself. With your permission, the company takes the amount directly from your account.
wichtigste: LSV is the Swiss abbreviation for the direct debit system.
With LSV, the recipient takes the amount from your account with your permission.
For this you give the company written permission in advance.
This is convenient for changing amounts, for example electricity.
If a debit is wrong, you can object to it.
With a standing order, by contrast, you send the same amount yourself every time.

abschnitte.text: With the **direct debit system**, you give a company **permission** to take bill amounts directly from your account. The company then does not send you the bill to pay, but collects the money itself. You say that the account is **debited**. This is convenient because you cannot forget a payment. Typical examples are **electricity**, telephone or health insurance.

For a company to be allowed to take money, it needs an **authorisation**. This is a permission that you sign or confirm online. The bank then knows that this company may collect money. You can also **withdraw** the permission later. Without permission, nobody may simply take money from your account.

With **LSV**, the recipient fetches the money. That is why it is suitable for **changing amounts**. With a **standing order**, you yourself regularly send the **same amount**, for example the rent. With both, there must be enough money in the account. Otherwise the payment cannot be made or fees are charged.

Even if the money is taken automatically, you should check your **bank statement** regularly. If an amount is wrong, you can **object** to the debit within a certain time limit. The bank then pays the money back. In Switzerland, the direct debit system is gradually being replaced by **eBill**. With eBill, the bill arrives in your online banking and you approve it yourself.

gewusst: In Switzerland there were two kinds of direct debit: LSV+ for banks and a separate system for PostFinance.
The German word “Lastschrift” comes from the fact that the account is “charged” (belastet) with the amount.

teile.einleitung: eBill is an electronic bill that appears directly in e-banking. You no longer have to type anything in; you check the bill and approve it. In Switzerland almost all banks offer eBill.
wichtigste: With eBill, bills come straight into e-banking.
You check the bill and approve it or reject it.
The amount, recipient and reference are already filled in.
This saves time and prevents typing mistakes.
You can also set up automatic approval.

abschnitte.text: Companies such as health insurance funds, telephone providers or electricity companies can send their bills as **eBill**. To do this, you register once with the company in **e-banking**. After that, every new bill appears directly in your e-banking. You look at it and approve it with a click. If something is not right, you can also **reject** it.

With eBill, the **amount**, **recipient** and **reference number** are already filled in. You do not have to type in long numbers. This saves time and prevents **typing mistakes**. You can choose the payment date yourself, for example shortly before the payment deadline ends. And no paper or stamp is needed.

For regular bills you can set up **automatic approval**. Then e-banking pays the bill by itself, often up to a maximum amount that you set. This is practical, but you should still look at the bills from time to time. And there must always be enough money in the account.

gewusst: As well as eBill, Switzerland has the paper QR bill. In 2022 it replaced the old orange and red payment slips.
Anyone without e-banking can still pay bills at the post office counter or with a payment order.

teile.einleitung: A Sparkässeli is a small container into which you put coins and notes to save them. In Switzerland this is what people call a money box or piggy bank. With it, many children learn to put money aside.
wichtigste: Sparkässeli is the Swiss word for a money box.
You put money into it regularly, for example part of your pocket money.
If you do not open the Kässeli every day, you spend your savings less quickly.
That way the money slowly grows.
When there is a lot of money in it, you can take it to a savings account at the bank.

abschnitte.text: A **Sparkässeli** comes in many shapes: as a pig, a little house or a tin. At the top it has a **slot** for coins and notes. Some have a fastener at the bottom; others can hardly be opened at all. Many children are given their first Kässeli as a present, sometimes from a bank.

abschnitte.titel: Saving works better when it is closed
abschnitte.text: If you open the Kässeli every day, you see the money and may want to spend it straight away. If it stays closed, the **temptation** is smaller. The money slowly builds up. You can, for example, decide to open the Kässeli only once a month to count it. That way you can see how much has already been collected.

abschnitte.titel: From the Kässeli to the bank
abschnitte.text: When the Kässeli is full, you can take the money to a **savings account**. There it is kept safe and sometimes earns a little **interest**. Many banks invite people in at the end of October for **World Savings Day**. Then children bring their savings to the bank and often get a small present.

gewusst: World Savings Day was decided on in 1924 at an international meeting of savings banks in Milan.

teile.einleitung: A savings account is an account at a bank where you can keep money safely and save it. Unlike in a piggy bank, the money there is protected from loss and theft. Later you can withdraw it again, and often you even get interest for it.
wichtigste: A savings account is a bank account meant for saving.
The money is kept safe there, and you can withdraw it again later.
The bank pays interest on the money in the savings account.
Many banks offer special youth savings accounts with better conditions.
For children, the parents usually open the account.
In Switzerland, bank deposits of up to 100,000 francs per person and bank are specially protected.
From a savings account you often cannot withdraw as much as you like all at once.

abschnitte.text: A **savings account** is an account at a bank where you keep money for later. You can pay money into it, for example the money collected in your money box. When you need it, you can **withdraw** it again. In the past you got a savings book for this; today you usually see your balance in e-banking or in an app.

At the bank, the money is protected from theft, fire or being lost. In Switzerland there is also **deposit protection**. It guarantees that customers get back up to 100,000 francs per bank if a bank goes bust. So your savings are doubly protected.

The bank works with the money in the savings accounts and lends it, for example, to people who are buying a house. In return it pays the savers **interest**. How much depends greatly on the economic situation and on the National Bank’s policy rate. In recent years interest rates in Switzerland have been rather low, sometimes almost zero.

Many children are given a savings account at birth by their parents or godparents (Gotte or Götti). Banks offer special **youth savings accounts**, which often have slightly higher interest and no fees. For small children, the parents manage the account. As they get older, young people can have more say themselves.

A savings account is not meant for everyday use; for that there is the **private account** with a card. From a savings account you can often only withdraw a certain amount per month without giving notice. If you want more, you sometimes have to announce it weeks in advance. This is so that the money is really saved and not spent on impulse.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of money compartment at the bank where it is recorded how much money you have.
Money the bank pays you for keeping your money with it.
Protection so that you get your money back if a bank goes bust.
To take money out of your account, for example at the bank counter or a cash machine.

gewusst: In the past, every payment was entered by hand in a small savings book.
Gotte and Götti are the Swiss words for godmother and godfather, and they often pay something into their godchild’s savings account.
For a time, because of negative interest rates, some Swiss banks even charged fees instead of paying interest on very large deposits.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who buys a house or a flat usually borrows a large part of the money from a bank. This loan is called a **mortgage**. With a SARON mortgage, the interest depends on a reference rate of the Swiss money market.
wichtigste: SARON stands for Swiss Average Rate Overnight.
SARON is a reference rate of the Swiss money market.
The interest on a SARON mortgage keeps adjusting to the level of interest on the money market.
On top of SARON there is a fixed margin that the bank charges.
If market interest rates rise, the mortgage becomes more expensive; if they fall, it becomes cheaper.
In Switzerland, SARON has replaced the former reference rate Libor.

abschnitte.text: Banks often lend each other money for very short periods, for example overnight. This trading is called the **money market**. SARON shows the average interest for such deals in francs. It is recalculated every trading day and published by the Swiss stock exchange SIX. Because it is based on real deals, it is seen as a reliable benchmark.

With a SARON mortgage, the interest is made up of two parts: **SARON** and the bank's **margin**. The margin stays the same for the length of the contract. The SARON part is recalculated regularly, usually for the past few months. That is why you do not know in advance exactly how high the interest will be in a few years' time. Usually you sign a framework contract for several years.

abschnitte.titel: The role of the National Bank
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** (SNB) sets the key interest rate. It steers monetary policy so that SARON stays close to this key rate. If the SNB lowers the key rate, SARON usually falls too, and with it the interest on the mortgage. If it raises the rate, living with a SARON mortgage becomes more expensive.

Compared with a **fixed-rate mortgage**, where the interest stays the same for many years, a SARON mortgage can be cheaper if interest rates stay low. In return you carry an **interest rate risk**: if interest rates rise sharply, the costs rise too. That is why people with few reserves often prefer a fixed rate. Many people also combine both kinds.

gewusst: Libor was discontinued at the end of 2021; since then SARON has been the most important reference rate for francs in Switzerland.
Because SARON is linked to the key rate, it was also below zero during the period of negative interest rates.

teile.einleitung: Means of payment are everything you can pay with. As well as coins and notes, many people today pay with a card or their phone.
wichtigste: **Cash** means coins and banknotes.
In Switzerland, the **Swiss franc** is the official money.
With a **bank card** or an app on your phone, you can pay without cash.
Even when paying by card or phone, real money is taken from the account.
Bills are often paid by **bank transfer** or with the QR payment slip.
The Swiss National Bank issues the banknotes.

abschnitte.text: **Cash** consists of coins and banknotes. In Switzerland you pay with **francs** and **centimes** (Rappen): 100 centimes make one franc. The banknotes are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**, and the coins are made by the federal mint, Swissmint. With cash, you can see exactly how much you still have in your purse.

Many adults pay in shops with a **bank card** or a **credit card**. With a debit card, the money is taken straight from your own account. With a credit card you pay later, usually once a month. Often you just hold the card briefly to the machine at the till; this is called paying **contactlessly**.

You can also pay with an **app** on your phone. In Switzerland, for example, **TWINT** is widely used. With it you can pay in shops or send money to friends. Here, too, it is real money that leaves your account. Because you cannot see the money, it is easier to lose track of how much you have already spent.

Larger amounts such as rent or health insurance are usually paid by **bank transfer** from a bank account. In Switzerland there is the **QR bill** for this, with a square code that you can scan with your banking app. It has replaced the old red and orange payment slips. That way the money arrives safely without you having to carry cash.

gewusst: Before there were coins, people paid with shells, salt or livestock.
Since the ninth series, Swiss banknotes no longer show people, but themes such as water, wind or light.

teile.einleitung: On the internet, in magazines and on television you see a lot of advertising. Paid content is meant to be clearly recognisable. That is why it carries labels such as “advertising”, “advert” or “sponsored”.
wichtigste: The label “advertising” or “advert” shows that content has been paid for.
A company has paid for it or given something as a present.
Advertising must be distinguishable from the rest of the content.
In Switzerland, the Swiss Commission for Fairness, among others, keeps watch over this.
Influencers must also label paid posts.
The label helps you judge content critically.

abschnitte.text: If a post says **“advertising”**, **“advert”**, **“sponsored”** or **“paid partnership”**, there is a **company** behind it. It has paid for it or given the person something as a present. So the post is meant to sell something. This is not forbidden, but you should know about it.

You should be able to tell advertising apart from **information**. That is why the principle applies that advertising must be **recognisable**. In Switzerland, the **Unfair Competition Act** bans deceiving customers. The **Swiss Commission for Fairness** examines complaints about advertising and has set out principles. If you feel you have been deceived, you can contact it.

On social media, **influencers** often show products. If they are paid for it or are given the products as presents, they should **label** the post. Many platforms have their own feature for this. But sometimes the label is small or hidden. That is why it is worth looking closely.

Even if a post is labelled as advertising, it often seems like an honest recommendation. Ask yourself: **Who benefits** if I buy this? Do I really need it? On the internet, paid results are often right at the top of search engines, also with the label “ad”. The best is not always what comes first.

gewusst: Newspapers also have articles that look like normal reports but are paid for. They are called “Publireportage” (advertorial).
Some influencers earn their whole income from paid posts.

teile.einleitung: A bank works for people and companies that keep their money with it. These people are called customers. Even children can already be customers of a bank.
wichtigste: Anyone who has an account with a bank is a customer there.
Companies, clubs and municipalities can also be customers of a bank.
The bank must know who its customers are.
Customers pay fees for some of the bank's services.
In Switzerland you can freely choose which bank you are a customer of.

abschnitte.text: A person who keeps their money with a bank is called a **customer**. You are a customer, for example, if you have an **account**, use a card or have been given a loan. Even children with a **savings account** are already customers. Besides private individuals, **companies**, clubs and municipalities are also customers of banks.

When an account is opened, the bank checks an **identity document**. Because of the rules against **money laundering**, it must know who its customers are. At the same time, it must keep its customers' details **secret**. In Switzerland this is called **banking secrecy**. So the bank may not simply tell people how much money someone has.

The bank offers its customers various **services**. These include accounts, cards, **online banking**, loans and advice on saving. Customers pay **fees** for some services. For money in a savings account they sometimes receive **interest**. If you have questions, your **customer adviser** will help.

There are many banks in Switzerland, for example **cantonal banks**, Raiffeisen banks, big banks and **PostFinance**. You can freely choose which bank you want to be a customer of. Many people have accounts with more than one bank. If you are unhappy, you can **switch** banks. That is why banks make an effort for their customers.

gewusst: For disputes between customers and banks, Switzerland has an independent office, the Swiss Banking Ombudsman.
Almost every canton in Switzerland has its own cantonal bank.

teile.einleitung: A Lombard loan is a special way of borrowing money from a bank. Securities such as shares or bonds serve as collateral. This type of loan is used mainly by people who have already invested money.
wichtigste: A Lombard loan is a loan for which securities serve as a pledge.
Securities are, for example, shares and bonds.
The bank lends only part of the value of the securities.
If their value falls sharply, the bank can demand additional security.
The securities remain the customer's property, but are pledged.

abschnitte.text: With a **Lombard loan**, the bank lends money and receives a **pledge** in return. A pledge is a security that the bank may keep if the loan is not paid back. With a Lombard loan these are **securities**, for example **shares** or **bonds**. You say that the securities are **pledged**. They still belong to the customer.

The bank does not lend the full value of the securities. It works with a **lending value**. This is the part of the value that it considers safe. For shares whose prices go up and down, it is lower than for safe bonds. This gives the bank a buffer in case prices fall.

The value of securities can **fall** sharply. If it drops too low, the bank can demand **additional security**. The customer then has to provide more securities or money, or pay back part of the loan. If they do not, the bank may **sell** securities. This can lead to a loss.

The name is a reminder of **Lombardy**, a region in northern Italy. In the Middle Ages, many moneylenders who were active all over Europe came from there. They lent money against pledges. Today the Lombard loan is common mainly among people who already have a **securities account**.

gewusst: Many national banks used to have a special interest rate for such loans to banks, the Lombard rate.

teile.einleitung: A cooperative bank belongs to its members. Customers can buy shares and so have a say. In Switzerland, the Raiffeisen banks are the best-known example.
wichtigste: A cooperative bank is organised as a cooperative.
Customers can buy shares and become members.
The members are called cooperative members (Genossenschafter).
In a cooperative, each member usually has one vote, no matter how many shares they have.
The best-known cooperative bank in Switzerland is Raiffeisen.
Cooperative banks are often firmly rooted in their region.

abschnitte.text: A **cooperative** is an association of people who want to help each other. Instead of having a single owner, it belongs to all its **members** together. In Switzerland there are many cooperatives, for example for housing, shops or in farming. Banks can also be organised like this.

At a **cooperative bank** you can buy a **share certificate**. With it you become a member, a cooperative member. The members meet at the **general meeting** and vote on important questions. There, each member usually has exactly one vote.

The idea goes back to **Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen**, who lived in Germany in the 19th century. He wanted to help farmers and craftsmen get loans cheaply. In Switzerland, the first Raiffeisen savings and loan bank was founded in 1899 in **Bichelsee** in the canton of Thurgau. Today there are Raiffeisen banks in many municipalities in Switzerland.

Cooperative banks often work **regionally**. They know the people and companies in their area well. Their aim is not only profit, but also benefit for their members. Profits often stay in the bank or benefit the members.

gewusst: Other well-known Swiss companies, such as large retailers, are also organised as cooperatives.
Raiffeisen’s guiding idea was, in essence: what one person cannot achieve alone, many can.

teile.einleitung: Play money looks a bit like real money, but it is only meant for games. With it you can practise how paying and doing sums with money work. In real life, however, it is worth nothing.
wichtigste: Play money belongs to board games or to playing shop.
You cannot pay with it in a shop.
Real money in Switzerland is francs and centimes.
Real banknotes have special security features.
Play money is good for practising sums and paying.

abschnitte.text: Many board games have **play money**. With it you buy streets, houses or other things in the game. In a **toy shop** at home or at nursery school, people also go shopping with play money. It is fun and helps with sums. Whoever wins may have lots of play money at the end, but after the game it all goes back in the box.

abschnitte.titel: Why it does not count in a shop
abschnitte.text: Real money has value because everyone in a country accepts it as a means of payment. In Switzerland this is the **franc**, which is divided into 100 **centimes** (Rappen). The banknotes are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**. Play money, on the other hand, is simply printed by a games company. That is why the cashier may not accept it.

Real banknotes are hard to copy. They have **security features**, for example pictures that change when you tilt the note, or places you can feel. Play money deliberately looks different so that nobody mixes them up. Anyone who copies real money in order to pay with it is making **counterfeit money**. That is forbidden and is punished.

Play money is a good **learning aid**. You can practise how much change you get when you pay with a note. You also learn that you can only spend money once. If you spend everything straight away in the game, you have nothing left later. This experience also helps with your real pocket money.

gewusst: Many schools use play money so that children can practise doing sums with francs and centimes.
There are games in which you buy whole cities with play money, but in real life not a single bread roll.

teile.einleitung: When you pay by card, you use a bank card instead of cash. The money is taken from your own account and credited to the shop. This is practical, but it is easier to lose track of your spending.
wichtigste: When you pay by card, the money is taken from your own account.
The bank transfers the amount to the shop.
With a debit card, the money is taken from your account immediately or very soon.
With a credit card, you pay later with a monthly bill.
Because you cannot see the money, you notice less how much you are spending.
Money on a card is real money too.

abschnitte.text: In the shop, you hold the card against the **card terminal** or insert it. Sometimes you enter your **PIN**. The terminal asks the bank whether there is enough money in the account. Then the amount is taken from the **account** and credited to the shop.

There are different kinds of card. With a **debit card**, the money is taken directly from your account. With a **credit card**, the card company collects all your payments and sends you a **bill** at the end of the month. If you do not pay it on time, you have to pay high interest.

With a card, you do not need to carry cash. You do not need change and can pay exact amounts. Later you can see all your **payments** in the app. If you lose the card, you can have it blocked, whereas lost cash is usually gone for good.

Because the money flows away **invisibly**, you notice less how much you are spending. That makes it easier to lose **track**. It helps to check your balance regularly or to make a **budget**. That way you keep your money under control.

gewusst: In Switzerland today, a large share of shopping in stores is paid for by card or mobile phone.
You can often pay with a mobile phone or a watch too; behind this there is usually a stored card.

teile.einleitung: Bitcoin is the first and best-known cryptocurrency, a digital money that exists only on the internet. It is not issued by a bank or a state, but managed by a worldwide computer network. Its value can go up and down a lot, and there is no deposit protection.
wichtigste: Bitcoin is a digital currency that was launched in 2009.
Bitcoin was invented by a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto.
All payments are stored in a public list, the blockchain.
There can be at most 21 million bitcoins.
The value of Bitcoin can go up and down a lot.
There is no deposit protection for Bitcoin as there is for a bank account.
Anyone who loses their access keys also loses their bitcoins.

abschnitte.text: **Bitcoin** is a **cryptocurrency**, money that consists only of data and is secured with encryption. There are no coins or notes, even though pictures often show a golden coin. Bitcoin is kept in a digital purse, the **wallet**. Bitcoin can also be divided into small parts; the smallest unit is called a satoshi.

In 2008, an unknown person or group using the name **Satoshi Nakamoto** published a plan for a new digital money. In January 2009 the Bitcoin network started running. To this day nobody knows for certain who Satoshi Nakamoto really is. The idea was to be able to send money directly from person to person without banks or states.

All Bitcoin payments are stored in the **blockchain**, a kind of public cash book that is kept on thousands of computers around the world. The entries are grouped into blocks that are linked together, hence the name. New bitcoins come into being through **mining**, in which computers solve difficult calculations. This uses a great deal of electricity, which is often criticised.

The price of a bitcoin has changed enormously since 2009, with big gains but also violent crashes. Within a few days the value can fall by a quarter or more. Unlike money in a Swiss bank account, bitcoins are not protected by **deposit protection**. If a crypto exchange goes bust or you forget your password, the money can be gone for ever.

Because of the many companies from the blockchain industry, the region around Zug is called **Crypto Valley**. Since 2016, small administrative fees in the town of Zug can be paid in Bitcoin. The city of Lugano is also a strong supporter of Bitcoin. Cryptocurrencies are not official legal tender in Switzerland; only the Swiss franc is.

begriffe.erklaerung: Digital money that is secured with encryption.
A public, linked list of all payments.
A digital purse for cryptocurrencies.
Creating new bitcoins through calculations done by computers.

gewusst: In May 2010, a programmer in the USA bought two pizzas for 10,000 bitcoins; this is considered the first purchase made with Bitcoin.
The reward for mining halves about every four years; this is called halving.
In 2021, El Salvador became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender.

teile.einleitung: A stock exchange is a marketplace where securities such as shares are bought and sold. The price, known as the share price, comes about there from supply and demand.
wichtigste: Securities such as shares are traded on the stock exchange.
The price comes about from supply and demand.
Switzerland’s most important stock exchange is the SIX Swiss Exchange in Zurich.
The SMI shows how the shares of 20 large Swiss companies are doing.
Today trading is done almost entirely electronically.
Private individuals usually trade on the stock exchange through a bank.

abschnitte.text: At a **stock exchange**, buyers and sellers of **securities** meet. These are, for example, **shares**, meaning parts of a company, or **bonds**, with which you lend money to a company or a state. If many people want to buy a share, its price rises. If many want to sell, it falls. This price is called the **share price**.

Switzerland’s most important stock exchange is the **SIX Swiss Exchange** in Zurich. In the past, traders stood in a hall and called out their offers to each other. Today trading is done almost entirely by **computer**. Private individuals usually buy and sell shares through their bank or a trading platform. For this you need a **securities account**.

The **Swiss Market Index**, **SMI** for short, is a share index. It shows how the share prices of the 20 largest companies on the Swiss stock exchange are doing overall. If the SMI rises, these shares have on average become worth more. On the news you often hear whether the SMI has risen or fallen. Other well-known indices are the Dow Jones in the USA or the DAX in Germany.

Share prices can **go up and down** a lot. You can win money with shares, but you can also lose it. That is why people who invest on the stock exchange often spread their money across many companies. Experts advise only investing money that you will not need for a long time. A big fall in prices is also called a **crash**.

gewusst: The Amsterdam stock exchange from the 17th century is considered one of the first stock exchanges in today’s sense.
The German word Börse goes back to the van der Beurse merchant family in Bruges, in front of whose house traders met.

teile.einleitung: Money does not fall from the sky. Most adults earn it through their work and get wages for it. With these wages they pay for what the family needs to live.
wichtigste: For work you get wages.
With the wages, the family pays for housing, food and much more.
Contributions, for example for the AVS, are deducted from gross pay.
What is left is called net pay.
Apprentices also get wages.
Young people may do light work from the age of 13.

abschnitte.text: Adults work, for example, in an office, in a hospital, on a building site or in a shop. For their work they get **wages**, usually every month. People who are self-employed and have their own company earn money by selling goods or services. With the money they earn, the family pays for **rent**, **food**, **clothes**, insurance and free time.

The wage stated in the contract is called **gross pay**. Contributions are deducted from it, for example for the **AVS**, unemployment insurance and the pension fund. What arrives in the account is the **net pay**. From this money you later also pay **taxes**. That is why less is left over than you might first think.

Anyone who does a **vocational apprenticeship** after school already gets an **apprentice’s wage**. It is smaller than the wages of trained professionals and usually rises with each year of the apprenticeship. Depending on their job, training and experience, people earn different amounts.

Young people can already earn something too. In Switzerland, from the age of **13**, they may do **light work**, for example running errands or helping with babysitting. There are rules for this to protect young people. That way you notice how much work goes into one franc, and you value money more.

gewusst: As well as their monthly salary, many Swiss people get a 13th month’s salary.
Not all important work is paid: many people cook, clean and look after children at home without wages.

teile.einleitung: Banknotes are notes of money that you can pay with. In Switzerland there are six different notes, each with its own value, its own colour and its own theme.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there are 6 banknotes.
The values are 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs.
The smallest note is the 10-franc note, the largest the 1000-franc note.
For 5 francs there is no note, but a coin.
Glittering areas are security features against forgers.
Ten 10-franc notes or five 20-franc notes are worth as much as one 100-franc note.

abschnitte.text: Each Swiss note has its own **colour**. The **10-franc note** is yellow, the **20-franc note** red, the **50-franc note** green and the **100-franc note** blue. The **200-franc note** is brown, the **1000-franc note** purple. If you know the colours, you can quickly find the right note in your purse.

Banknotes are good for practising sums. Ten 10-franc notes together make 100 francs, because 10 times 10 is 100. Five 20-franc notes are also 100 francs. Two 50-franc notes also make a hundred. A 1000-franc note is worth as much as ten 100-franc notes.

The current series shows **the many sides of Switzerland**. Each note has a theme: the 10-franc note stands for time, the 20-franc note for light, the 50-franc note for wind. The 100-franc note shows water, the 200-franc note matter and the 1000-franc note language. Each note also shows a globe.

In some places the notes glitter and shimmer. These are **security features**. They change when you tilt the note and are very hard to copy. There are also signs that you can only see when holding the note up to the light. That is how the National Bank protects the notes against **forgers**.

gewusst: For 5 francs there is a large coin in Switzerland, the “Fünfliber”.
Every Swiss note of the ninth series shows a hand.

teile.einleitung: A savings picture is a picture of what you are saving for. You hang it on the wall, for example, or stick it on your money box. It reminds you of your goal every day and helps you keep going.
wichtigste: A savings picture shows what you are saving for.
If you see your goal every day, you think about it more often.
That makes it easier not to spend the money on other things.
You can draw the picture yourself or cut it out.
A progress bar on the picture shows how much you have already saved.

abschnitte.text: Saving takes **patience**. Sometimes you see something nice in a shop and want to spend the money straight away. A savings picture reminds you that you actually want something else. If it hangs somewhere you often walk past, you think about your **savings goal** more often. That way it is easier to keep going.

abschnitte.titel: How to make your savings picture
abschnitte.text: Draw your goal or cut out a picture from a brochure. Write the **price** next to it and the date by which you would like to have it. Next to it you can draw a **bar** or a ladder. Every time you put money in your money box, you colour in a piece of it. That way you can see how you are getting closer to your goal.

gewusst: People often pursue goals that they write down or make visible more consistently than goals they only keep in their heads.
