teile.einleitung: When you order online, you often pay not only for the goods but also for delivery. These delivery costs can quickly make a bargain more expensive. That is why you always include them when comparing.
wichtigste: You pay delivery costs for packing and sending.
They always belong in a price comparison.
Some shops deliver free above a minimum amount.
With orders from abroad, customs duty and VAT can be added.
Returns can also cost something.

abschnitte.text: When an online shop sends something, the goods have to be **packed** and **delivered** by Swiss Post or a courier. That costs money. The customer often pays these **delivery costs** on top of the price of the goods. They usually only appear in the shopping basket or just before you pay.

A T-shirt costs 15 francs online, and delivery costs 8 francs. Together that is **23 francs**. In the shop, the same T-shirt costs 20 francs. So the shop is **cheaper**, even though the online price looked lower at first. When comparing, what always counts is the **total price** you really pay in the end.

Many shops offer **free delivery** above a certain amount. This can be practical, but it tempts you to buy more than planned. If you add something just to get free delivery, you often end up spending more. Sometimes it is worth combining orders with your family.

With orders from **abroad**, further costs can be added. Switzerland often charges **VAT** and sometimes **customs duty**. On top of that comes a **fee** for customs clearance by Swiss Post or the courier. That way a cheap offer can suddenly become much more expensive. **Sending things back** abroad is also often expensive.

gewusst: With small orders from abroad, the customs clearance fees can be higher than the VAT itself.
Many shops let you order online and collect the goods free of charge in the shop.

teile.einleitung: A children's account is a bank account specially for young people. Many banks offer one so that children learn early on how to handle money. Often the parents open the account together with the child.
wichtigste: A children's account or youth account is an account for young people.
Many banks offer such accounts, often without fees.
For young children, the parents help to open the account.
You can save pocket money and gifts in the account.
Having your own account teaches you how to handle money.

abschnitte.text: Instead of leaving all your money in your **piggy bank**, you can put it into a **children's account**. There it is kept safe. The bank records exactly how much money belongs to you. Sometimes you even get a little **interest**.

Young children cannot open an account on their own. For that they need their **parents** or other **legal guardians**. They go to the bank with the child or do it online. The parents help and keep an eye on things until the child is older.

With your own account, you learn to plan how to use your money. You see how your balance grows when you save. But you also notice that money is gone once you spend it. This experience helps you later when you make a **budget**.

A children's account often receives **pocket money** and gifts of money from grandparents or godparents. Some parents pay in a small amount regularly. As you get older, you often get a **card** with it. Later it becomes a youth account and finally a normal account.

gewusst: Many banks give children a small money box or a little present when they open an account.
Even a few francs a month add up to a nice sum over many years.

teile.einleitung: Advertising is meant to make people aware of a product, a service or an idea and to get them to buy. We come across it everywhere: on posters, on television, on the internet and on social media. If you know how advertising works, you can decide better what you really need.
wichtigste: Advertising wants to attract attention and tempt you to buy.
It can create wishes that lead to spontaneous, unplanned purchases.
Advertising often works with feelings, music, colours and famous people.
On the internet, advertising is often tailored exactly to one person.
Influencers must label paid advertising.
Many free services on the internet are financed by advertising.
If you sleep on it before buying, you buy less on impulse.

abschnitte.text: **Advertising** is a message that is paid for in order to persuade people. Companies advertise products such as chocolate, phones or clothes. Parties, clubs and charities also advertise, for example for a vote or a fundraising campaign. Advertising is part of **marketing**, meaning all the measures a company uses to sell its products.

Advertising often appeals to our **feelings**, for example with happy families, funny animals or cool sports stars. Catchy tunes and slogans make sure that you remember a brand. Often the impression is given that you will belong if you have the product. That is how wishes arise that you did not have before, and it leads to **impulse buys**.

On the internet, companies collect data about what someone looks at, searches for or buys. From this comes **personalised advertising**, which matches a person’s interests exactly. On platforms such as Instagram, TikTok or YouTube, **influencers** show products, often for payment. Posts like these must be recognisable as advertising, for example with the label “advertising” or “advert”.

In Switzerland, the **Unfair Competition Act** bans misleading advertising. If you think an advert is unfair, you can complain to the **Swiss Commission for Fairness**. Special restrictions apply to alcohol and tobacco, above all to protect children and young people. With a “No advertising please” sticker on your letterbox, you can stop advertising leaflets.

Before buying, it helps to ask: Do I really need this, or do I only want it because I have seen it? A good trick is to write a wish down and wait a few days. Often the interest is already smaller by then. A **budget**, which says how much money you can spend on free time and wishes, also helps.

begriffe.erklaerung: A short, catchy advertising phrase.
A spontaneous purchase without planning beforehand.
A person on social media who has many followers and often advertises products.
The people an advert wants to reach.

gewusst: Even in ancient Pompeii there were painted adverts on the walls of houses.
Advertising meant to appeal to children is often placed at children’s eye level in shops, for example by the till.
Many apps are only free because they earn money from advertising.

teile.einleitung: Bank staff are the people who work in a bank. They help at the counter, advise customers and make sure behind the scenes that payments work.
wichtigste: At the counter, bank staff help with paying in, withdrawing and with questions.
Customer advisers explain accounts, saving and investing.
Many bank staff work behind the scenes, for example in IT.
In Switzerland, people often learn the job through a commercial apprenticeship at a bank.
Bank staff must keep their customers’ data confidential.

abschnitte.titel: At the counter and in advice
abschnitte.text: At the **counter**, bank staff take in cash, pay out money and answer questions. In **advice** sessions, they show which account suits you and how to save or invest money. Some also help with a mortgage for a house. Many bank branches have fewer counters today, because a lot can be done at a machine or in e-banking.

As a customer, you never see many of the people in a bank. They work, for example, in **IT**, check loans, look after payments abroad or make sure that laws are followed. This work is often called **compliance**. Security experts are also important, so that fraudsters have no chance.

In Switzerland, many people start with an **apprenticeship** as a commercial employee at a bank. Later they can go on to further training, for example at a university of applied sciences. All bank staff have an important duty: they may not pass on anything about their customers’ accounts. This is called **banking secrecy** (bank client confidentiality), and it is laid down in the Banking Act.

gewusst: A real bank employee will never ask you for your password or PIN by email or phone.
In Switzerland, banks are among the important employers.

teile.einleitung: A tip is a small amount that you pay voluntarily on top to say thank you. You give it, for example, in a restaurant or at the hairdresser’s. In Switzerland it is not compulsory.
wichtigste: A tip is a voluntary thank you for good service.
With “keep the change”, the staff may keep the change.
In Switzerland, service is already included in the price.
Many people simply round the amount up a little.
Other countries have other customs.

abschnitte.text: A **tip** is given to people who serve us, for example waiters, taxi drivers or hairdressers. You give it if you were happy. The German word Trinkgeld, “drink money”, comes from the fact that people used to give someone a little money so that they could buy themselves something to drink. Today it is simply a small **thank you**.

If a meal costs 37 francs and Dad gives 40 francs, he can say: “**Keep the change**.” That means the waiter may keep the 3 francs change. You can also name an amount, for example: “Make it 40.” When paying by card, the machine sometimes asks directly whether you would like to give a tip.

In Switzerland, **service is included in the price**. So the staff get a wage and do not depend on tips. That is why tipping is **voluntary**. Many people still round up if they were happy. If the service was bad, you do not have to give anything.

In some countries, tips are much more important. In the **USA**, for example, restaurant wages are often low, and a considerably higher tip is expected. In **Japan**, on the other hand, tipping is unusual and can even be considered rude. So if you are travelling, it is best to find out beforehand.

gewusst: In many restaurants, the tips are shared among the whole team at the end of the day, including the kitchen.
In French, a tip is called “pourboire”, which literally means “for drinking”.

teile.einleitung: A youth account is a bank account especially for children and teenagers. It usually costs little or nothing and cannot go into the red. That way you learn to handle money independently.
wichtigste: Many banks offer youth accounts for children and teenagers.
They are often free of fees or very cheap.
A youth account usually cannot be overdrawn.
If there is not enough money in the account, a payment is refused.
There is often a card for young people with it.
Above a certain age, the account is usually converted into a private account.

abschnitte.text: A **youth account** is tailored to the needs of young people. You can collect **pocket money** (Sackgeld), presents or, later, your apprentice’s wage in it. Many banks charge no **account fee** for it. Some even offer slightly better interest.

With a normal account you can sometimes spend more than there is in it. This is called **overdrawing**, and it costs interest. Youth accounts usually **cannot be overdrawn**. If there is no money left, the payment is refused. That way you cannot get into debt on the account.

A youth account often comes with a **debit card**. With it you can pay in shops and withdraw cash at a cash machine. With an **app** you can see at any time how much is still in the account. With younger children, parents can often see it too.

Youth accounts only apply up to a certain **age**, which differs from bank to bank. After that the account is usually converted into a normal **private account**. Then other conditions apply, for example new fees. It is worth comparing the offers again at that point.

gewusst: In Switzerland, a child may in principle decide for themselves about wages they have earned.
Many banks offer special accounts for students and apprentices that stay cheap for longer.

teile.einleitung: With payment in advance, you pay for goods before you receive them. This is common with well-known retailers, but risky with unknown online shops. If the goods never arrive, the money is often lost.
wichtigste: Payment in advance means: pay first, then delivery.
The person who pays bears the risk.
There are fake online shops that never deliver.
It is safer to pay on invoice, after receiving the goods.
Before buying, check the shop, for example its legal notice.
If an offer is far too cheap, be careful.

abschnitte.text: With **payment in advance**, you transfer the money before the goods are sent. That way the retailer does not have to bear any risk. Instead, the risk lies with the **customer**: if nothing arrives or the goods are broken, she has to sort out getting her money back. With well-known shops this usually works without any problems.

On the internet there are **fake shops**. They look like real shops but never deliver anything. They often lure people with **very low prices** and ask for payment in advance. Once the money has been transferred, it is almost impossible to get it back. The fraudsters are often abroad and hard to find.

Before buying, a quick check is worth it. Is there a **legal notice** with an address and phone number? Are the **reviews** from other customers genuine, and can they also be found on other sites? Does the shop only offer payment in advance? Then you need to be especially careful. If in doubt, ask an adult for advice.

The safest way is buying on **invoice**: you only pay once the goods have arrived. With **credit cards**, you can in some cases claim back a payment. **Cash on delivery**, where you pay the postman, is also possible. With unknown shops, you should never pay in advance by bank transfer.

gewusst: On classified ad platforms, too, there are fraudsters who ask for payment in advance and then disappear.
Anyone who has fallen victim to a fake shop can report it to the police.

teile.einleitung: A cash machine is a machine where you can withdraw cash with your bank card. In Switzerland people usually call it a Bancomat; elsewhere it is called a cash machine or cashpoint. If you know a few rules, you can withdraw money safely and cheaply.
wichtigste: At a cash machine you withdraw cash from your own account with your card and PIN.
If a machine looks strange, do not use it and tell the bank.
With skimming, fraudsters copy card data with hidden devices.
At your own bank, withdrawing is usually free; at other banks’ machines it can cost something.
After withdrawing, put your card and money away straight away.
Always cover your PIN with your hand when typing it.

abschnitte.text: You put your **bank card** into the machine or, with some machines, just hold it against it. Then you type in your secret **PIN** and choose the amount. The cash machine checks whether there is enough money in the account and gives out the notes. The amount is taken from the account. In Switzerland, cash machines are found at banks, at railway stations and in shopping centres.

With **skimming**, fraudsters fit a reading device over the card slot. It copies the card’s data. Often they also hide a small camera that films the PIN. With the data they make fake cards. A loose card slot, a keypad that has been placed on top or traces of glue are warning signs. Then the rule is: hands off and tell the bank.

At **your own bank**, withdrawing is usually free of charge. At other banks’ machines, some banks charge a **fee**. Costs often arise abroad too, sometimes with extra charges for changing into another currency. If you know your bank’s fees, you can save money. The exact prices are in the bank’s price list.

When typing, cover the keys with your hand. If someone is standing very close, wait or ask them to keep their **distance**. After withdrawing, take your card first, then the money, and put both away straight away. You can count it later in a safe place. If the machine keeps your card, tell the bank immediately.

gewusst: The world’s first cash machines came into use in the 1960s.
Many cash machines show their instructions in several languages.

teile.einleitung: A bond is one way of investing money. You lend money to a company or the state and receive interest in return. At the end of the term you get the amount back, provided the borrower is able to pay.
wichtigste: A bond is a loan to a company or the state.
In return you regularly receive interest.
At the end of the term you get the amount back.
The biggest risk is that the borrower cannot pay it back.
Unreliable borrowers have to pay higher interest.
In Swiss German, a bond is called an “Obligation” or “Anleihe”.

abschnitte.text: With a **bond**, you lend money. The **borrower** is a **company**, a **canton**, a town or the **Confederation**. It needs money, for example for new factories, roads or railway lines. Instead of taking out a loan from a bank, it issues bonds. Another word for a bond in German is **Anleihe**.

For the money you lend, you regularly receive **interest**, usually once a year. It is also called the **coupon**. Every bond has a fixed **term**, for example five or ten years. At the end of the term you get the original amount back. But this only applies if the borrower is able to pay.

The biggest risk is that the **borrower cannot pay back** the money. If a company or a state gets into **financial difficulties**, you lose part or all of it. That is why **unreliable borrowers** pay higher interest. Safe borrowers such as the **Swiss Confederation** pay lower interest. Experts assess how safe they are with a **rating**.

If you buy a **share**, you become a **part-owner** of a company. If you buy a **bond**, on the other hand, you are a **lender**. The value of shares usually goes up and down more. Bonds are often seen as a calmer investment. But bonds can also be traded on the stock exchange, and their price can change.

gewusst: The Swiss Confederation also issues bonds. They are called federal bonds.
When interest rates rise in general, the market price of existing bonds with lower interest falls.

teile.einleitung: A pocket money notebook is a small notebook in which you write down how much money you get and what you spend it on. That way you can always see how much is left. This helps you divide up your money well.
wichtigste: The pocket money notebook lists income and spending.
Income is, for example, pocket money or presents.
Spending is everything you buy.
That way you can see where your money goes.
With the notebook you can also plan for saving.

abschnitte.text: In a **pocket money notebook** you write the date, what the money was for and how much it was. Money you get is **income**, for example your pocket money or money from your grandmother. Money you spend is **spending**, for example on an exercise book, an ice cream or a present. At the end you work out how much is left.

Many people do not know exactly where their money goes. Small expenses are quickly forgotten. If you write everything down, you see it in black and white. Perhaps you notice that you spend a lot on sweets. Then you can decide for yourself whether you want to change that.

With the notebook you can also **plan**. If you want to buy something bigger, you write down a **savings goal**. Then every week you can see how close you already are to your goal. Adults do the same thing with a **budget**. If you practise early, it will be easier later with your wages.

gewusst: A pocket money notebook is really a small set of accounts, like the ones companies keep.
Instead of a notebook, you can also use a simple spreadsheet or an app.

teile.einleitung: A bank statement is an overview from the bank that shows all the money coming into and going out of an account. On it you can see who sent money, what was paid for and how much money is left. If you read your bank statements regularly, you stay in control of your money.
wichtigste: A bank statement shows all the money coming into and going out of your account.
It contains the date, description and amount of every transaction.
At the end is the current account balance.
Credits increase the balance, debits reduce it.
Today, bank statements usually come as a PDF in online banking.
By checking, you discover mistakes or fraud in good time.
You should keep important bank statements for a few years.

abschnitte.text: A **bank statement** is a list of all the transactions in a bank account over a certain period, for example a month. Each **transaction** shows when money came in or went out, how much it was and from whom or to whom. At the very top there is often the balance at the start, and at the very bottom the balance at the end. This way you can follow exactly how the money has changed.

When money comes into the account, it is called a **credit**, for example your wages or pocket money. When money goes out, it is called a **debit**, for example when you pay by card or withdraw cash at a cash machine. On the statement, the two are often in separate columns. The amount left at the end is called the **balance**.

In the past, the bank sent bank statements by post, or you printed them out at a machine in the branch. Today they can usually be downloaded as a PDF document in **online banking** or in the banking app. In the app you can even see every transaction straight away, not only at the end of the month. If you like, you can still order the statement on paper, often for a fee.

If you read your bank statement regularly, you quickly notice what your money has been spent on. This helps you stick to your **budget**. You also discover mistakes, double charges or subscriptions you have forgotten about. If an unknown payment appears, you should contact the bank immediately, because it could be **fraud**.

Bank statements are important **records**, for example for your tax return. In Switzerland, the tax authorities sometimes ask for proof of account balances at the end of the year. For this, the bank often sends a separate statement of interest and capital at the start of the year. In Switzerland, companies must keep business records for ten years.

begriffe.erklaerung: The amount in the account, meaning how much money there is in it.
Money that comes into the account.
Money that goes out of the account.
A single entry about a payment in the account.

gewusst: A minus sign in front of the balance means that the account is overdrawn.
For card payments, the bank statement often shows the name of the shop and the place.
In the past, many bank branches had special machines for printing bank statements.

teile.einleitung: Deposit protection protects bank customers’ money if a bank goes bust. In Switzerland, deposits of up to 100,000 francs per person and bank are protected. So savers do not have to be afraid of losing their savings.
wichtigste: Deposit protection protects bank deposits if a bank goes bankrupt.
In Switzerland, up to 100,000 francs per person and bank are protected.
It is organised by esisuisse, a joint body of the Swiss banks.
All banks in Switzerland must take part.
The protected money is to be paid out within a few days.
Securities such as shares belong to the customer and do not become part of the bankrupt estate.
Cryptocurrencies on platforms are usually not protected by deposit protection.

abschnitte.text: Money that you pay into an account at a bank is called a **deposit**. The bank works with this money; for example, it lends it on as loans. If the bank goes bust, customers could lose their money. **Deposit protection** makes sure that at least part of the deposits is still paid back.

In Switzerland, deposits of up to **100,000 francs** per person and per bank are protected. If someone has 30,000 francs in their account, all of it is protected. If someone has 150,000 francs at the same bank, only 100,000 francs are safe. That is why people with a lot of money can spread it across several banks.

Deposit protection is organised by **esisuisse**, an association based in Basel. All banks and securities firms with a head office or branch in Switzerland must be members. If a bank fails, the other banks pay into the protection scheme together. Supervision of the banks is the job of the financial market supervisory authority **FINMA**.

In the past, only 30,000 francs per customer were specially protected in Switzerland. During the worldwide **financial crisis**, the amount was raised to 100,000 francs at the end of 2008. Since 2023, new rules have applied that provide for faster payment, within seven working days of FINMA’s decision. That way customers are meant to get their money back quickly.

Deposit protection applies to credit balances in accounts such as private, savings and salary accounts. **Securities** such as shares or fund units are not part of it, but they belong to the customer and are handed over in the event of bankruptcy. Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies on trading platforms are usually not protected at all. Nor does deposit protection make up for losses caused by falling share prices.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that you pay into a bank account.
When a company can no longer pay its debts and is wound up.
The organisation that runs deposit protection in Switzerland.
The authority that supervises the banks in Switzerland.

gewusst: Many EU countries also protect bank deposits up to 100,000 euros.
Deposit protection is also meant to prevent all customers from withdrawing their money at the same time out of fear, which is known as a bank run.
Pillar 3a savings are protected up to 100,000 francs in addition to and separately from a normal account.

teile.einleitung: E-banking means doing your banking on a computer, tablet or phone. You can see your account balance, pay bills and transfer money without going to the bank.
wichtigste: In e-banking you can see your account balance and all account movements.
You can pay bills and transfer money.
You type the address in yourself or use the bank’s official app.
After e-banking, always log out properly.
Public or other people’s computers are not suitable for e-banking.
With eBill, bills come straight into e-banking.

abschnitte.text: In **e-banking** you can see how much money is in your account and which **payments** have come in and gone out. You can **pay bills**, transfer money to another account or set up a **standing order**, for example for the rent. Many banks offer an app for this; this is also called **mobile banking**.

To log in you usually need a username, a **password** and a second step, such as a code or a confirmation in an app. This is called **two-factor authentication**. You type the bank’s address in yourself or use the official app. Links in emails or text messages can lead to fake websites. Memory aid: type it yourself instead of clicking.

abschnitte.titel: Logging out and your own device
abschnitte.text: After e-banking, always **log out properly**. Otherwise someone else could carry on using the same device. It is best to do your banking only on **your own device**. On public computers, for example in an internet café, **malware** could read passwords. You also keep the operating system and the app up to date.

With **eBill**, bills come straight into your e-banking. You check them and approve them for payment with a click. Paper bills in Switzerland have a **QR code**. You can scan it with your phone camera in the banking app, and then all the details are already filled in. That way fewer typing mistakes happen.

gewusst: eBill is a service of the Swiss banks and is used by a great many companies.
A real bank never sends a link through which you are supposed to enter your password.

teile.einleitung: An investment fund is like a big pot into which many people put their money. This money is then invested in many different shares, bonds or other investments. That way, even with little money, you can invest in a widely spread way.
wichtigste: In an **investment fund**, the money of many investors is pooled.
The money is invested in many different **securities**.
Because it is spread out, the **risk** is smaller than with a single share.
Anyone who joins buys **fund units**.
You pay **fees** for the management.
In Switzerland, **FINMA** supervises the funds.

abschnitte.titel: Not all your eggs in one basket
abschnitte.text: If you put all your money into a single company, you lose a lot if that company does badly. A fund spreads the money across many companies or countries. This is called **diversification**, meaning spreading. If one investment falls, others may rise and make up for the loss. That is why people say: don’t put all your eggs in one basket.

With many funds, **experts** decide which shares or bonds the money goes into. Other funds simply follow a fixed rule, for example an **index** such as the SMI. Funds like these are often called **index funds** or **ETFs** and are traded on the stock exchange. They usually have lower fees, because there is less work involved.

Anyone who invests in a fund buys **units**. If the value of the investments in the fund rises, the value of the units rises too. If it falls, the units lose value. So a fund is not without risk, but the risk is spread more widely. Many people use a **fund savings plan** to save a small amount every month.

In Switzerland, the **Collective Investment Schemes Act** governs funds, and the financial market supervisory authority **FINMA** supervises them. The money in a fund counts as **segregated assets**. This means that if the fund company goes bust, the money still belongs to the investors. Fees and risks must be looked at carefully before buying.

gewusst: ETF stands for “exchange-traded fund”.
Pension funds also invest the money for retirement provision in a widely spread way.

teile.einleitung: The IBAN is the international account number. With it, a transfer finds its way to the right account, in Switzerland and abroad. A Swiss IBAN has 21 characters and begins with CH.
wichtigste: IBAN stands for International Bank Account Number.
A Swiss IBAN has 21 characters and begins with CH.
After CH come two check digits, then the bank’s number and the account number.
The check digits help to spot typing mistakes.
You may pass on your IBAN; nobody can withdraw money with it.
For a payment you need the IBAN and the name of the recipient.

abschnitte.text: Every bank account has its own **IBAN**. It works like an address: anyone who wants to send you money needs it. The IBAN is used in Europe and in many other countries. That way payments arrive reliably even across national borders.

A Swiss IBAN has **21 characters**. At the beginning is the **country code**, **CH** for Switzerland, **LI** for Liechtenstein. After that come two **check digits**. Then comes the number of the **bank** and finally the actual **account number**.

The two check digits are calculated from the other characters using a fixed rule. If you make a typing mistake when entering it, the calculation no longer works out. **E-banking** usually notices the mistake straight away and reports it. That way the money does not end up in the wrong account by accident.

abschnitte.titel: Share it, but never your PIN
abschnitte.text: You may pass on your IBAN, for example to your employer or to friends. With it, people can only **pay money in**, not take any out. It is quite different with your **PIN** and **passwords**: they always stay secret. No bank ever asks for them by phone or email.

In Switzerland there is the **QR bill**. It contains a code that you can scan with your phone. Among other things, it contains the IBAN and the name of the recipient. That way you no longer have to type in the number.

gewusst: The length of the IBAN differs from country to country; a German IBAN, for example, has 22 characters.
Liechtenstein uses francs, but it has its own country code in the IBAN, LI.

teile.einleitung: If a bank card is stolen, you must have it blocked immediately. The sooner this happens, the less damage can be done. You can do it through a card-blocking number or directly in the bank’s app.
wichtigste: Have a stolen card blocked immediately.
You can do this through the bank’s card-blocking number or in the banking app.
Nobody can use a blocked card any more.
After a theft, report it to the police.
The bank then sends a new card.
It is best to note down the card-blocking number beforehand in a safe place.

abschnitte.text: If your card has been stolen, every minute counts. Whoever has the card could go shopping with it, especially **contactlessly** for small amounts. That is why you have the card **blocked** straight away. A blocked card is no longer accepted by any terminal or machine.

Many banks offer a feature in their **app** with which you can block the card in a few clicks. There is also a **card-blocking number** that can be reached round the clock. You can find this number on the bank’s website or in the card documents. It is wise to save it in your phone or somewhere else safe.
After a **theft**, report it to the **police**. The police take down a report. The bank sometimes needs this confirmation if money has been taken. It can also be important for an insurance claim.

A blocked card usually cannot be unblocked. That is why the bank sends a **new card**, often with a new PIN. Afterwards you check your **bank statements** to see whether there are any payments you did not make. If you notice anything, report it to the bank straight away.

gewusst: With some banks you can also block the card temporarily in the app if you have only mislaid it.
If you never keep your PIN together with your card, you protect yourself particularly well.

teile.einleitung: Twint is a Swiss app that lets you pay cashlessly with your smartphone. You can use it in shops, in online shops, at machines or simply to send money between friends. Twint is so widespread in Switzerland that “twinten” has almost become a word of its own.
wichtigste: Twint is a Swiss payment app for smartphones.
With Twint you can pay cashlessly in shops, online and at machines.
You can also use it to send money to friends and family.
Twint is run jointly by several Swiss banks.
The app is linked to a bank account or to credit.
You often pay by scanning a QR code.
As with a bank card, you have to protect your code and phone well with Twint too.

abschnitte.text: **Twint** is an app for smartphones that lets you pay in Switzerland without cash or a card. You download it and link it to your **bank account**. After that you can pay or send money with a few clicks. The app was developed in Switzerland and is run by large Swiss banks.

In a shop you usually scan a **QR code** at the till or hold your phone to a terminal. In online shops you choose Twint as the payment method and confirm the payment in the app. You can also pay this way at many parking meters, ticket machines and farm shops. The amount is taken directly from the linked account.

A particularly popular feature is sending money to other people. You simply choose a contact from your phone book and enter the amount. If you have eaten a pizza together, you can **split** the bill this way. You can also request money if someone still owes you something.

Twint came onto the market in 2015. Shortly afterwards it merged with a similar app, **Paymit**, which was also backed by Swiss banks. Since then the number of users has grown strongly every year. Today Twint has several million users and is the best-known mobile payment system in Switzerland.

Twint is protected with a **PIN code**, a fingerprint or face recognition. You must not tell anyone these codes. Fraudsters on online marketplaces sometimes try to trick people with fake Twint payment requests. That is why you should check every payment carefully before confirming it.

Because Twint is so easy, it is easy to spend more money than planned. It helps to look regularly at the list of payments in the app. Some banks also offer Twint for young people with their own **youth account**. That way you can practise handling money digitally without losing track.

begriffe.erklaerung: Paying without coins and notes, for example by card or app.
A program for a smartphone or tablet.
A square pattern of black and white dots that a phone can read.
A message in which someone asks you for money.

gewusst: In Switzerland, many people say “Ich twinte dir das Geld” (I’ll twint you the money) when they send money by app.
Twint works at many farm shops and market stalls where there used to be only a cash box.
In 2022, the old payment slips in Switzerland were replaced by the QR bill, which you can also scan with your phone.

teile.einleitung: Second-hand means things that have already belonged to someone else. They are often still in good condition and much cheaper than new ones.
wichtigste: Second-hand means used, from a second owner.
At a flea market, people sell things they no longer need.
Other places are charity shops (Brockenhäuser), second-hand shops and online platforms.
Used things are often much cheaper than new ones.
Second-hand is also good for the environment.

abschnitte.text: At a **flea market**, people lay out their old things on tables and sell them. In Switzerland there are also **Brockenhäuser**, also called **Brocki**, which are second-hand stores often run for charity. There you can buy used furniture, clothes, books and crockery. There are also **children’s clothes sales** and online platforms where you can buy and sell used things.

Children quickly grow out of clothes and shoes. Toys are often only used for a short time. Used, these things usually cost only a small part of the price when new. You can also sell things yourself that you no longer need. That way you get some money back. But before buying, you should look at things closely to see whether everything works.

When things are used for longer, fewer new things have to be made. This saves **raw materials**, **energy** and **water**. In addition, less ends up in the rubbish. That is why second-hand is a form of **sustainability**. What you no longer need yourself can bring someone else joy.

gewusst: The word flea market is said to come from the fact that old clothes were once sold at such markets, and sometimes there were fleas in them.

teile.einleitung: On a wish list you write down what you would like. That way you keep track and can decide which wish to save for first.
wichtigste: A wish list is a list of all the wishes you have.
You can put the wishes in order: the most important one goes at the top.
You save for the most important wish first.
Next to each wish you can write roughly how much it costs.
A wish list may change over time.
A wish list is also handy for birthdays or Christmas.

abschnitte.text: A **wish list** is a sheet of paper or a note on which you collect your wishes. It can be a bike, a game or going to a concert. If you write everything down, you do not forget anything. And you can see at a glance how many wishes you actually have.

Not every wish is equally important. That is why it is worth putting the list **in order**. The wish that means the most to you goes in first place. Then you know what you want to save for first. That way you do not spread your money over lots of small things that later turn out not to matter so much.

Next to each wish you can write the approximate **price**. Then you work out how long you need to save for it. An example: a game costs 40 francs, and you put 5 francs aside every week. After eight weeks you have the money. A **savings plan** like this helps you keep your goal in sight.

A wish list is never quite finished. Some wishes drop off because you no longer find them so exciting. New wishes are added. It is good to look at the list from time to time and put it in order again. That way you learn what really matters to you.

gewusst: If you leave a wish on the list for a while, you often notice whether you really want it.
Many families use wish lists before birthdays so that presents are not bought twice.

teile.einleitung: You need a password for online banking. It protects your account from strangers getting into it. A good password is long, unique and not used anywhere else.
wichtigste: A secure password is long, random and unique.
You do not use your bank password anywhere else.
If another website is hacked, your bank account stays protected.
Online banking usually needs a second step too, for example an app.
The bank never asks for your password by email or phone.
A password manager helps you store many passwords safely.

abschnitte.text: A secure **password** is **long** and **random**. The more characters it has, the harder it is to guess. Mixtures of letters, numbers and special characters are good. Another option is a long sentence made of several words that do not belong together. Names, birthdays or words such as “password”, on the other hand, are bad.

Your **online banking** password should be **unique**. So you do not use it anywhere else. Many websites get **hacked** at some point. Criminals can then try out the stolen passwords on other sites. If you have a separate password for your bank, you stay protected anyway.

In online banking, the password alone is usually not enough. There is also a **second step**, for example a confirmation in an **app** or a code sent by message. This is called **two-factor authentication**. Even if someone knows your password, they cannot get into the account this way. You should only confirm log-ins that you started yourself.

The **bank** **never** asks for your password by email, text message or phone. Such messages are **phishing**, meaning attempts to steal data. You do not click on links in such messages. You always open online banking yourself, using the bank's address or the official app. A **password manager**, a program that stores passwords securely, is helpful.

gewusst: A long sentence made of four random words can be safer than a short password with lots of special characters.
In Switzerland, the Confederation runs a National Cyber Security Centre that warns about current scams.

teile.einleitung: In every budget there are expenses that are the same every month and others that change. The changing ones are called variable costs. They are where it is easiest to save.
wichtigste: Variable costs differ from month to month.
Examples are eating out, going out, clothes and presents.
Fixed costs are regularly the same, such as rent or health insurance.
Fixed costs are usually tied to contracts.
Variable costs depend on your own behaviour.
That is why they are where it is easiest to save in the short term.

abschnitte.text: In a **budget** you divide up your expenses. **Fixed costs** are amounts that are regularly the same, for example rent, health insurance or a phone contract. **Variable costs** change from month to month. They include eating while out, going out, clothes, hobbies or presents. Food at home is usually variable too.

Fixed costs often cannot be changed straight away, because they are laid down in **contracts**. If, for example, you want a cheaper flat, you have to give notice and move. Variable costs, on the other hand, depend on **your own behaviour**. If you eat out less or buy new clothes less often, you save in the very same month.

Because they vary, variable costs are hard to predict. That is why in a budget you set an **amount per month**, for example for free time. If you write down your expenses for a while, you can see how much you really need. Rare expenses such as holidays or Christmas presents can be saved for over the year.

The term is also known from **business studies**. For a bakery, flour and ingredients are variable costs: the more bread it bakes, the more it needs. The rent for the shop, on the other hand, is fixed, no matter how much is sold. That is how companies work out when their business becomes profitable.

gewusst: Lots of small variable expenses, such as a drink while out, often add up to a surprisingly large amount over a year.
Budgetberatung Schweiz offers budget templates in which fixed and variable costs are listed separately.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Banking Ombudsman is a neutral office that bank customers can turn to if they have a dispute with their bank. The ombudsman mediates free of charge and helps to find a solution without going to court.
wichtigste: The banking ombudsman is a neutral mediation office.
The ombudsman helps with disputes between customers and a bank in Switzerland.
The service is free of charge for customers.
The ombudsman can suggest solutions but cannot give judgements like a court.
Before you contact the ombudsman, you should first discuss the problem with the bank itself.

abschnitte.text: The word **ombudsman** comes from Swedish. It means a person or office that **mediates** in disputes. They listen to both sides and look for a fair solution. In Switzerland there are offices like this for various areas, for example for banks, insurance companies or telephone providers.

If, for example, you have a problem because of a fee or a wrong payment, you first talk to the bank. If you cannot find a solution, you can write to the **banking ombudsman**. The ombudsman examines the case, makes enquiries at the bank and makes a **proposal**. The bank and the customer do not have to accept it, but an agreement is often reached this way. Going to court still remains an option.

The banking ombudsman was set up in 1993 and is based in Zurich. It is run by a **foundation** that is financed by the banks. Even so, it works **independently** and does not take sides. Its help costs customers nothing. Banks in Switzerland must be affiliated to a mediation office like this.

gewusst: You can also contact the banking ombudsman in French, Italian or English.
Every year, the banking ombudsman deals with thousands of enquiries.

teile.einleitung: Cash means coins and banknotes that you can touch, count and pass on. It is the oldest way of paying with money that is still in use today.
wichtigste: Cash consists of coins and banknotes.
In Switzerland, cash is the franc; one franc has 100 centimes.
With cash you can see immediately how much money you still have.
Cash works even without electricity and internet.
Lost cash is usually gone, so you look after it carefully.

abschnitte.text: **Cash** includes **coins** and **banknotes**. In Switzerland there are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes as well as half a franc, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The banknotes have values from 10 to 1000 francs. The coins are made by **Swissmint** in Bern, and the notes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.

With cash in your purse, you can see immediately how much is left. This helps you not to **spend** too much. Cash also works when there is a power cut or your phone battery is flat. You can simply pass it on to a friend, and no data is left behind when you pay.

Cash can be **lost**, or it can be stolen. Then it is usually gone. Carrying large amounts around is impractical and unsafe. You cannot pay with cash on the internet. That is why many people today use cash as well as cards or their phone.

Compared with many other countries, cash is still used a lot in Switzerland. In recent years, however, more and more people pay by **card** or with **TWINT**. In politics there is debate about whether cash should be specially protected. The National Bank makes sure that enough notes are in circulation.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the 5-franc coin is called the “Fünfliber”.
The edge of the 5-franc coin bears the words “Dominus providebit”, which means “The Lord will provide”.

teile.einleitung: A mortgage is a loan for a house or a flat, secured by the property itself. Because hardly anyone can pay for a house entirely with their own money, the bank lends a large part. If you can no longer pay, the bank may have the property sold.
wichtigste: A mortgage is a loan for a house or a flat.
The property serves as security for the bank.
In Switzerland you usually need at least 20 per cent own funds.
You pay the bank interest for the mortgage.
Housing costs should make up at most about a third of income.
There are mortgages with fixed and with variable interest.
Swiss households are among the most indebted in the world, mainly because of mortgages.

abschnitte.text: A **mortgage** is a loan that a bank gives for buying a house or a flat. The **property**, meaning the house with its land, serves as security. This is entered in the land register, an official register of all plots of land. If the borrower can no longer pay the interest, the bank may have the property sold.

In Switzerland, buyers usually have to provide at least 20 per cent of the purchase price themselves as **own funds**. At least half of this must come from savings or other own resources, not from the pension fund. The bank also checks **affordability**: housing costs should make up at most about a third of income. In doing so, it calculates with a higher interest rate than the current one, usually about 5 per cent, so that you can still pay if interest rates rise.

With a **fixed-rate mortgage**, the interest stays the same for a certain period, for example 5 or 10 years. With a **SARON mortgage**, the interest adjusts regularly to a reference rate that depends on the National Bank’s policy rates. There are also variable mortgages, whose interest the bank can adjust. Many families combine several models to spread the risk.

A mortgage is often not paid back completely. It is usual to pay off the **second mortgage**, meaning the part above about two thirds of the value, within 15 years or by retirement. This paying off is called **amortisation**. Many home owners keep the rest for their whole lives and only pay the interest.

In Switzerland only just over a third of households live in a house or flat they own; most rent. Even so, Swiss households together have mortgages of more than 1000 billion francs. This makes Switzerland one of the countries with the highest household debt per person. When the National Bank changes the **policy rate**, home owners feel it, and so do tenants, because rents are based on the reference interest rate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plot of land with or without a building on it.
Your own money that you contribute yourself when buying.
Paying back a loan step by step.
An official register that shows who owns a plot of land and which mortgages are secured on it.

gewusst: The word mortgage in German, “Hypothek”, comes from Greek and means roughly “pledge”.
You may withdraw money from your pension fund early to buy a home of your own.
So when buying a house for 1 million francs, you need at least 200,000 francs of own funds.

teile.einleitung: **Pillar 3a** is a voluntary form of pension provision in Switzerland. Anyone who works and has income on which AVS contributions are due can pay money in every year. In return there is a tax deduction, but the money is normally tied up until shortly before retirement.
wichtigste: Pillar 3a is restricted private pension provision, part of the three-pillar system.
Anyone with earned income in Switzerland on which AVS contributions are due may pay in, including apprentices who earn a wage.
The payments can be deducted from taxable income.
There is a maximum amount per year, set by the Confederation.
Normally you can draw the money at the earliest five years before the AVS reference age.
Early withdrawals are allowed only in exceptional cases, for example for a home you live in yourself.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland's pension system is based on **three pillars**. The first is the AVS, which is meant to cover basic needs. The second is occupational pension provision with the pension fund. The third is private pension provision. It is divided into the **restricted pillar 3a** with tax advantages and the unrestricted pillar 3b. The system is laid down in the Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.titel: Who may pay in and how much
abschnitte.text: Only people with **earned income on which AVS contributions are due** can pay in. This includes apprentices who earn a wage. Every year the Confederation sets a **maximum amount**. In 2025 it was 7,258 francs for employees with a pension fund. For people without a pension fund, such as many self-employed people, it is much higher. You do not have to pay in the full amount every year.

Whatever you pay into pillar 3a can be deducted from your income in your **tax return**. This lowers your income tax in the same year. When you draw the money later, you do have to pay tax on it, but separately from your other income and at a lower rate. If you start early, you benefit for many years from the tax deduction and from **compound interest**.

The money can be kept in a **3a account**. There it earns interest and its value does not go up and down. You can also invest it in **3a funds** with securities such as shares. In the long run this often earns more, but the value can fall in between. The longer the time until retirement, the easier it is to cope with such ups and downs.

The 3a savings are meant for old age and are therefore **tied up**. Normally you can draw them at the earliest five years before the AVS reference age. An **early withdrawal** is only allowed in certain cases: for a home you live in yourself, when starting your own business or when emigrating for good. There are further legal exceptions, for example in the case of a disability pension.

gewusst: You can have several 3a accounts and draw them later in different years in order to save tax.
Pillar 3a money is offered not only by banks but also by insurance companies, in the form of pension policies.

teile.einleitung: With fraud, people try to deceive others in order to get their money or their data. There are many tricks around banks and the internet. If you know them, you will fall for them less often.
wichtigste: Fraudsters deceive people to get money or data.
Anyone who lets their account be used for other people’s payments can commit a criminal offence.
Genuine prizes do not require payment in advance.
A bank never asks for your password or PIN by email or phone.
Anyone who has been defrauded should tell the bank and their parents straight away.
A long password of your own protects your e-banking.

abschnitte.text: With **phishing**, fraudsters send emails, text messages or messages that look as if they come from a bank or Swiss Post. They want you to click on a link and enter passwords or card details. The page behind it is fake. Real banks never ask for secret data in this way. If in doubt, type the bank’s address in yourself.

A message promises a great **prize**, but you are supposed to pay a fee first. This is almost always **advance-fee fraud**. Genuine prizes do not require payment in advance. It is similar with offers that sound too good to be true, for example very cheap phones in an unknown online shop.

Sometimes strangers online offer you money if you **pass on payments through your account**. That sounds like easy money. But often the money comes from crime and is meant to be hidden. This is called **money laundering**. Anyone who helps with it is called a **money mule** and can commit a criminal offence. Your account is for you alone.

If you think you have fallen for fraudsters, talk to your **parents** and the **bank** straight away. The sooner the bank knows, the more likely it is to be able to stop payments or block cards. **Reporting it** to the police can also help. There is no need to feel ashamed; fraudsters are very clever. For protection, a long password that you only use for e-banking helps.

gewusst: The term phishing is an invented word that is reminiscent of the English “fishing”.
In Switzerland, the Federal Office for Cybersecurity provides information about current scams on the internet.

teile.einleitung: A share is a small part of a company. Anyone who buys shares becomes a co-owner of that company. They can share in its success, but they also take a risk.
wichtigste: With a **share** you buy a small part of a company.
Anyone who owns shares is called a **shareholder**.
Companies with shares are **public limited companies**, abbreviated to **AG** in Switzerland.
Shares are traded on the **stock exchange**.
The price of a share is called the **share price** and can rise or fall.
Part of the profit can be paid out as a **dividend**.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a company as a big cake that is divided into many pieces. Each **share** is one of those pieces. Anyone who has many shares owns a bigger part. By selling shares, the company gets money with which it can grow. As a shareholder you become a **co-owner**.

Shares are bought and sold on the **stock exchange**. Switzerland’s largest stock exchange is the **SIX Swiss Exchange** in Zurich. The price of a share is called the **share price**. It rises when many people want to buy the share and falls when many want to sell. That is why it often changes every day.

If the company makes a profit, it often pays part of it out to the shareholders. This payment is called a **dividend**. If the share price rises, the share is worth more than when it was bought. But if the company does badly, the share price can fall sharply. In the worst case, if the company goes bust, the money is lost completely.

Once a year, shareholders may take part in the **general meeting**. There they vote on important questions, for example on the dividend or the election of the management. The more shares someone has, the more votes they usually have. That way the owners have a say in what happens to their company.

gewusst: Many well-known Swiss companies are public limited companies, which is why “AG” comes after their name.
The Swiss Market Index, SMI for short, shows how the shares of the largest Swiss companies are doing on the stock exchange.

teile.einleitung: Coins are pieces of money made of metal. In Switzerland there are coins from 5 centimes to 5 francs. They are made by Swissmint in Bern and show well-known pictures such as Helvetia.
wichtigste: The smallest Swiss coin today is the 5-centime piece.
The 5-centime coin is the only golden-yellow one; the others are silver-coloured.
The largest and most valuable coin is the 5-franc piece, known as the “Fünfliber”.
The coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern.
The banknotes, by contrast, are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
CHF stands for Confoederatio Helvetica franc.

abschnitte.text: Today in Switzerland there are coins of **5, 10 and 20 centimes** and of **½, 1, 2 and 5 francs**. The smallest is the **5-centime piece**. The 1-centime coin was abolished in **2007**, and the 2-centime coin even earlier. The largest and most valuable coin is the **Fünfliber**. There is no 10-franc coin in normal circulation.

The **5-centime piece** is the only Swiss coin that is **golden-yellow**. All the other coins are **silver-coloured**. The half-franc, 1-franc and 2-franc coins show **Helvetia** with a spear and shield. She is a female figure and a symbol of Switzerland. The 5-franc coin shows the head of an **Alpine herdsman**, and the small centime coins show a woman's head, **Libertas**.

The coins are made by the **Federal Mint Swissmint** in **Bern**. Making coins is called **minting**. In this process the picture is pressed into a small metal disc with great force. The **banknotes**, by contrast, are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**. Swissmint also makes special **commemorative coins** for collectors.

The abbreviation for the Swiss franc is **CHF**. **CH** stands for **Confoederatio Helvetica**, the Latin name of Switzerland. The **F** stands for **franc**. One franc has **100 centimes**. You often see this abbreviation on price tags, bills and at bureaux de change.

In everyday life, the 5-franc coin is often called the **Fünfliber**. This **nickname** is very old and well known in German-speaking Switzerland. It recalls old names for money such as the French “livre”. Around the edge of the Fünfliber there is a Latin inscription: **DOMINUS PROVIDEBIT**. It means “The Lord will provide”.

gewusst: The design of the 10-centime coin has hardly changed since 1879. It is one of the oldest coin designs in the world still in circulation.
Swiss coins do not say “Switzerland” but, in Latin, “Helvetia” or “Confoederatio Helvetica”.

teile.einleitung: The PIN is a secret number that you use to prove your identity with bank cards. Only someone who knows it can withdraw money or pay with the card. That is why it is very important to protect your PIN well.
wichtigste: PIN stands for “Personal Identification Number”.
The safest PIN is a random number that has nothing to do with you.
After several wrong entries, usually three, the card is blocked.
When typing it in, you cover the keypad with your hand.
You must never write your PIN on the card.
Only you may know your PIN.

abschnitte.text: The safest **PIN** is a **random number** that has nothing to do with you. Thieves can easily guess **dates of birth**, house numbers or simple **number sequences** such as 1234. With many banks you can change your PIN yourself, for example at the **cash machine**. A random PIN is much harder to crack.

If you enter your PIN **wrongly** several times, you have a problem. Usually the card is **blocked** after **three** wrong attempts. That way a thief cannot simply try out PINs. Sometimes the cash machine even keeps the card. Then you have to contact the bank.

When typing in your PIN, you cover the keypad with your **hand**. Thieves sometimes look over your **shoulder** or secretly film with small cameras. With your hand covering it, your PIN stays secret. You should also keep your **distance** from other people. If a cash machine looks as if it has been tampered with, it is better to use a different one.

Your PIN is **personal**. You must **never write it on the card**. Otherwise a finder has everything they need. If there is damage, you then often have to **pay for it yourself**. The **bank** never asks for your PIN either, neither on the **phone** nor by **email**. Anyone who does ask for it is a fraudster.

If your card is lost or stolen, you must have it **blocked** immediately. For this, banks have a **blocking number** that you can call around the clock. With many banks you can also do it directly in the **app**. After that you get a new card. The new PIN usually comes by post separately from the card.

gewusst: The bank usually sends the card and the PIN separately, so that a thief cannot get both at once.
When paying small amounts contactless, you often do not need a PIN, but for larger amounts you do.

teile.einleitung: A Betreibung is a legal procedure in Switzerland that someone can use to recover an unpaid claim for money. It can follow if you do not pay bills despite reminders.
wichtigste: With debt enforcement, a creditor claims money through legal channels.
The debt enforcement office is responsible.
It starts with the payment order.
You can raise an objection to a payment order within 10 days.
Debt enforcement proceedings are entered in the debt enforcement register.
An entry can, for example, make it harder to find a flat.

abschnitte.text: If you do not pay a bill, you usually get a **reminder** first. If it still is not paid, the **creditor**, meaning the person or company you owe money to, can start debt enforcement proceedings. To do so, they make a request for debt enforcement at the **debt enforcement office**. The office does not check whether the claim is correct; it simply starts the procedure.

The debt enforcement office sends the **debtor** a **payment order**. It states how much they are to pay. If you think that you owe nothing or less, you can raise an **objection** within 10 days. Then the creditor must show in court that their claim is justified. Without an objection, the procedure continues.

If the debt still is not paid, the office can **seize** money or belongings of the debtor. Only so much may be taken that they still have the bare essentials to live on. For companies, debt enforcement can also lead to **bankruptcy**. The rules for this are set out in the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy, **SchKG** for short.

Every debt enforcement case is entered in the **debt enforcement register**. When you are looking for a flat, landlords often ask for an **extract from the debt enforcement register**. Many entries can then be a disadvantage. That is why it is worth paying bills on time or talking to the creditor early if there are problems. Debt advice centres also help if you have money worries.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can start debt enforcement proceedings without first proving that the claim is correct.
You can order an extract from the debt enforcement register at the debt enforcement office of the municipality where you live.

teile.einleitung: Banking secrecy obliges banks to treat their customers’ data confidentially. In Switzerland it has been laid down by law since 1934 and was famous worldwide for a long time. Today banks may not pass on customer data to unauthorised people, but an automatic exchange of information applies towards the tax authorities of many countries.
wichtigste: Banking secrecy protects information about bank customers’ accounts and assets.
In Switzerland it has been part of the Banking Act since 1934.
Bank staff who breach banking secrecy commit a criminal offence.
Banks may not pass on customer data to unauthorised people.
Towards the tax authorities of many countries, an automatic exchange of information applies today.
In the case of crimes such as money laundering, banking secrecy can be lifted.
Protecting privacy is at the heart of banking secrecy.

abschnitte.text: **Banking secrecy** means that a bank may not reveal who has an account with it and how much money is in it. It is similar to medical confidentiality, which protects patients’ health data. Bank staff must keep quiet about everything they learn about their customers. This duty even continues after they have left their job at the bank.

In 1934, banking secrecy was written into the **Banking Act**, in Article 47. Since then it has been a criminal offence to pass on customer data without permission. For a long time, people from all over the world brought their money to Switzerland, partly because here it was protected from access by foreign authorities. This made the **Swiss financial centre**, with Zurich and Geneva, internationally known.

After the financial crisis of 2008, pressure from other countries grew, because some people were hiding their money in Switzerland from the tax authorities of their home country. The USA, Germany and the EU in particular demanded more openness. In 2009 the big bank UBS had to hand over customer data to the USA. After that, Switzerland changed its policy step by step.

Since 2017, Swiss banks have collected the account data of customers who pay tax abroad. Since 2018, this data has been sent automatically every year to the tax authorities of many partner countries. This procedure is called the **automatic exchange of information**, AEOI for short (AIA in German). That way, money in Switzerland can no longer be hidden from the tax authorities of these countries.

Towards unauthorised people, such as neighbours, companies or journalists, banking secrecy still applies strictly. If there is a suspicion of crimes such as **money laundering** or fraud, a court or a criminal authority can demand that data be handed over. For people who live in Switzerland, the Swiss tax authorities usually have no direct access to bank data. So banking secrecy mainly protects customers’ **privacy**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bank’s duty to keep its customers’ data confidential.
When money from crime is hidden so that it looks clean.
The automatic exchange of account data between countries for tax purposes (AIA in German).
Your personal sphere, which is nobody else’s business.

gewusst: Swiss banking secrecy became a cliché for secret accounts in many crime novels and films.
In Switzerland, anyone who breaches banking secrecy can be punished with a prison sentence.
Even retired bank staff may not reveal anything about former customers.

teile.einleitung: A cash discount (Skonto) is a small price reduction you get if you pay a bill particularly quickly. Some bills say, for example: “payable within 10 days with 2 % cash discount or within 30 days net”. So if you pay early, you save money.
wichtigste: A cash discount is a price reduction for paying a bill quickly.
The cash discount is usually two to three per cent.
The deadline for the cash discount is short, often ten days.
If you pay later, you have to pay the full amount; this is called net.
Cash discounts are mainly found between companies and on tradespeople’s bills.
The word comes from Italian.
A cash discount is not the same as an ordinary discount.

abschnitte.text: A **cash discount** is a deduction from the amount of the bill if you pay within a short period. The seller uses it to reward customers who pay on time and quickly. Typically it is a deduction of two per cent for payment within ten days. The German word Skonto comes from the Italian sconto, which means deduction.

A painter sends a bill for 1000 francs with a 2 per cent cash discount within 10 days. If you pay quickly, you deduct 20 francs and transfer only 980 francs. If you only pay after three weeks, the full 1000 francs are due. This full amount is called **net**, meaning without a deduction.

Companies need their money as quickly as possible to pay wages and materials. With the cash discount they encourage customers to pay early. This improves their **liquidity**, meaning the money that is available straight away. It also lowers the risk that a bill is never paid at all.

A **discount** is a reduction in the price, for example in a special offer or for regular customers. A cash discount, on the other hand, is only given for paying quickly. Both can also happen together. Then the discount is deducted first, and the cash discount is taken off the new amount afterwards.

Two per cent sounds like little, but with large amounts it adds up. For companies it is often even worth borrowing money briefly in order to pay with the cash discount. In everyday life you mainly see cash discounts on bills from **tradespeople** or garages. It is important to keep exactly to the deadline, otherwise you may not deduct anything.

begriffe.erklaerung: A price reduction for paying a bill quickly.
Here: the full amount of the bill without the cash discount.
The time by which a bill must be paid.
Money that a company has available straight away.

gewusst: If you miss a 2 per cent cash discount and pay 20 days later, you are giving up the equivalent of an annual interest rate of more than 30 per cent.
The plural of Skonto in German is Skonti or Skontos.
In commercial lessons at vocational school, calculating with cash discounts is part of the basic knowledge.

teile.einleitung: Many products tempt you with a free extra, for example a figure or a sticker. Free gifts like these are meant to get us to buy. If you know this, you can decide better.
wichtigste: A free gift is an extra that is meant to tempt you to buy.
You still pay for the whole product.
Companies want to win attention and new customers this way.
Collecting campaigns are meant to make you buy again and again.
The most important question: Do I really want the product?

abschnitte.text: A **free gift** is something you get with a product without paying extra for it. It can be a figure in a packet, a pen with a company logo or a small toy. The packet then says “free” in big letters. But it is not completely free, because you are buying the packet.

Companies hand out free gifts because they want to **sell more**. The extra is a **lure**: it is meant to get you to choose that particular product. The gift is often made for children, because children then ask their parents. The cost of the figure is usually included in the price.

abschnitte.titel: Collecting and buying again and again
abschnitte.text: In **collecting campaigns** there are many different figures or pictures. But you never get them all at once. So some people buy again and again to complete the collection. **Loyalty points** in the supermarket work in a similar way. They are meant to make you always shop in the same shop.

Before you buy, ask yourself one question: **Would I buy the product even without the gift?** If not, you may not need it at all. Also compare the **price** with similar products without an extra. Some free figures break quickly or soon end up in a drawer.

gewusst: Sticker albums for big football tournaments are very popular in Switzerland with children and adults.
Many free gifts carry a company’s logo, so that you think of the company every time you use them.

teile.einleitung: A debit card is a bank card with which you pay directly from your own account. The money is taken straight away or within a few days. That way you can only spend what is in the account.
wichtigste: With a debit card, the amount is taken directly from your own account.
The money is taken straight away or within a few days.
You can use it to pay in shops, online and at cash machines or to withdraw money.
Unlike with a credit card, you do not pay later.
Debit cards are well suited to young people, because you cannot get into debt.

abschnitte.text: The word **debit** comes from Latin and means roughly “he owes”. With a **debit card**, every payment is **charged to your own account**. If Mia buys a book with her card, the price is taken from her account straight away or within a few days. If there is not enough money, the payment is usually refused.

With a debit card you pay in **shops**, often **contactlessly** too. You can use it to withdraw cash at a **cash machine**. Today, many debit cards also work for **online shopping**. In Switzerland, cards from the big card companies are widespread, and PostFinance also has its own card.

With a **credit card**, you pay first and get a **bill** later, usually once a month. If you do not pay it in full, high interest is charged. With a debit card there is hardly any such danger, because the money goes out directly. That is why young people are often given a debit card first. Memory aid: debit, the money goes out directly.

gewusst: On your bank statement you can see every debit card payment with its date and place.
Some banks charge an annual fee for the debit card; others do not.

teile.einleitung: A cash machine is a device at which you can withdraw cash from your own account round the clock. In Switzerland it is usually called a Bancomat. You need a bank card and a secret PIN code for it.
wichtigste: At a cash machine you can withdraw cash with your card and PIN.
In Switzerland, the cash machine is usually called a Bancomat.
The world’s first cash machine came into use in London in 1967.
Many machines give out francs and also euros.
At some machines you can also pay money in.
When typing your PIN, you should always cover the keypad.
Because more payments are made digitally, there are fewer cash machines today than before.

abschnitte.text: A **cash machine** is a device that gives out cash. You put in your bank card, enter your **PIN** and choose the amount you want. Through the bank’s network, the machine checks whether there is enough money in the account. Then it gives out the card and the notes, and the amount is taken from the account.

In Switzerland people almost always say **Bancomat**, a word that is also used in Italy. Bancomats are found at railway stations, at bank branches, in shopping centres and on the walls of buildings. Many machines offer francs and euros, which is practical for travelling. At some machines you can also pay money in or top up your phone credit.

The world’s first cash machine was opened on 27 June 1967 at a bank branch in London. It belonged to **Barclays** bank and still worked with special vouchers instead of cards. Machines soon followed in many countries, including Switzerland. Today there are millions of cash machines around the world.

When typing your PIN, you should **cover** the keypad with your hand so that nobody can watch. Criminals sometimes secretly fit devices to the card slot to copy card data; this is called **skimming**. If a machine looks altered or damaged, it is better to use another one. If the card is not given back, you should have it blocked by the bank straight away.

For some years, more and more people have been paying by card, phone or **TWINT**. That is why the number of cash machines in Switzerland is slowly falling. Even so, **cash** is important to many Swiss people, for example as an emergency reserve or for small purchases. The Swiss National Bank stresses that cash should remain available to everyone.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss word for a cash machine.
A secret number with which you identify yourself at the machine.
Fraud in which card data is secretly copied at a cash machine.
Money in the form of coins and notes.

gewusst: The inventor John Shepherd-Barron is said to have had the idea for the cash machine in the bath.
Other banks sometimes charge a fee for withdrawing money at their machines.
If the money is not taken out of the dispenser within a short time, the machine pulls it back in.

teile.einleitung: A bank account is a place at the bank where it is recorded how much money belongs to you. You can pay money in, withdraw it and transfer it. The money in the account always remains your money.
wichtigste: In an account, the bank records how much money belongs to you.
The money is not kept in a separate box with your name on it.
The money in your account belongs to you, not to the bank.
For young children, the parents open the account together with the child.
The current amount in the account is called the balance.
In Switzerland, deposits of up to 100,000 francs per person and bank are specially protected.

abschnitte.text: A **bank account** is like a notebook in which the bank writes everything down. If you pay money in, it is added. If you take money out, it is subtracted. What is left is your **account balance**, also simply called the **balance**.

Many people think their money is kept in a separate box with their name on it. That is not true. The bank works with the money and lends some of it to other people, for example. Even so, it remains **your money**, and you can get it back at any time. The bank must record exactly who owns how much.

Adults can open an account themselves. For **young children**, the **parents** or other legal guardians do this together with the child. The parents help and keep an eye on things. The older you get, the more you are allowed to decide for yourself.

Switzerland has a **deposit protection scheme**. If a bank goes bust, balances of up to **100,000 francs** per person and bank are specially protected. On top of that there are rules and checks by **FINMA**. That is why money in an account is safer than under the mattress.

There are different kinds of account. You need a **personal account** for everyday life, for example for your wages and bills. In a **savings account** you put money aside for later. For children and teenagers there are special accounts with low fees.

gewusst: Every account has its own IBAN, which works like an address.
In Switzerland, almost everyone now receives their wages directly into their account rather than in cash.

teile.einleitung: Every bank card comes with a PIN code. This is a secret number that only you know. With it, you show at the cash machine or at the till that the card really belongs to you.
wichtigste: The PIN code is a secret number for your card.
A PIN code usually has 4 or 6 digits.
You never tell anyone your PIN code, not even good friends.
It is best to keep it only in your head.
Numbers such as 1234 or 0000 are bad, because they are easy to guess.
