abschnitte.text: The **PIN code** is a **secret number** for your bank card. Only you know it. That way nobody else can use your card. You enter the PIN code, for example, at the **cash machine** when you take out money. You often need it when paying at the **till** too. A PIN code usually has **4 or 6 digits**.

Your best friend asks for your PIN code? Then you say: “I don't tell anyone that.” You **never** give away your PIN code, not even to good friends. That way your money stays **protected**. The bank never asks for it either. Anyone who asks for your PIN code on the phone or by message wants to **cheat** you.

Where is the best place to keep your PIN code? **Only in your head**. If you write it on a piece of paper next to the card, a finder can take out money straight away. That is why it is best to learn your PIN code **by heart**. A little trick: say it to yourself in your head a few times. Soon you will know it without thinking.

The worst PIN code is one that is **easy to guess**. Thieves try numbers such as **1234** or **0000** first. Your **birthday** is not a good idea either. A good PIN code has **no simple pattern**. If you enter your PIN code wrongly several times, your card is usually blocked.

gewusst: PIN is an English abbreviation meaning “Personal Identification Number”. So when you say “PIN code” or “PIN number”, you are really saying “number” twice.
When typing it in, you cover the keys with your hand so that nobody can watch.

teile.einleitung: You cannot shop without limits with a credit card. The bank sets a maximum amount, the credit limit. It shows how much borrowed money you may spend per billing period.
wichtigste: The credit limit is the highest amount you can spend per billing period.
The bank sets the limit.
Once the limit is reached, further payments are refused.
The money within the limit is borrowed and must be paid back.
A high limit does not mean you can afford that much.

abschnitte.text: The **credit limit** is the highest amount you may spend with your credit card in one **billing period**. A billing period usually lasts a month. The bank or card company sets the limit. Once it is reached, further payments are **refused**. Only when the bill has been paid can you shop again.

Before the bank sets a limit, it checks your **income** and your financial situation. People who earn more often get a higher limit. People who are just starting out or earn little get a lower limit. Sometimes you can ask for the limit to be **lowered** yourself. This helps you not to spend too much.

Nina has a credit limit of 2,000 francs. That does not mean she owns 2,000 francs. It is **borrowed money** that she must **pay back** at the end of the period. With a credit card, the card company pays first. Then the bill comes to Nina. So a high limit does not mean you should spend that much.

If you have a credit card, you should only spend as much as you can also **pay**. It helps to check your spending regularly in the **app**. Your own **budget** shows how much money you really have available each month. If you do not pay the bill in full, high interest is added.

gewusst: Prepaid cards have a limit too, namely the amount that has been loaded onto them.
Some card apps show exactly how much of the limit has already been used.

teile.einleitung: If you have little money, you have to think carefully about what you spend it on. The most important rule is: necessities come first, wishes afterwards.
wichtigste: First you pay for what you really need, for example food.
Wishes only come afterwards, if there is still money left.
Necessities include food, housing, clothes, electricity and health insurance.
A **budget** helps you divide up your money properly.
If you pay for necessities first, you will not run short of money.
Children can also practise planning the important things first with their pocket money.

abschnitte.text: Necessary means everything you need in order to live. This includes **food** and drink, a **home**, warm clothes and electricity. In Switzerland, **health insurance** is part of it too, because it is compulsory for everyone. You cannot simply leave out these expenses. That is why you always plan for them first.

abschnitte.titel: First the necessities, then the rest
abschnitte.text: Imagine a family has only a little money left at the end of the month. Then they first buy the **food for the week**. A new game or a trip to the cinema has to wait. If there is still money left afterwards, you can fulfil a wish. That way the money is enough for everything important.

A **budget** is a plan for your money. You write down how much money comes in and what you spend it on. First you enter the fixed expenses, such as rent and insurance. Then come food and other everyday things. What is left can be saved or used for wishes. Budget templates for families and young people are available, for example, from **Budgetberatung Schweiz**.

You can practise this rule with your **pocket money** too. If, for example, you pay for your mid-morning snack (Znüni) or school materials yourself, you put money aside for these first. Only after that do you spend the rest on sweets or toys. That way you learn early how to handle money. This helps later when you have to divide up your own wages.

gewusst: Many municipalities and cantons offer free debt advice if the money is no longer enough.
In Switzerland, basic health insurance is compulsory for all residents.

teile.einleitung: Your account balance shows how much money is in your account right now. It changes every time money comes in or goes out. If you know your balance, you keep track of your money.
wichtigste: The account balance shows how much money is in the account at the moment.
Paying money in makes the balance bigger.
Withdrawing money or paying makes the balance smaller.
Another word for the account balance is simply the balance.
You can see your balance in online banking, in the app or on your bank statement.

abschnitte.text: Your **account balance** tells you how much money you have in your account **at the moment**. Experts also simply call it the **balance**. You can see it in the bank's **app**, in **online banking**, at the cash machine or on your **bank statement**. The balance is always a snapshot. By tomorrow it may already be different.

When money comes into the account, the balance gets **bigger**. This happens, for example, when you pay money in or someone transfers money to you. Example: Mia has 20 francs in her account and pays in 10 francs. 20 plus 10 makes 30, so she now has **30 francs**. Wages, pocket money and **interest** also increase the balance.

When money leaves the account, the balance gets **smaller**. This happens when you **withdraw** money at a cash machine or pay by card. Example: Tim has 50 francs and withdraws 20 francs. 50 minus 20 is **30 francs**. Bank fees are also taken off the balance.

abschnitte.titel: When the balance goes into the minus
abschnitte.text: If you spend more than there is in the account, the balance becomes **negative**. You then say that the account is **overdrawn**. This is really money borrowed from the bank. The bank usually charges high **interest** for it. With youth accounts, going overdrawn is normally not possible at all.

gewusst: A negative balance is often shown with a minus sign or in red.
Many banking apps can send you a message as soon as money arrives in your account.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes you need more money than you have at the moment, for example for a house. Then a bank can lend you money. This is called a loan or credit. Later you have to pay the money back and pay interest on it.
wichtigste: A loan is money that the bank lends.
Borrowed money must be paid back.
You pay interest for borrowing, so you usually pay back more than you received.
A loan for a house is called a mortgage.
Before giving a loan, the bank checks whether you can pay it back.
Debts can become a big problem.

abschnitte.text: A **loan** or **credit** means that the bank **lends** someone money. The word “credit” comes from the Latin “credere”, which means “to believe” or “to trust”. The bank trusts that the money will come back. Anyone who takes out a loan has **debts** with the bank. These must be paid back in instalments or all at once.

The bank charges **interest** for lending money. Interest is the price of the borrowed money. It is usually given as a **percentage** per year. That is why in the end you pay back more than you received. The longer you keep the money, the more interest adds up.

The Meier family wants to buy a house but does not have enough money. Then the bank can give them a loan. A loan for a house or a flat is called a **mortgage**. The house serves as **security**. In Switzerland, you normally have to pay part of the purchase price yourself; this is called **equity**.

There are also loans for cars, holidays or furniture. They are called **consumer loans** or personal loans. In Switzerland, the bank must first check whether you **can pay the loan back**. This is called a **creditworthiness check**. Even so, some people fall into a **debt trap**. That is why you should think carefully about whether you really need such a loan.

gewusst: States, cantons and municipalities also take out loans, for example for school buildings or roads.
In Switzerland there are debt advice centres that help people with debts free of charge.

teile.einleitung: The key interest rate is the most important interest rate that a national bank sets. In Switzerland it is decided by the Swiss National Bank, in order to keep prices stable and steer the economy. It affects how much interest you get on a savings account and how much a loan costs.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, the key interest rate is set by the Swiss National Bank.
It is used to keep prices stable and to steer the economy.
A high key rate makes loans more expensive and slows down inflation.
A low key rate makes loans cheaper and boosts the economy.
The National Bank reviews the key rate four times a year.
From 2015 to 2022 the key rate in Switzerland was even negative.
The key rate affects savings interest, mortgages and, indirectly, rents.

abschnitte.titel: What is the key interest rate?
abschnitte.text: The **key interest rate** is an interest rate that the National Bank sets and that banks use as a guide. It roughly determines the interest at which banks lend money to each other for short periods. That is why it is said to be the rate that “leads” the other rates. In Switzerland it is officially called the **SNB policy rate** and has been used in this form since 2019.

If prices rise too much, this is called **inflation**. Then the National Bank can raise the key rate, loans become more expensive and people spend less, which slows down prices. If the economy is doing badly or prices are falling, it lowers the key rate. Then loans become cheaper, and companies and people invest and buy more.

In Switzerland, the **Governing Board** of the Swiss National Bank decides on the key rate. It normally meets for this four times a year, in March, June, September and December. The aim is **price stability**, which the National Bank understands as inflation of less than 2 per cent a year. In doing so, the National Bank is independent of the government.

In January 2015 the National Bank introduced a negative interest rate of minus 0.75 per cent in order to weaken the strong franc. Banks had to pay if they held a lot of money at the National Bank. When prices rose sharply worldwide from 2022, the SNB raised the key rate step by step to 1.75 per cent in 2023. After that inflation fell, and in June 2025 the National Bank lowered the key rate to 0 per cent.

abschnitte.titel: What does it mean for me?
abschnitte.text: A high key rate usually means a bit more interest on your **savings account**, but more expensive loans. Anyone with a SARON mortgage notices the change quickly, because the interest is adjusted regularly. Rents in Switzerland also depend on it indirectly, through what is known as the **reference interest rate**. A low key rate, on the other hand, helps companies that need loans.

begriffe.erklaerung: The National Bank's most important interest rate, which banks use as a guide.
When prices rise in general and money becomes worth less.
Interest that you have to pay instead of receiving it.
When prices change only a little.

gewusst: The European Central Bank in Frankfurt and the US Federal Reserve in Washington also set their own key interest rates.
At the time of negative interest, some Swiss banks also charged wealthy private customers fees on large balances.
The National Bank's decisions on the key rate are often followed live in the news.

teile.einleitung: A foreign currency is any currency that is not your own. For us in Switzerland these are, for example, the euro, the dollar or the pound. If you pay abroad, you have to have francs converted.
wichtigste: Switzerland’s currency is the franc; all others are foreign currencies for us.
The exchange rate says how much one currency is worth in another.
Exchange rates change all the time.
When paying by card abroad, it is usually cheaper to pay in the local currency.
If you choose francs at the terminal, the retailer often converts at a worse rate.
Banks often charge a fee for conversions.

abschnitte.text: Almost every country has its own **currency**. In Switzerland and Liechtenstein you pay with **francs**. In Germany, France, Italy and Austria the **euro** is used, in the USA the dollar. For us, all these currencies are **foreign currencies**.

The **exchange rate** states how many francs you get for one euro or one dollar. It depends on supply and demand and changes every day. Banks have two rates: one for buying and one for selling. The difference is what they earn.

When you pay by card abroad, the terminal sometimes asks whether you want to pay in francs or in the local currency. If you choose francs, the **retailer** often does the conversion, usually at a worse rate. If you choose the **local currency**, your own bank does the conversion. This is usually cheaper.

Even in Switzerland you can sometimes pay in euros, for example near the border or at railway stations. But the change is often given in francs, and the rate is not always good. So if you are travelling, it is best to compare the costs. That way there is more money left for your holiday.

gewusst: The euro is used in many European countries, but Switzerland has kept its franc.
Because the franc is considered very stable, many people all over the world buy it in uncertain times.

teile.einleitung: With a credit card you can pay in shops, on the internet and when travelling. But the money is not taken from your account straight away. You get a bill later. That is why people say: buy first, pay later.
wichtigste: With a credit card, the card company pays first.
Once a month a bill arrives with all your purchases.
If you only pay part of the bill, you pay high interest on the rest.
In Switzerland you can normally get a real credit card from the age of 18.
The bank checks your income first.
Younger people can use a prepaid card or a debit card.

abschnitte.text: If you pay with a **credit card**, the card company is really lending you the money for a short time. The company collects all your purchases for a month. Then it sends a **monthly bill**. You must pay this **on time**. Well-known credit cards in Switzerland run through companies such as **Visa** or **Mastercard**.

abschnitte.titel: Paying in part costs a lot
abschnitte.text: You can often pay only **part** of the bill. The rest then counts as a **loan**. For this the card companies charge **high interest**, much higher than for a mortgage. The interest is calculated on the amount still owed. This way debts can grow quickly. It is best always to pay the whole bill.

In Switzerland you can normally get a proper credit card **from the age of 18**. So you have to be **of age**. The bank first checks your **income** and sets a **limit**. Younger people can get at most a **prepaid card** or a **debit card**. With these cards you can only spend what is already there.

Credit cards are practical when **travelling**, for hotels and for shopping on the **internet**. The card company often helps if a payment was wrong. At the same time, it is easy to lose track because you do not see the money disappear straight away. Some cards also cost an **annual fee**. And when paying in foreign currencies, extra fees are often added.

gewusst: Many credit cards can now be held contactless against the card terminal or stored in a mobile phone.
On the back of many cards there is a short security code that you need for shopping on the internet.

teile.einleitung: If you pay a debt of money too late, you often have to pay more than the original amount. This extra charge is called default interest. In Switzerland it is governed by the Code of Obligations.
wichtigste: Default interest is interest for paying too late.
It applies when you are in default with a debt of money.
The statutory default interest is 5 per cent a year.
It applies if nothing else has been agreed in the contract.
Reminder fees are something different from default interest.

abschnitte.text: **Interest** is a price for money that you have at your disposal. If you pay a bill too late, you keep the money longer than you are allowed to. For this you owe the creditor **default interest**. It starts to run as soon as you are **in default**, that is after a reminder or after a fixed payment date that was agreed.

The **Code of Obligations** lays down: default interest is **5 per cent a year** unless something else has been agreed. An example: anyone who pays 1,000 francs a whole year too late owes 50 francs in default interest. For half a year it is about 25 francs. A contract can also set a different interest rate.

Default interest is not the same as a **reminder fee**. A company may only charge reminder fees if they have been agreed, for example in the terms and conditions. With **debt enforcement proceedings**, **debt enforcement costs** are added too. So anyone who pays late often ends up paying considerably more.

The simplest way to avoid default interest is to **pay on time**. That is why you should collect your bills and keep an eye on the deadline. If you are short of money, it is better to ask early for **payment by instalments**. That way you avoid interest, fees and entries in the debt enforcement register.

gewusst: For small amounts, default interest is often low, which is why many companies do not charge it at all.
Tax offices also charge default interest if you pay your taxes late.

teile.einleitung: The chip is the small gold or silver part on a bank card. It stores important data about the card and makes paying safer.
wichtigste: The chip is a tiny computer on the card.
It stores card data that card readers recognise.
Chips are much harder to copy than the old magnetic stripe.
With every payment, the chip creates new, one-off data.
Contactless payment also works through a chip and a small antenna.

abschnitte.text: The **chip** on a bank card is a tiny **computer**. The gold or silver areas are its contacts. When you put the card into a card reader, these contacts touch the machine. That way the shop, cash machine and bank can **exchange data** with the chip. The chip also checks whether the PIN entered is correct.

In the past, bank cards mainly had a **magnetic stripe** on the back. Fraudsters could copy it fairly easily. The chip is much safer, because it creates **new, one-off data** with every payment. A copy of this is of little use to fraudsters. There is a common worldwide standard for this, which is called **EMV**.

With many cards you can just hold them briefly to the machine. This is called paying **contactlessly**. For this, a small **antenna** connected to the chip is built into the card. The data is transmitted by radio over a few centimetres. For larger amounts, the machine still asks for the PIN.

gewusst: Similar chips are also found in passports, SIM cards and many ID cards.
The chip on a bank card does not need its own battery; it gets power from the card reader.

teile.einleitung: Diversification means spreading money across many different investments. That way you lose less if a single investment does badly. A well-known saying puts it like this: don’t put all your eggs in one basket.
wichtigste: Diversification means spreading money widely.
If one investment does badly, it only affects part of the money.
Anyone who puts everything into a single share has a concentration risk.
You can spread across different companies, industries, countries and types of investment.
Funds are a simple way of spreading widely.
Diversification lowers the risk, but it does not protect against every loss.

abschnitte.titel: Don’t put all your eggs in one basket
abschnitte.text: If you put all your eggs in one basket and drop it, you lose them all at once. It is similar with investments. **Diversification** means **spreading** money across many different investments. If one of them does badly, the others make up for part of it. It is also called **spreading the risk**.

If Jan puts all his money into the shares of a single company, everything depends on that company. If it gets into difficulties, Jan loses a lot. This is called **concentration risk**. If he had spread his money across many companies, the damage would be smaller. Anyone who only invests in one country or one industry also has a risk like this.

You can spread in different ways: across many **companies**, across different **industries** such as pharmaceuticals, banks or technology, across several **countries** and across different **types of investment** such as shares, bonds or property. A simple option is **funds**. A fund collects the money of many investors and uses it to buy many different securities.

Diversification lowers the risk without giving up chances completely. But it does not protect against every loss. If almost all prices on the stock exchange fall at the same time, widely spread investments lose value too. That is why the **investment horizon** remains important: anyone who has time can sit out such phases more easily.

gewusst: In 1990, the economist Harry Markowitz received the Nobel Prize in Economics, partly for his research on spreading risk.
A single fund can contain hundreds or even thousands of different shares.

teile.einleitung: A bank card is easy to lose: on the bus, at school or during sport. When that happens, it is important to stay calm and have the card blocked straight away. Good habits help to make sure no harm is done.
wichtigste: You have a lost card blocked by the bank straight away.
You can do this by phone using the blocking number or in the app.
After that, nobody can pay with the card any more.
You never keep your PIN together with the card.
If you follow the bank's rules, you are better protected if something goes wrong.

abschnitte.text: If your card is missing, first have a quick look in the usual places. If you cannot find it, have it **blocked immediately**. Someone who finds the card could use it, for example for **contactless** payments. It is better to block it too early than too late.

The bank has a **blocking number** that you can call day and night. Many banks also offer a blocking function in their **app**. Children and teenagers can also ask their parents for help. The bank then orders a **new card**.

Banks expect you to handle your card **carefully**. You learn your **PIN** by heart and never write it on the card. It does not belong in your wallet either. If you follow these rules, the bank will usually give you more support if something goes wrong.

After blocking the card, you look at your **account transactions**. If there are payments you do not recognise, you report them to the bank. If the card was stolen and not just lost, you also go to the **police**. This often helps to sort out any damage.

gewusst: Some banks let you block your card briefly in the app and unblock it again if you had only mislaid it.
If you find someone else's card, the best thing is to take it to the bank or to the police.

teile.einleitung: At the bank there are two kinds of interest. You pay debit interest (Sollzins) when you owe the bank money. You receive credit interest (Habenzins) when you have money in your account.
wichtigste: **Debit interest** is the interest you pay for debts at the bank.
**Credit interest** is the interest you receive on your savings.
Debit interest is usually much higher than credit interest.
Part of the bank’s income comes from this difference.
If you overdraw your account, you often pay particularly high debit interest.

abschnitte.text: The words come from **bookkeeping**. “Soll” (debit) stands for what you owe someone. “Haben” (credit) stands for what you have. If you borrow money from the bank, for example with a **loan**, you pay **debit interest**. If you put money into a **savings account**, the bank pays you **credit interest**.

The bank takes savers’ money and lends it on to others. For lending, it charges more interest than it pays the savers. With this difference the bank covers its costs and the **risk** that someone will not pay back. That is why debit interest is almost always considerably higher than credit interest.

If you take out more money than there is in your account, you **overdraw** the account. For this, banks often charge high **overdraft interest**. **Credit cards** also involve high interest if you do not pay the bill in full. That is why it is wise only to spend what you have.

gewusst: A memory aid: Soll means owing, Haben means having.

teile.einleitung: The payment order (Zahlungsbefehl) is a document from the debt enforcement office. In Switzerland it is the first official step when someone wants to recover their debts.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, debt enforcement begins with the **payment order**.
The payment order comes from the **debt enforcement office**.
It demands that you pay the debt or raise an objection.
You have ten days to raise an **objection**.
The rules are set out in the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy (SchKG).
Debt enforcement proceedings are entered in the debt enforcement register.

abschnitte.text: If you do not pay a bill, you usually get reminders first. If you still do not pay, the **creditor**, meaning the person or company you owe money to, can make a **request for debt enforcement** at the debt enforcement office. The office then sends the **debtor** a payment order. It is often handed over in person by Swiss Post or by staff from the office.

The payment order states the creditor’s name, the amount owed and the reason for the claim. It demands that the debtor pays within **20 days**. If you think the claim is wrong, you can raise an objection within **10 days**. This is very simple: verbally or in writing at the debt enforcement office, or directly when the order is handed over.

With an **objection** you are saying: I do not agree with this claim. Then the debt enforcement stops for the time being. The creditor must now show in court that they are in the right. This is done by asking the court to set aside the objection (**Rechtsöffnung**) or by a court action. Only if the court rules in their favour does the debt enforcement continue.

If you do not pay and do not raise an objection, the creditor can ask for the debt enforcement to **continue**. Then the office can, for example, **seize** part of your wages or belongings. The debt enforcement also appears in the **debt enforcement register**. Landlords or employers often ask for an extract from it, so debt enforcement proceedings can bring disadvantages later.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can start debt enforcement proceedings against someone without first proving that the debt really exists. That is why the objection is so important.
You do not have to give a reason for an objection.

teile.einleitung: Handling money is about dividing up money wisely, saving and avoiding debt. In Switzerland you pay with the Swiss franc, in cash, by card or with your phone. If you learn early to handle pocket money, it will be easier later with wages, rent and bills.
wichtigste: Switzerland’s money is called the Swiss franc; one franc has 100 centimes.
A budget is a plan of how much money comes in and what you spend it on.
Needs such as food are more important than wishes such as a new game.
If you want something expensive, you can save for a few weeks.
If you do not pay a credit card bill in full, high interest is usually charged on the rest.
If you lease a car, you pay monthly to use it, but the car does not belong to you.
Debts often build up gradually, through lots of small expenses.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland’s currency is the **Swiss franc**, abbreviated to CHF or Fr. It is also used in the Principality of Liechtenstein. The banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank, and the coins are minted by the federal mint, **Swissmint**, in Bern. The franc is considered a very stable currency worldwide.

With **pocket money**, children learn to make their own decisions about money. If, for example, you get 5 francs every week and want a game costing 20 francs, you can save for four weeks. Waiting is not always easy, but you learn to plan goals. Many parents and advice services recommend paying pocket money regularly and at a fixed amount.

A **budget** is a plan that shows how much money comes in and what it is spent on. On one side is the income, such as pocket money or wages. On the other side are the expenses, for example for your phone, clothes, going out and saving. The organisation **Budgetberatung Schweiz** offers templates and sample budgets for young people and families.

**Needs** are things you really need in order to live, such as food, housing, clothing and health. **Wishes** are things that would be nice but are not necessary, for example a new video game or branded shoes. If you cover your needs first and then decide about wishes, it is easier to stay in control. Advertising often tries to make wishes look like needs.

With a **debit card** you pay with money that is already in your account. With a **credit card** the bank pays first and you get a bill later; if you do not pay it in full, high interest is charged. When **leasing** a car, you pay monthly to use it, but the car belongs to the leasing company. In Switzerland, before a small loan or leasing is granted, it must be checked whether you can afford the instalments.

Many young adults in Switzerland have debts, for example because of unpaid taxes, health insurance premiums or phone bills. Debts often arise when you spend more than you take in. Anyone with problems can get free help from a **debt advice service**. The earlier you get help, the easier it is to find a way out.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plan for income and spending.
Something you really need in order to live.
You rent something, for example a car, for a monthly fee.
Money that you still have to pay someone.
A price that you pay for borrowed money or receive for saved money.

gewusst: The Swiss franc was introduced in 1850 as the single currency of the whole of Switzerland.
Swiss coins bear the words “Confoederatio Helvetica”, the Latin name for Switzerland.
In Switzerland you come of age at 18 and can sign contracts yourself, which also means you can get into debt.

teile.einleitung: A receipt is a slip of paper that shows what has been paid. You get one in a shop, at the bank counter or at a machine. It is proof that money has been paid or paid in.
wichtigste: A receipt shows what has been paid or paid in.
It is proof of a payment.
A receipt shows the amount, the date and often the things that were bought.
You often need the receipt for an exchange or a guarantee.
Other words for it are till receipt, slip or sales slip.

abschnitte.text: A **receipt** shows how much money has been **paid** or **paid in**. Usually it also shows the **date** and the time. In a shop you can also see which things you bought and what they cost. Often the name of the shop is printed on it too. In everyday life people also say **till receipt** or **slip**.

The receipt is **proof**. It shows that a payment really took place. If there is a dispute later, you can show it. That is why you should **keep** receipts for important payments. At the bank counter or at a machine you get a receipt for a **deposit**.

If you want to **exchange** something, the shop often asks for the receipt. You also need it for a **guarantee**. A guarantee means that a device will be repaired or replaced if it breaks. Without a receipt, it is hard to prove when and where you bought it. For expensive devices it is therefore worth keeping the receipt safe.

Many receipts are printed on thin **thermal paper**. This writing can **fade** over time. That is why it is best to take a photo of important receipts. More and more shops also offer **digital receipts** in an app or by email. In online banking, every payment also has an entry on the bank statement.

gewusst: In Switzerland, companies normally have to keep their business records for ten years.

teile.einleitung: A cash withdrawal means taking out cash, for example at a cash machine. Depending on the card and the place, this can be free or cost quite a lot.
wichtigste: A cash withdrawal means taking out cash.
With a debit card, withdrawing at your own bank is usually free.
With a credit card, there is often a percentage fee plus interest.
Abroad, extra costs for changing currency can be added.
The exact fees are in the price list of the bank or card provider.

abschnitte.text: You usually get cash at a **cash machine**, with your bank card and PIN. You can also withdraw money at the **bank counter**. In some shops, when you pay by card, you can also get some cash. In each case the money is taken from your own account.

With a **debit card**, the money comes directly from your own account. At your own bank this usually costs nothing. With a **credit card** it is different: many providers charge a **fee** for cash, as a percentage of the amount. Often **interest** is added from the day of the withdrawal. That is why the rule is: better to get cash with a debit card.

If you withdraw money abroad, you often pay a fee per withdrawal. On top of that comes the **exchange rate**, meaning the price for changing into another currency. Some machines ask whether you want to be charged in francs or in the local currency. Being charged in francs is often more expensive. Before a trip, it is worth looking at your own bank’s prices.

gewusst: Many cash machines have a maximum limit on how much you can withdraw per day.
Fees for cash can differ greatly between banks.

teile.einleitung: Amortisation means paying back a debt step by step. You hear the word most often in connection with mortgages, which are loans for a house or a flat. If you amortise, you have less debt over time.
wichtigste: To **amortise** means to pay off.
A **mortgage** is a loan with which you buy a house or a flat.
With amortisation, you pay back part of the mortgage.
This reduces the **debt** and the **interest costs**.
In Switzerland there is **direct** and **indirect** amortisation.

abschnitte.text: A house costs a lot of money, and hardly anyone can pay for it entirely themselves. That is why you borrow part of it from the bank. This loan is called a **mortgage**. The house serves as **security** for the bank. For the borrowed money you pay **interest** every year.

With **amortisation** you regularly pay back part of the mortgage. That way the debt becomes a little smaller every year. Because you only pay interest on the money you still owe, the **interest costs** fall too. In Switzerland, banks require part of the mortgage to be paid off within a certain period.

With **direct amortisation** you pay the money directly to the bank, and the mortgage becomes smaller. With **indirect amortisation** you first pay the money into a pension account, for example into **pillar 3a**. Later the mortgage is paid back with this money all at once. Which type suits better depends, among other things, on taxes.

Amortisation comes from the French “amortir”, which means roughly “to deaden” or “to weaken”. In business, people also say that a purchase has **paid for itself** (amortisiert). This means that it has brought in or saved as much as it cost. A solar installation, for example, pays for itself after a few years through the electricity saved.

gewusst: Many mortgages in Switzerland are never paid back completely, but only up to a certain part.
Pillar 3a is part of Swiss retirement provision and is supported by the state with tax advantages.

teile.einleitung: PostFinance is the financial institution of Swiss Post. Many people in Switzerland have an account there for making payments. It is one of the most important financial institutions in the country.
wichtigste: PostFinance belongs to Swiss Post.
Swiss Post belongs to the Confederation.
Many people have an account with PostFinance for making payments.
PostFinance has its head office in Bern.
By law it may not grant loans and mortgages itself.
PostFinance has had a banking licence since 2013.

abschnitte.text: **PostFinance** belongs to **Swiss Post**. Swiss Post in turn belongs to the **Confederation**. PostFinance has its head office in **Bern**. It is one of the largest financial institutions in Switzerland. Many people have an **account** there for **payments**, meaning for deposits, transfers and bills.

The roots of PostFinance go back to the **postal cheque service**. This was introduced at the beginning of the 20th century. It allowed people to send money through the post without cash. For many years people had a **postal account**, even if they were not with any bank. Since **2013**, PostFinance has been a separate public limited company with a **banking licence**.

In Switzerland, Swiss Post has a special task: the **universal service**. This means that everyone in the whole country should be able to make payments. That is why you can pay in money and pay bills at many **post office counters**. On top of this there is **e-finance**, an app and **Postomats**. Postomat is the name of PostFinance's cash machines.

Unlike other banks, PostFinance may not, by law, grant **loans** and **mortgages** to customers itself. It offers mortgages only together with **partner banks**. This rule is debated again and again in politics. Some want to relax it, others want to keep it. It is meant to prevent a company owned by the Confederation from competing too strongly with private banks.

gewusst: The Swiss National Bank has classified PostFinance as systemically important. This means it is especially important for the Swiss economy.
Swiss Post's yellow payment slips were typical of Switzerland for a long time. Today they have been replaced by the QR-bill.

teile.einleitung: The Fünfliber is the popular nickname for the 5-franc coin. It is the largest and most valuable coin in circulation in Switzerland. It shows an Alpine herdsman.
wichtigste: “Fünfliber” is the nickname for the 5-franc coin.
It is the largest coin in circulation in Switzerland.
The front shows the head of an Alpine herdsman.
The edge bears the Latin inscription “DOMINUS PROVIDEBIT”.
The Fünfliber used to be made of silver; today it is made of copper and nickel.
It is minted by Swissmint in Bern.

abschnitte.text: The name **Fünfliber** is very old. “Liber” comes from the French word “livre”, an earlier unit of money. In everyday speech the name has stuck to the 5-franc coin to this day. Many people also simply say “a Fünfer”.

On one side you can see the head of an **Alpine herdsman**, who stands for Switzerland’s mountain people. On the other side is the **Swiss coat of arms** with the value. The edge is special: it bears the words **“DOMINUS PROVIDEBIT”**, which means “The Lord will provide”. The inscription is surrounded by stars.

In the past, the Fünfliber was minted from **silver**. When the price of silver rose sharply, the metal in the coin was worth almost more than 5 francs. That is why from 1968 it was switched to a mixture of **copper and nickel**. Old silver Fünfliber coins are popular with collectors today.

All Swiss coins are minted by **Swissmint** in Bern. This is the federal mint. The banknotes, on the other hand, are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**. The Fünfliber is heavy and big; you notice it straight away in your purse.

gewusst: The Fünfliber is bigger than a 2-euro coin.
Many children get a Fünfliber as pocket money (Sackgeld) or as a reward; almost everyone in Switzerland knows the word.

teile.einleitung: A deposit is an amount of money that is put into an account. In Switzerland you can pay in cash at banks and at the post office. But a lot of money also reaches accounts electronically today.
wichtigste: A deposit increases the account balance.
You pay in cash at the bank counter or at a deposit machine.
You can also pay in cash at post office counters.
Transfers, for example wages, are also deposits into the account.
For every deposit there is a receipt or an entry on the bank statement.

abschnitte.text: If you want to put **cash** into an account, you go to the **bank counter** or a **deposit machine**. You can also pay in at **post office counters**. The machines check that the notes are genuine and count them. The amount is then credited to the account. With large amounts, the bank may ask where the money comes from.

Many deposits today happen without cash. **Wages**, for example, are **transferred** by the employer directly into the account. Money from parents, grandparents or friends can also come by bank transfer or TWINT. For a transfer, the sender needs the account’s **IBAN**.

For every deposit there is **proof**. At the counter or machine you often get a **receipt**. In e-banking and on the **bank statement** you can see every deposit with its date and amount. That way you can check at any time whether the money has arrived. Receipts should be kept for a while.

gewusst: In the past, people in Switzerland often filled in a red or orange payment slip for deposits at the post office counter.
Since 2022, the QR bill has replaced these payment slips.

teile.einleitung: A joint account is a bank account that belongs to two or more people together. It is often used by couples, families or people sharing a flat. When setting it up, you decide who may make decisions about the money alone.
wichtigste: A joint account is held in the names of several people.
Couples, families or people sharing a flat often use it for shared expenses.
You agree whether each person may use the money alone or only all of them together.
All the account holders are responsible for the account.
An account like this needs trust and clear agreements.

abschnitte.text: Normally an account belongs to a single person. With a **joint account**, several people are **account holders**. They can be, for example, a couple, brothers and sisters or the members of a **shared flat** (WG). All of them get access to the account.

With a joint account you pay shared expenses. Typical examples are **rent**, shopping or bills for electricity and internet. Everyone pays in their share, and the bills are paid from the joint account. That way nobody has to keep sending money back and forth.

When opening the account, you agree with the bank who has **signing authority**. Often each person may withdraw money and make payments alone. But you can also decide that everyone may only act **together**. This is safer, but less practical in everyday life.

With a joint account, everyone must be able to rely on each other. It is worth agreeing clearly who pays in how much. If someone moves out or a couple separates, the account must be rearranged or closed. That is why clear rules from the start are helpful.

gewusst: As well as the joint account, many couples each have an account of their own.
Clubs also often have an account that several committee members can make decisions about.

teile.einleitung: Cash transport vehicles are special armoured vehicles that carry large amounts of cash safely from place to place. They travel between banks, shops and cash machines. Trained staff make sure everything is safe.
wichtigste: A cash transport vehicle is an armoured car for cash and valuables.
It has thick walls, reinforced windows and good locks.
The drivers are specially trained.
Cash transport vehicles take money to banks, shops and cash machines.
The journeys are planned and often monitored.

abschnitte.text: A **cash transport vehicle** looks like a van, but it is heavily protected. It has **armour**, meaning thick, reinforced walls and windows. The doors can only be opened with special locks. Inside, the money is kept in secure containers.

Shops take in a lot of **cash** every day. This money has to be taken to the bank. At the same time, **cash machines** keep needing new notes. Cash transport vehicles connect all these places and also take cash to the National Bank and back.

**Security staff** who are trained for this work are employed in cash transport vehicles. They follow fixed rules, for example when loading and unloading. The journeys are planned and often **monitored** by radio and tracking. In Switzerland, this work is done by private security companies.

Some cash boxes have an **ink-staining system**. If the box is forced open, the money is stained with ink. That way the notes are marked and worthless to thieves. Ideas like this make robberies hardly worth it.

gewusst: Because more and more people pay by card or phone, less cash is transported today than in the past.
Gold and other valuables are also transported in armoured vehicles like these.

teile.einleitung: Pocket money is money that children regularly get from their parents to manage themselves. With it they learn to handle money, to save and to make decisions. Older teenagers sometimes get a youth allowance and plan even more themselves with it.
wichtigste: Pocket money is money you regularly get from your parents to manage yourself.
With pocket money you learn to handle money and to save.
Budget experts recommend pocket money from about the age of six.
Younger children usually get it weekly, older ones monthly.
A youth allowance is a fixed monthly amount with which teenagers plan many expenses, such as clothes or free time, themselves.
With small jobs such as mowing lawns or babysitting, you can earn a bit extra.
How much pocket money you get is decided by your parents.

abschnitte.text: **Pocket money** is an amount of money that children regularly receive from their parents. The special thing is that the children may decide for themselves what to spend it on. They can use it for sweets, trading cards or books, or save it. That way they learn step by step to take on responsibility.

Experts such as **Budgetberatung Schweiz** recommend starting pocket money at about six years old. Younger children are best given it every week, because a month is very long for them. From about ten, a monthly amount makes sense. The budget advice service publishes guideline figures that rise with age, but in the end the parents decide.

If you have pocket money, you soon notice that money is not endless. If you spend everything on the first day, nothing is left for the rest of the week. You learn to set **priorities** and to save for bigger wishes. Mistakes are part of it too, because you learn a lot from a bad buy.

The **youth allowance** (Jugendlohn) is a larger, fixed amount for teenagers, often from about the age of twelve. With it they pay for things such as clothes, their phone contract, free time or school materials themselves. Parents and teenagers decide together which expenses it covers. That way teenagers practise planning a budget, as they will later as adults.

Many children and teenagers earn a bit extra, for example by **babysitting**, mowing lawns, delivering newspapers or helping neighbours. In Switzerland, young people from the age of 13 may do light work, with clear rules on working hours. By law, children may in principle manage what they earn themselves. Anyone who does a babysitting course with the Swiss Red Cross finds jobs more easily.

A small notebook or an app helps you write down income and spending. A proven method is to put part of it aside as soon as you receive it. With different money boxes you can separate the money for **saving**, spending and donating. It is important that parents pay pocket money reliably and do not cancel it as a punishment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A regular amount of money from your parents for you to manage yourself.
A larger monthly amount with which teenagers pay many expenses themselves.
A plan of how much money you have and what you spend it on.
Something that is especially important to you and comes first.

gewusst: The youth allowance model was developed and made known in Switzerland by experts in youth and budget advice.
The German word Taschengeld (pocket money) comes from the fact that people used to carry this money in their trouser pocket.
Teenagers who attend a babysitting course also learn first aid for small children.

teile.einleitung: A certificate of loss is an official document from debt enforcement proceedings. It confirms that a creditor did not receive all their money. But this does not mean the debt has disappeared.
wichtigste: A certificate of loss is issued by the debt enforcement office.
It confirms that the seizure did not cover the debt.
There are also certificates of loss after a bankruptcy.
The debt remains and can be claimed again later.
Claims from a certificate of loss only become time-barred after 20 years.
The debtor does not have to pay interest on claims from a certificate of loss.

abschnitte.titel: How a certificate of loss comes about
abschnitte.text: If someone does not pay a debt, the creditor can start **debt enforcement proceedings** against them. In the end the debt enforcement office can **seize** wages or valuables. If the seized assets are not enough to pay the debt, the office issues a **certificate of loss**. It shows how much money is still missing. After a **bankruptcy**, too, creditors receive a certificate of loss for what they have lost.

A certificate of loss does not mean that the debt has been cancelled. The creditor can **claim it again later**, for example if the debtor earns more again or inherits money. The certificate of loss counts as strong proof of the debt. It can also be sold to someone else, for example to a debt collection agency.

Claims from a certificate of loss only become **time-barred** **20 years** after it was issued. This is laid down in the Federal Act on **Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy**. So debts can stay with a person for a very long time. In return, the debtor does **not have to pay interest** on this claim. Anyone who pays a certificate of loss in full can ask for it back and apply to have it deleted from the register.

Certificates of loss appear in the **debt enforcement register**. Many landlords and companies ask for an **extract from the debt enforcement register** before they rent out a flat or sign a contract. That is why people with certificates of loss find it harder to get a flat or do not get a loan. If you have debt problems, **debt advice centres**, which exist in all regions of Switzerland, can help.

gewusst: Against the debtor’s heirs, a claim from a certificate of loss becomes time-barred just one year after the debtor’s death if it has not been made before then.
There are companies that buy up old certificates of loss cheaply and try to collect the money after all.

teile.einleitung: Paying contactless means you just hold your card briefly against the card terminal and you have paid. You can recognise it by the wave symbol on the card. For small amounts you usually do not need a PIN.
wichtigste: When paying contactless, you hold the card briefly against the terminal.
The wave symbol on the card shows that it works contactless.
For small amounts you usually do not need a PIN.
For larger amounts the terminal asks for your PIN.
After several payments without a PIN, the PIN is requested again too.
Mobile phones and watches can also pay contactless.

abschnitte.titel: Hold it up and you're done
abschnitte.text: Many cards have a small **wave symbol**. It shows that you can pay **contactless** with them. You hold the card just a few centimetres in front of the **card terminal**. A beep confirms that the payment has worked.

Inside the card there is a small **chip** with an aerial. The technology is called **NFC**, which stands for near field communication. It only works over a very short distance. That is why you have to hold the card close to the device.

For small amounts it works without a **PIN**. In Switzerland, this limit is 80 francs for many cards (as of 2024). For higher amounts you have to enter your PIN. Even after several payments without a PIN, the terminal asks for it again, so that a thief cannot spend as much as they like.

You can also pay contactless with a **mobile phone** or a **watch**. To do this, you store your card in an app. Often you have to confirm the payment with a fingerprint, face recognition or a code. This makes this way of paying fairly safe.

gewusst: Contactless payment became popular especially quickly in Switzerland when many people did not want to touch anything while paying.
If your card is lost, you should block it straight away, because small amounts can be paid without a PIN.

teile.einleitung: A donation is a gift to people, animals or projects that need help. You give money, things or time voluntarily, without asking for anything in return. In Switzerland, a great many people donate regularly to good causes.
wichtigste: Donating means giving something voluntarily without asking for anything in return.
You can donate money, things such as clothes or toys, and also time.
Donations often go to charities that help people in need, animals or the environment.
In Switzerland, the Zewo seal of approval shows that an organisation can be trusted.
After big disasters, Swiss Solidarity (Glückskette) collects donations from all over Switzerland.
Donations to charitable organisations can be deducted from your taxes.
Blood donations and organ donations are also important forms of donating.

abschnitte.text: A **donation** is a voluntary gift to someone who needs support. People who donate do not expect anything in return. You can give money, but also clothes, books, food or toys. People who give their time and help out are donating something too; this is called **volunteering**.

Donations help, for example, people after earthquakes, floods or wars. Many people also support projects for children, sick people, animals or nature. Organisations that collect donations and use them to help are called **charities** or aid organisations. Well-known examples from Switzerland are the Swiss Red Cross, Caritas or the Winterhilfe.

It is important that the money really arrives where it is needed. In Switzerland, the Zewo foundation awards a **seal of approval** to organisations that handle donations carefully. Be careful with collectors at your front door or appeals on the internet that you do not know. With reputable charities, you can read what the money is used for.

**Swiss Solidarity** (Glückskette) is the fundraising organisation of the Swiss radio and television stations and was founded in 1946. After big disasters it organises national fundraising days. Then many people phone in or transfer money, and millions of francs are often collected. The money is distributed to partner charities that help on the spot.

Altogether, people in Switzerland donate about two billion francs every year. Many donate regularly, for example once a year before Christmas. Donations to charitable organisations can be deducted in the **tax return**. In this way the state also indirectly supports donating.

Children can donate too, for example part of their pocket money or toys they no longer need. Some school classes do a sponsored run, in which money is donated for every lap. A separate money box for donations helps you collect something regularly. From the age of 18 you can also **give blood** and save lives.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation that helps people, animals or nature in need.
A sign that shows that something has been checked and can be trusted.
For the good of the community and not for one’s own profit.
Work that you do for others without pay.

gewusst: The Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863; one of its founders was Henry Dunant from Geneva.
For some disasters, Swiss Solidarity has collected more than 100 million francs in donations.
Giving blood only takes about ten minutes, but it can help several people.

teile.einleitung: Counterfeit money is copied money that looks like the real thing but has no value. Anyone who makes it or deliberately passes it on commits a criminal offence. That is why real banknotes have many security features.
wichtigste: Counterfeit money is copied money and not a real means of payment.
Counterfeiting money is forbidden in Switzerland and is severely punished.
Anyone who knowingly passes on counterfeit money also commits a criminal offence.
Real banknotes have security features that you can feel, see and tilt.
If you receive counterfeit money, you get no replacement for it.
Take suspicious notes to the police or a bank.

abschnitte.text: **Counterfeit money** means banknotes or coins that do not come from the official body. In Switzerland, the **Swiss National Bank** issues the banknotes, and the coins are minted by **Swissmint** in Bern. Anything else that looks like francs is a copy. Such money is worthless, even if it looks real.

Real notes are printed on special material and have **security features**. Some areas feel rough when you run your finger over them. If you tilt the note, colours and pictures change. If you hold it up to the light, you see things that an ordinary printer cannot copy. It is best to compare a suspicious note with a real one.

**Counterfeiting money** is a crime. Anyone who makes or alters money or deliberately puts counterfeit money into circulation is punished. Anyone who receives a fake note and knowingly passes it on to get rid of it also commits an offence. In this way the law protects trust in money.

abschnitte.titel: What to do if you are suspicious
abschnitte.text: If you think you have a fake note, do not pass it on. Take it to the **police** or to a bank. There it is checked. If it is fake, it is taken away, and you get no money for it. That is why it is worth taking a quick look when paying.

gewusst: Counterfeiters used to be called “Falschmünzer” (false coiners) in German, because it was mainly coins that were copied.
Many shop tills and cash machines check banknotes automatically before accepting them.

teile.einleitung: Many games on the internet and on phones can be downloaded for free. But in the game there are often buttons like “Buy now”. Behind them is real money, so you ask your parents first.
wichtigste: Many free games make money from purchases in the game.
Purchases like these are called **in-app purchases**.
Behind game currencies such as coins or diamonds there is real money.
Before any purchase, you ask your parents first.
On a phone or tablet, purchases can be locked with a password.

abschnitte.text: Games that cost nothing are called **free-to-play**. The companies still earn money. In the game you can buy extras, for example new characters, clothes for your character or more lives. These **in-app purchases** cost real money, even if they only cost a few francs.

Many games have their own **game currency**, for example coins, gems or jewels. You buy it with real money. Because you no longer see francs, you hardly notice how much you are spending. Some games tempt you with offers that only last a short time. That way you are meant to buy quickly and without thinking.

If a button like “Buy now” appears, always ask your **parents** first. They can set up a **purchase lock** on the phone or tablet, so that purchases only work with a password. Adverts in the game can also tempt you to buy things. If you know this, you can play in peace without spending money.

gewusst: Some games have surprise boxes called **loot boxes**. You do not know beforehand what is inside, which is why they are compared with gambling.

teile.einleitung: The investment horizon is the time during which you probably will not need money you have invested. It helps with the question of where it is best to keep or invest money.
wichtigste: The investment horizon says how long money will probably not be needed.
Roughly speaking, there are short, medium and long investment horizons.
Money for the next few months is better kept in an account.
Shares go up and down a lot, so they suit a long investment horizon better.
The longer you can wait, the better you can sit out bad years.
The investment horizon, the goal and the willingness to take risks belong together.

abschnitte.text: The **investment horizon** is the planned length of an investment. It begins when you invest money and ends when you need it again. Anyone who is saving for a bike in a year’s time, for example, has a short investment horizon. Anyone saving for old age often has a horizon of many decades.

**Short term** usually means a period of up to about two years. **Medium term** is roughly two to five years, and **long term** is anything beyond that. The limits are not fixed exactly; banks and experts draw them slightly differently. Above all, it is important to estimate honestly when you will need the money.

The value of **shares** can rise sharply or fall sharply in a single year. These ups and downs are called **fluctuations**. Over many years, good and bad years often balance each other out. But if you need the money soon, you may have to sell exactly when prices are low. That is why the rule is: do not put short-term money into shares.

abschnitte.titel: The right place for the money
abschnitte.text: For a short time, a **savings account** or a payment account is suitable, because the amount there does not go up and down. For a long time, many people invest part of their money in shares or in **funds**. In Switzerland, **pillar 3a** is an example of very long-term saving, because the money is usually tied up until shortly before retirement. People often divide up their money depending on what it is meant for.

gewusst: For the same money, the investment horizon can change, for example when a goal gets closer.
Before giving investment advice, many banks ask exactly about the investment horizon.

teile.einleitung: A comparison website is a site where you can see the prices and services of many providers side by side. That way you can quickly find the cheapest phone contract, the right health insurance or the cheapest television. But you should know how such websites earn money.
wichtigste: Comparison websites are sites that compare the offers of many providers.
People use them to compare prices and services before buying something or signing a contract.
They compare, for example, electronics, insurance, phone contracts, hotels or flights.
Well-known Swiss comparison websites include Comparis, Toppreise and Moneyland.
Many websites earn money from commissions when you sign up for something through them.
Not every website shows all the providers on the market.
It is worth using more than one website.

abschnitte.text: A **comparison website** collects information about products and offers and presents it clearly. You enter, for example, which phone you are looking for, and you can see straight away which shop offers it most cheaply. Often you can sort the list by price, rating or delivery time. That way you save time and often money too.

There are comparison websites for almost everything: electronics, insurance, health insurance funds, phone contracts, electricity, hotels and flights. In Switzerland, **Comparis** is one of the best-known websites; it was founded in 1996. For electronics many people use **Toppreise**, and for bank accounts and credit cards Moneyland. In autumn especially, many people compare health insurance premiums for the following year.

Most comparison websites are free for their users. They earn money from **advertising** and from commissions. A **commission** is an amount that a provider pays when someone signs a contract through the website. That is why some offers are shown higher up even though they are not the best.

Not every website lists all providers; some are simply missing. That is why you should compare several websites or check directly with the provider. The **small print**, the length of the contract and hidden fees are also important. A cheap phone contract, for example, can become much more expensive after a year.

Before you compare, first think about what you really need. Look out for labels like “sponsored” or “ad”, because these are paid entries. Also read reviews from other customers, but with a critical eye. With contracts such as insurance or subscriptions, young people should always decide together with their parents.

begriffe.erklaerung: A website that shows the offers of different providers side by side.
Money that an intermediary receives for a contract that has been signed.
Important contract conditions that are often written in small letters.
A company that sells something or offers a service.

gewusst: If you want to change your basic health insurance, you usually have to cancel by the end of November, which is why comparison websites are particularly in demand in autumn.
Some websites also show how the price of a product has changed over months.
On hotel booking websites, the same room can cost different amounts depending on the website.

teile.einleitung: Debts do not last for ever. After a certain time, a claim can become time-barred. Then the debtor can refuse to pay, and the creditor can no longer enforce the debt through the courts.
wichtigste: Limitation means that after a certain period, a claim can no longer be enforced.
The rules are set out in the Code of Obligations.
The general limitation period is 10 years.
Rents and other periodic payments become time-barred after 5 years.
The period begins when the claim falls due.
Debt enforcement proceedings or an acknowledgement of debt interrupt the limitation period.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who owes money must in principle pay it. But after a certain time a claim can become **time-barred**. Then the **debtor** may rely on this and no longer has to pay. The debt does not disappear completely, but the **creditor** can no longer enforce it in court. This is meant to create clarity, so that old matters are closed at some point.

abschnitte.titel: Ten years as the basic rule
abschnitte.text: The rules are set out in the **Code of Obligations**. The **general limitation period** is **10 years**. It applies to many claims, for example from a loan. The period begins as soon as the claim is **due**, meaning it ought to be paid.

A shorter period of **5 years** applies to some claims. These include **periodic payments** such as **rents** or interest on capital. Claims for craft work, for medical treatment or from an employment relationship also become time-barred after 5 years. Other periods apply again to compensation for damage and other cases.

The creditor can **interrupt** the limitation period. This happens, for example, through **debt enforcement proceedings** or a court action. It is also interrupted if the debtor **acknowledges** the debt, for example with a part payment. Then the period starts again from the beginning. Important: a court does not check limitation on its own initiative. The debtor must rely on it.

gewusst: If someone voluntarily pays a debt that is already time-barred, they cannot ask for the money back.
Claims from a certificate of loss only become time-barred after 20 years.

teile.einleitung: When you are out and about, you keep coins, notes and cards in a wallet or purse. That way you always have your money with you and nothing gets lost. The usual Swiss German word for it, “Portemonnaie”, comes from French.
wichtigste: You keep coins, notes and cards in a wallet.
The German word “Portemonnaie” comes from French and means roughly “money carrier”.
Other German words for it are “Geldbeutel” or “Börse”.
A wallet often has compartments for notes, coins and cards.
When you are out, you should protect your wallet well from thieves.

abschnitte.text: A **wallet** keeps your **money** and your **cards** together. It has room for **coins**, **notes** and, for example, your bank card. Often an ID card or a public transport pass goes in it too. That way nothing gets lost when you are out. In Switzerland people also say **Geldbeutel** or write **Portmonee**.

The word **Portemonnaie** comes from **French**. “Porter” means **to carry**, and “monnaie” means **coins** or small change. So a Portemonnaie is something you carry money in. In Switzerland the word is very common in everyday life. In parts of Germany people more often say **Geldbörse**.

A wallet usually has several **compartments**. A long compartment is for **notes**. A compartment with a zip or a press stud is for **coins**. Small slots hold the **cards**. There are wallets made of leather, fabric or plastic, large or very small.

When you are out, you should **protect** your wallet well. On crowded trains or at railway stations there are sometimes **pickpockets**. It is safest in a closed bag at the front of your body. You should only take as much cash as you need. Your **PIN** never belongs in your wallet.

gewusst: Today many people pay with their mobile phone. That is why people also talk about a “digital wallet”.
If your wallet is stolen, you must have your cards blocked straight away.

teile.einleitung: **Pocket money** is money that children regularly get from their parents. You can plan it yourself, spend it or save it. This is how you learn, step by step, to handle money.
wichtigste: Many children get pocket money every week or every month.
You are allowed to decide for yourself what to do with your pocket money.
With pocket money you learn to do sums, plan and save.
Younger children often get it weekly, older ones more often monthly.
The parents decide how much pocket money a child gets.
Whatever you do not spend can go into your money box.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss German word “Sackgeld” comes from **Hosensack**, the trouser pocket. Pocket money is money for your own pocket. It is not a wage for helping at home but an amount to practise with. Many families agree on what the pocket money is meant for, for example sweets, comics or small toys. You can then decide yourself what you buy with it.

Younger children often get their pocket money **every week**. A week is a length of time that is easy to keep track of. Older children and teenagers often get it **every month**. Then you have to plan further ahead so that the money lasts until the end of the month. Advice services such as Budgetberatung Schweiz give parents recommendations on how much is right at which age.

With pocket money you practise **arithmetic** without even noticing. If you get 4 francs and spend 1 franc, you have 3 francs left. You soon notice: once it is gone, it is gone. Some children divide their money into parts, one for spending and one for saving. That way there is always something left.

One week's pocket money is usually not enough for something expensive. But if you regularly put something aside, your savings grow in your **money box**. At some point there is enough for the bigger wish. This takes patience, but it makes you proud. When the money box is full, you can take the money to the bank with your parents.

gewusst: The word “Sackgeld” is typical of Switzerland; in Germany people usually say “Taschengeld”.
Under Swiss law, children may freely decide what to do with their own pocket money.

teile.einleitung: If you pay with a note or coin that is worth more than the price, you get money back. This money is called **change**. With a little arithmetic you can check for yourself whether it is right.
wichtigste: Change is the difference between the amount paid and the price.
You work it out like this: amount paid minus price.
Example: you pay 5 francs for an ice cream costing 3 francs and get 2 francs back.
You should always count your change, ideally right at the till.
In Switzerland, cash amounts are rounded to 5 centimes.

abschnitte.text: To work out change, you do a **subtraction**. You take the amount you handed over and subtract the price. If you pay with 10 francs for an exercise book costing 4 francs, you get 6 francs back. It works the same way with centimes: 2 francs minus 1 franc 50 is 50 centimes. If you are good at mental arithmetic, you notice straight away when something is wrong.

abschnitte.titel: Counting up like at the till
abschnitte.text: Many shop assistants count the change **up**. They start at the price and keep counting until they reach the amount paid. With a price of 3 francs and a 5-franc coin, they count: 4 francs, 5 francs. As they do so, they put two 1-franc coins into your hand. That way you do not have to subtract, only add. You can practise this method yourself too.

In Switzerland there are coins of **5, 10 and 20 centimes** and of half a franc, 1, 2 and 5 francs. Notes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. There are no longer any coins smaller than 5 centimes. That is why cash payments are rounded to 5 centimes. If something costs 2 francs 98, you usually pay 3 francs in cash.

Anyone can make a mistake when giving change. That is why it is wise to count your change **straight away**, while you are still standing at the till. Later, a mistake can hardly be proved. If something is missing, say so politely. And if you have been given too much, it is fair to say that too.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the 1-centime coin was taken out of circulation in 2007.
Switzerland has a 1000-franc note, one of the most valuable banknotes in the world.

teile.einleitung: A right of withdrawal lets you cancel a contract within a short time. In Switzerland it only exists for certain contracts. For consumer loans and leasing, the period is 14 days.
wichtigste: Withdrawing means cancelling a contract that has been made.
For consumer loans and leasing, there is a right of withdrawal of 14 days.
This is laid down in the Consumer Credit Act.
The withdrawal must be made in writing or in a way that can be proved.
For doorstep sales, too, there is a right of withdrawal of 14 days.
For normal online purchases there is no legal right of withdrawal in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: What is a right of withdrawal?
abschnitte.text: Normally a contract is valid as soon as both sides have agreed. But with a **right of withdrawal** you can still **cancel** it within a certain period without giving a reason. This is meant to protect you from **hasty decisions**. In Switzerland, the right of withdrawal only exists for certain kinds of contract.

The **Consumer Credit Act** gives a right of withdrawal of **14 days** for a **consumer loan** and for **leasing**. That gives you two weeks to think the contract over carefully once more. The withdrawal must be made **in writing** or in another way that can be **proved**. It is important to send it off in time.

For **doorstep sales** too, there is a right of withdrawal of **14 days**. This applies if you are talked into a contract at your front door, at work, in the street or on a promotional trip. It also applies to certain contracts made by **phone**. These rules are in the **Code of Obligations**.

Unlike in the European Union, Switzerland has **no legal right of withdrawal** for normal **online purchases**. Even so, many shops voluntarily allow **returns**. The rules are in their terms and conditions. That is why it is worth reading before you buy whether and for how long you may send something back.

gewusst: The period for withdrawing from a consumer loan only begins once you have received a copy of the contract.
The right of withdrawal does not apply to doorstep sales under 100 francs.

teile.einleitung: When prices rise in general, people in Switzerland often call it “Teuerung”. Another word for it is inflation. You can then buy less with the same money.
wichtigste: Teuerung means: prices rise in general.
Another word for it is inflation.
With inflation, money loses purchasing power.
The Federal Statistical Office measures inflation with the Swiss Consumer Price Index.
The Swiss National Bank makes sure prices are stable.
When prices fall in general, this is called deflation.

abschnitte.text: People speak of **Teuerung** when not just one thing but many goods and services become more expensive. The technical term for it is **inflation**. If only one thing becomes more expensive, for example strawberries in winter, that is not yet inflation. It is about prices in general.

The **Federal Statistical Office** measures inflation every month. To do this it uses a **basket of goods**: a selection of things that households typically buy, such as food, rent, clothes or tickets. From this comes the **Swiss Consumer Price Index**, CPI for short (LIK in German). It shows how much prices have risen compared with the previous year.

When prices rise, you can buy less with the same money. The money loses **purchasing power**. Anyone who has money in an account with little interest slowly loses value this way. That is why **inflation compensation** is often discussed for wages and pensions. It is meant to let people buy just as much despite rising prices.

abschnitte.titel: The role of the National Bank
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** has the task of ensuring **price stability**. By this it means inflation of less than 2 per cent a year. One important tool is the **policy rate**. If inflation is high, it can raise interest rates so that less money is spent. Falling prices, known as **deflation**, are also considered harmful to the economy.

gewusst: The Federal Statistical Office’s basket of goods contains hundreds of different goods and services.
In some countries, prices have risen so much that money became almost worthless within a short time.

teile.einleitung: A money counting machine counts banknotes much faster than a person. Banks, shops and cash transport companies use them to count large amounts of cash accurately. Many machines also detect fake notes.
wichtigste: A money counting machine counts banknotes automatically.
It can manage hundreds of notes per minute.
Many machines check at the same time whether a note is genuine.
There are also machines that count and sort coins.
Banks, shops and cash transport companies use such machines.

abschnitte.text: You put a stack of **banknotes** into the machine. Rollers pull the notes through the machine one by one. A **sensor** counts every note that goes past. At the end, the display shows the number or even the total amount.

Many money counting machines also check whether the notes are **genuine**. They work, for example, with **UV light**, which makes certain features visible. Others measure size, thickness or magnetic ink. If something is not right, the machine stops and reports the suspicious note.

There are separate **coin counting machines** for coins. They sort the coins by size and weight. That way Fünfliber, francs and centimes each end up in their own compartment. Some banks have machines like these into which customers can pour their small change.

In a bank, a lot of **cash** is counted every day. Large shops and companies that transport money also need exact figures. By hand this would take a long time, and it would be easy to miscount. The machine works quickly and reliably.

gewusst: Some machines can even recognise which banknote has which value and sort mixed stacks.
Even today, bank staff often recount important amounts by hand as well.
